paragraphs: This paper models self-organization in recurrent networks by allowing both neuron states and their interactions to change. The neurons take binary values, while their symmetric connections have continuous values and evolve in response to neuronal activity. The central assumption is a separation of timescales: neuronal changes happen much faster than connection changes.

Because of that separation, the neurons can be treated as effectively at Boltzmann equilibrium on the timescale of the slower interactions. The authors derive an effective statistical-mechanical description whose partition function involves an average over replicated versions of the system. This resembles the replica method used for spin glasses, but the replication parameter has a different status.

Here, the number of replicas represents a ratio of two temperatures and can vary over real values. It therefore has a physical interpretation within the model rather than serving only as a mathematical device. The abstract reports phase consequences as this ratio and external stimuli change, and states that the framework can extend to other models.
summary.tldr: Separating fast neuronal activity from slow connection changes yields a statistical-mechanical model with a physically meaningful replica parameter.

title: Coupled Dynamics of Fast Neurons and Slow Interactions

abstract: Recent work has exploited boundedness of data in the unsupervised learning of new types of generative model. For nonnegative data it was recently shown that the maximum-entropy generative model is a Non(cid:173) negative Boltzmann Distribution not a Gaussian distribution, when the model is constrained to match the first and second order statistics of the data. Learning for practical sized problems is made difficult by the need to compute expectations under the model distribution. The computa(cid:173) tional cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods and low fidelity of naive mean field techniques has led to increasing interest in advanced mean field theories and variational methods. Here I present a second(cid:173) order mean-field approximation for the Nonnegative Boltzmann Machine model, obtained using a "high-temperature" expansion. The theory is tested on learning a bimodal 2-dimensional model, a high-dimensional translationally invariant distribution, and a generative model for hand(cid:173) written digits.

paragraphs: The paper studies generative modeling for data whose values cannot be negative. Under constraints matching first- and second-order statistics, the relevant maximum-entropy model is a Nonnegative Boltzmann Distribution. The nonnegativity restriction therefore affects the appropriate model family, making the support of the observations a substantive part of the statistical formulation.

Learning this model requires computing expectations under its distribution, which becomes difficult at practical problem sizes. The abstract identifies a tradeoff: Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are computationally costly, while naive mean-field approximations have low fidelity. The paper addresses this calculation with a second-order mean-field approximation derived using a high-temperature expansion.

The approximation is tested on three settings: a two-dimensional distribution with two modes, a high-dimensional translationally invariant distribution, and a generative model of handwritten digits. These tests examine the theory across different distributional structures and scales. The central contribution is a more developed approximation for the expectations needed in learning, with the stated experiments providing applications rather than a quantified claim of superiority.
summary.tldr: A high-temperature expansion provides a second-order mean-field approximation for learning Nonnegative Boltzmann models.

title: High-temperature Expansions for Learning Models of Nonnegative Data

abstract: Modern classification applications necessitate supplementing the few available labeled examples with unlabeled examples to improve classi(cid:173) fication performance. We present a new tractable algorithm for exploit(cid:173) ing unlabeled examples in discriminative classification. This is achieved essentially by expanding the input vectors into longer feature vectors via both labeled and unlabeled examples. The resulting classification method can be interpreted as a discriminative kernel density estimate and is read(cid:173) ily trained via the EM algorithm, which in this case is both discriminative and achieves the optimal solution. We provide, in addition, a purely dis(cid:173) criminative formulation of the estimation problem by appealing to the maximum entropy framework. We demonstrate that the proposed ap(cid:173) proach requires very few labeled examples for high classification accu(cid:173) racy.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification settings with few labeled examples and additional unlabeled data. It proposes a tractable way for both kinds of examples to contribute to the classifier. The central operation expands each input into a longer feature vector using information from labeled and unlabeled examples.

This feature expansion gives unlabeled data a role in the representation used for discriminative classification. The resulting method can be interpreted as a discriminative kernel density estimate. The authors train it using an expectation-maximization algorithm that, for this formulation, is discriminative and reaches the optimal solution. That optimality claim concerns the proposed estimation problem.

The paper also develops a purely discriminative formulation through the maximum-entropy framework. These two perspectives describe how the expanded representation supports estimation and training. The authors demonstrate high classification accuracy with very few labeled examples. The contribution is thus a specific mechanism for exploiting unlabeled examples, paired with tractable optimization and evidence that the resulting classifier can work with limited labeled data.
summary.tldr: Expanding features with labeled and unlabeled examples yields a tractable discriminative classifier demonstrated to achieve high accuracy with few labels.

title: Kernel Expansions with Unlabeled Examples

abstract: Probabilistic mixture models are used for a broad range of data anal- ysis tasks such as clustering, classiﬁcation, predictive modeling, etc. Due to their inherent probabilistic nature, mixture models can easily be combined with other probabilistic or non-probabilistic techniques thus forming more complex data analysis systems. In the case of online data (where there is a stream of data available) models can be constantly up- dated to reﬂect the most current distribution of the incoming data. How- ever, in many business applications the models themselves represent a parsimonious summary of the data and therefore it is not desirable to change models frequently, much less with every new data point. In such a framework it becomes crucial to track the applicability of the mixture model and detect the point in time when the model fails to adequately represent the data. paragraphs: Probabilistic mixture models can summarize data for clustering, classification, and prediction. With a continuing stream of observations, such a model could be updated repeatedly to follow the incoming distribution. The paper focuses on business settings where the model itself is a compact summary and frequent changes to that summary are undesirable.

In this setting, the central task is to monitor whether the existing model remains applicable. The authors formulate change detection as identifying when a mixture model no longer adequately represents incoming data. This places attention on the continued validity of a retained model, providing a basis for deciding when the observed population has changed enough to matter.

The paper proposes a principled solution and presents empirical results on synthetic and real-life datasets. The supplied formulation starts with independent, identically distributed observations. Its practical contribution is to make model applicability an explicit monitoring problem, connecting distribution-change detection with the need to preserve useful, stable summaries of data as new observations arrive.
summary.tldr: The paper monitors when a retained mixture model stops adequately representing incoming data, supporting distribution-change detection without continual model updates.

title: Model Based Population Tracking and Automatic Detection of Distribution Changes

abstract: We show that Queyranne's algorithm for minimizing symmetric submodular functions can be used for clustering with a variety of different objective functions. Two specific criteria that we consider in this paper are the single linkage and the minimum description length criteria. The first criterion tries to maximize the minimum distance between elements of different clusters, and is inherently "discriminative". It is known that optimal clusterings into k clusters for any given k in polynomial time for this criterion can be computed. The second criterion seeks to minimize the description length of the clusters given a probabilistic generative model. We show that the optimal partitioning into 2 clusters, and approximate partitioning (guaranteed to be within a factor of 2 of the the optimal) for more clusters can be computed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that a tractable algorithm for finding the optimal clustering with respect to the MDL criterion for 2 clusters has been given. Besides the optimality result for the MDL criterion, the chief contribution of this paper is to show that the same algorithm can be used to optimize a broad class of criteria, and hence can be used for many application specific criterion for which efficient algorithm are not known.

paragraphs: Q-Clustering applies Queyranne's algorithm for minimizing symmetric submodular functions to clustering. The central contribution is that one algorithm can optimize a broad class of clustering criteria. This matters because different applications may require different definitions of a good partition, including criteria without previously known efficient algorithms.

The paper examines single linkage and minimum description length. Single linkage seeks to maximize the smallest distance between members of different clusters, emphasizing separation. Minimum description length instead seeks a concise description of the clusters under a probabilistic generative model. These objectives illustrate distinct ways to judge a clustering.

For the minimum description length criterion studied, the authors obtain an optimal two-cluster partition and a factor-of-two approximation guarantee for more clusters. They identify the tractable optimal two-cluster result as a first to their knowledge. Optimal polynomial-time clustering for any specified number of clusters was already known for the single-linkage criterion. The paper's significance combines the MDL result with a reusable optimization approach, while distinguishing exact solutions from approximation guarantees.
summary.tldr: Queyranne's algorithm supports multiple clustering objectives, including exact two-cluster MDL optimization and a factor-of-two approximation for more clusters.

title: Q-Clustering

abstract: Blind source separation, i.e. the extraction of unknown sources from a set of given signals, is relevant for many applications. A special case of this problem is dimension reduction, where the goal is to approximate a given set of signals by superpositions of a minimal number of sources. Since in this case the signals outnumber the sources the problem is over-determined. Most popular approaches for addressing this problem are based on purely linear mixing models. However, many applications like the modeling of acoustic signals, EMG signals, or movement trajectories, require temporal shift-invariance of the extracted components. This case has only rarely been treated in the computational literature, and specifically for the case of dimension reduction almost no algorithms have been proposed. We present a new algorithm for the solution of this problem, which is based on a timefrequency transformation (Wigner-Ville distribution) of the generative model. We show that this algorithm outperforms classical source separation algorithms for linear mixtures, and also a related method for mixtures with delays. In addition, applying the new algorithm to trajectories of human gaits, we demonstrate that it is suitable for the extraction of spatio-temporal components that are easier to interpret than components extracted with other classical algorithms.

paragraphs: Blind source separation seeks unknown underlying sources from observed signals. This paper focuses on a dimension-reduction setting in which there are more observed signals than sources. The aim is to explain those signals using a small collection of components, while allowing a component to appear at different temporal offsets.

Allowing delays matters for applications such as acoustic signals, muscle measurements, and movement trajectories. Purely linear mixing methods do not provide the required temporal shift invariance. The authors introduce an algorithm based on transforming the generative model into a time-frequency representation using the Wigner-Ville distribution, addressing delayed mixtures specifically in this over-determined setting.

The reported comparisons favor the new algorithm over classical methods for linear mixtures and a related method that handles delays. Applied to human gait trajectories, it also extracts spatial and temporal components that are easier to interpret than those obtained with other classical algorithms. These results connect the method's treatment of timing differences with both separation performance and the interpretability of movement components.
summary.tldr: A time-frequency approach separates delayed signal mixtures and extracts interpretable components from human gait trajectories.

title: Blind source separation for over-determined delayed mixtures

abstract: Geometrically based methods for various tasks of machine learning have attracted considerable attention over the last few years. In this paper we show convergence of eigenvectors of the point cloud Laplacian to the eigen- functions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on the underlying manifold, thus establishing the ﬁrst convergence results for a spectral dimensionality re- duction algorithm in the manifold setting.
originalAbstract: Geometrically based methods for various tasks of machine learning have attracted considerable attention over the last few years. In this paper we show convergence of eigenvectors of the point cloud Laplacian to the eigen- functions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on the underlying manifold, thus establishing the ﬁrst convergence results for a spectral dimensionality re- duction algorithm in the manifold setting.

paragraphs: Geometric dimensionality reduction tries to describe data through the shape of an underlying manifold. In practice, an algorithm receives a cloud of sampled points rather than the continuous manifold itself. This paper addresses the theoretical connection between a spectral construction on those points and the geometry it is intended to represent.

The authors prove convergence of the point cloud Laplacian's eigenvectors to eigenfunctions of the manifold's Laplace-Beltrami operator. These are the discrete and continuous objects on the two sides of the result. In plain language, the theorem connects patterns computed from sampled data with corresponding patterns defined on the underlying geometric surface.

That connection gives theoretical support to Laplacian Eigenmaps as a spectral dimensionality reduction method in the manifold setting. The abstract identifies the result as the first convergence result for such an algorithm in that setting. Its contribution is a mathematical foundation: the quantities used by the discrete method converge to meaningful continuous counterparts, linking a data-based representation to the geometry of the space being sampled.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that point cloud Laplacian eigenvectors converge to their continuous manifold counterparts, establishing a foundation for Laplacian Eigenmaps.

title: Convergence of Laplacian Eigenmaps

abstract: Reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) has recently emerged as a candidate for a learning rule that could explain how local learning rules at single synapses support behaviorally relevant adaptive changes in com- plex networks of spiking neurons. However the potential and limitations of this learning rule could so far only be tested through computer simulations. This ar- ticle provides tools for an analytic treatment of reward-modulated STDP, which allow us to predict under which conditions reward-modulated STDP will be able to achieve a desired learning effect. In particular, we can produce in this way a theoretical explanation and a computer model for a fundamental experimental ﬁnding on biofeedback in monkeys (reported in [1]).

paragraphs: Reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity combines a local synaptic learning rule with a reward signal. It is a candidate mechanism for explaining how changes at individual synapses can produce behaviorally useful adaptation in networks of spiking neurons. This paper addresses the need to understand when such learning will produce an intended effect.

Earlier investigations of the rule's potential and limits relied on computer simulations. The authors provide tools for an analytic treatment, allowing conditions for a desired learning effect to be predicted theoretically. This changes the kind of question that can be answered: the analysis can identify when learning should work, rather than only observing outcomes in simulated cases.

As a concrete application, the framework yields a theoretical explanation and a computer model of an experimental finding involving biofeedback in monkeys. The contribution links a candidate synaptic mechanism to a behavioral learning result through mathematical analysis and modeling. Its claim is conditional: the tools characterize circumstances supporting a desired effect, rather than guaranteeing successful adaptation in every spiking network.
summary.tldr: Analytic tools identify conditions for successful reward-modulated STDP and support a theoretical model of a monkey biofeedback finding.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Learning with Reward-Modulated Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity

abstract: We consider multi-label prediction problems with large output spaces under the assumption of output sparsity – that the target (label) vectors have small support. We develop a general theory for a variant of the popular error correcting output code scheme, using ideas from compressed sensing for exploiting this sparsity. The method can be regarded as a simple reduction from multi-label regression problems to binary regression problems. We show that the number of subprob- lems need only be logarithmic in the total number of possible labels, making this approach radically more efﬁcient than others. We also state and prove robustness guarantees for this method in the form of regret transform bounds (in general), and also provide a more detailed analysis for the linear prediction setting.

paragraphs: Multi-label prediction becomes expensive when each example could receive labels from a very large collection. This paper assumes that each target vector has only a small number of active entries. That output-sparsity assumption creates an opportunity to represent the prediction problem compactly, even though the full set of possible labels is large.

The authors develop a variant of error-correcting output codes using ideas from compressed sensing. They describe it as a reduction from multi-label regression to binary regression subproblems. Under the sparse-output setting, the number of subproblems needs to grow only logarithmically with the total number of possible labels. This is the central source of the method's efficiency.

The paper also provides robustness guarantees through regret transform bounds, relating performance on the reduced problems to performance on the original task. A more detailed analysis covers linear prediction. The contribution is therefore both computational and theoretical: it reduces the number of prediction problems while establishing how errors in the reduction affect the final result.
summary.tldr: Assuming sparse label vectors, a compressed-sensing reduction needs only logarithmically many prediction subproblems and comes with robustness guarantees.

title: Multi-Label Prediction via Compressed Sensing

abstract: A kernel embedding of probability distributions into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) has recently been proposed, which allows the comparison of two probability measures P and Q based on the distance between their respective embeddings: for a sufficiently rich RKHS, this distance is zero if and only if P and Q coincide. In using this distance as a statistic for a test of whether two samples are from different distributions, a major difficulty arises in computing the significance threshold, since the empirical statistic has as its null distribution (where P=Q) an infinite weighted sum of $\chi^2$ random variables. The main result of the present work is a novel, consistent estimate of this null distribution, computed from the eigenspectrum of the Gram matrix on the aggregate sample from P and Q. This estimate may be computed faster than a previous consistent estimate based on the bootstrap. Another prior approach was to compute the null distribution based on fitting a parametric family with the low order moments of the test statistic: unlike the present work, this heuristic has no guarantee of being accurate or consistent. We verify the performance of our null distribution estimate on both an artificial example and on high dimensional multivariate data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to decide whether two collections of observations come from different probability distributions. Kernel methods represent each distribution in a mathematical feature space and compare the resulting representations. When that space is sufficiently rich, a zero distance means the distributions are identical. Turning this distance into a statistical test, however, requires knowing how much apparent difference can arise when the distributions actually match.

The main contribution is a consistent estimate of this null distribution, which determines the test's significance threshold. The method uses the eigenvalues of a Gram matrix built from the combined samples. This tackles the difficult distribution of the test statistic through information calculated directly from the observed data.

The estimate can be computed faster than an earlier consistent bootstrap approach. It also has a consistency guarantee that a previous moment-fitting heuristic lacks. Tests on artificial and high-dimensional multivariate data assess its performance. The advance is therefore in calibrating the kernel test reliably and potentially more quickly.
summary.tldr: The paper estimates a kernel two-sample test's null distribution consistently from matrix eigenvalues, potentially faster than bootstrap calibration.

title: A Fast, Consistent Kernel Two-Sample Test

abstract: Image representation based on image bases provides a framework for understanding neural representation of visual perception. A recent fMRI study has shown that arbitrary contrast-defined visual images can be reconstructed from fMRI activity patterns using a combination of multi-scale local image bases. In the reconstruction model, the mapping from an fMRI activity pattern to the contrasts of the image bases was learned from measured fMRI responses to visual images. But the shapes of the images bases were fixed, and thus may not be optimal for reconstruction. Here, we propose a method to build a reconstruction model in which image bases are automatically extracted from the measured data. We constructed a probabilistic model that relates the fMRI activity space to the visual image space via a set of latent variables. The mapping from the latent variables to the visual image space can be regarded as a set of image bases. We found that spatially localized, multi-scale image bases were estimated near the fovea, and that the model using the estimated image bases was able to accurately reconstruct novel visual images. The proposed method provides a means to discover a novel functional mapping between stimuli and brain activity patterns.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a viewed image from brain activity requires a representation of the image and a mapping from neural measurements to that representation. Earlier work used fixed image bases at several scales and learned how fMRI responses predicted their contrasts. This paper asks whether the image bases themselves can instead be learned from the measured data.

The authors build a probabilistic model connecting fMRI activity and visual images through latent variables. The mapping from those hidden variables into image space acts as the set of image bases. Learning this mapping allows the reconstruction model to discover its visual building blocks together with their relationship to brain activity, rather than fixing their shapes in advance.

The estimated bases near the fovea were spatially localized and appeared at multiple scales. Using these learned bases, the model accurately reconstructed novel visual images. These findings show that a useful reconstruction representation can emerge from the measured brain–image relationship. The method also provides a way to investigate functional mappings between visual stimuli and neural activity through the image structures it learns.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model learns image bases from fMRI and visual data, discovering localized multiscale structure and accurately reconstructing novel images.

title: Estimating image bases for visual image reconstruction from human brain activity

abstract: Recent experimental work has suggested that the neural firing rate can be interpreted as a fractional derivative, at least when signal variation induces neural adaptation. Here, we show that the actual neural spike-train itself can be considered as the fractional derivative, provided that the neural signal is approximated by a sum of power-law kernels. A simple standard thresholding spiking neuron suffices to carry out such an approximation, given a suitable refractory response. Empirically, we find that the online approximation of signals with a sum of power-law kernels is beneficial for encoding signals with slowly varying components, like long-memory self-similar signals. For such signals, the online power-law kernel approximation typically required less than half the number of spikes for similar SNR as compared to sums of similar but exponentially decaying kernels. As power-law kernels can be accurately approximated using sums or cascades of weighted exponentials, we demonstrate that the corresponding decoding of spike-trains by a receiving neuron allows for natural and transparent temporal signal filtering by tuning the weights of the decoding kernel.

For such signals, the online power-law kernel approximation typically required less than half the number of spikes for similar SNR as compared to sums of similar but exponentially decaying kernels. paragraphs: This paper connects the timing of neural spikes to fractional differentiation. Earlier experimental work had suggested that firing rates could have this interpretation when changing signals induce adaptation. The authors extend the interpretation to the spike train itself, provided that the underlying neural signal is approximated as a sum of power-law kernels.

A standard threshold-based spiking neuron can produce this approximation when equipped with a suitable refractory response. Empirically, the representation benefits signals with slowly changing components, including long-memory self-similar signals. For those signals, it typically needs fewer than half as many spikes as comparable exponentially decaying kernels to achieve similar signal-to-noise ratios.

The paper also considers how a receiving neuron could decode the spikes. Power-law kernels can be approximated accurately through weighted sums or cascades of exponentials. Adjusting the decoding weights then provides a direct way to filter the reconstructed signal over time. Together, the results connect a conditional mathematical interpretation of spikes with efficient encoding and adjustable temporal decoding.
summary.tldr: Power-law signal representations give spike trains a fractional-derivative interpretation and empirically encode certain slowly varying signals with substantially fewer spikes.

title: Fractionally Predictive Spiking Neurons

abstract: We present a new algorithm for Independent Component Analysis (ICA) which has provable performance guarantees. In particular, suppose we are given samples of the form $y = Ax + \eta$ where $A$ is an unknown $n \times n$ matrix and $x$ is chosen uniformly at random from $\{+1, -1\}^n$, $\eta$ is an $n$-dimensional Gaussian random variable with unknown covariance $\Sigma$: We give an algorithm that provable recovers $A$ and $\Sigma$ up to an additive $\epsilon$ whose running time and sample complexity are polynomial in $n$ and $1 / \epsilon$. To accomplish this, we introduce a novel ``quasi-whitening'' step that may be useful in other contexts in which the covariance of Gaussian noise is not known in advance. We also give a general framework for finding all local optima of a function (given an oracle for approximately finding just one) and this is a crucial step in our algorithm, one that has been overlooked in previous attempts, and allows us to control the accumulation of error when we find the columns of $A$ one by one via local search.

paragraphs: The paper studies independent component analysis under a specific noisy observation model. Each sample is y = Ax + η, where A is an unknown square matrix, x is uniformly distributed over vectors of plus and minus ones, and η is Gaussian noise with unknown covariance. The goal is to recover both the mixing matrix and the noise covariance.

The proposed algorithm provides additive-error recovery guarantees, with running time and sample requirements polynomial in the dimension and inverse error tolerance. A key ingredient is a quasi-whitening step designed for the case where the Gaussian noise covariance is unavailable. The authors suggest that this step may also be useful in other settings with unknown Gaussian noise.

Another contribution is a framework for finding all local optima using a procedure that can approximately find one. This is crucial when recovering the columns of A sequentially through local search, because it lets the analysis control accumulating error. The recovery guarantee is tied to the stated observation model, including its binary latent variables.
summary.tldr: An ICA algorithm provably recovers a mixing matrix and unknown Gaussian noise covariance for uniformly random binary latent sources.

title: Provable ICA with Unknown Gaussian Noise, with Implications for Gaussian Mixtures and Autoencoders

abstract: The question of aggregating pairwise comparisons to obtain a global ranking over a collection of objects has been of interest for a very long time: be it ranking of online gamers (e.g. MSR’s TrueSkill system) and chess players, aggregating social opinions, or deciding which product to sell based on transactions. In most settings, in addition to obtaining ranking, finding ‘scores’ for each object (e.g. player’s rating) is of interest to understanding the intensity of the preferences. In this paper, we propose a novel iterative rank aggregation algorithm for discovering scores for objects from pairwise comparisons. The algorithm has a natural random walk interpretation over the graph of objects with edges present between two objects if they are compared; the scores turn out to be the stationary probability of this random walk. The algorithm is model independent. To establish the efficacy of our method, however, we consider the popular Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model in which each object has an associated score which determines the probabilistic outcomes of pairwise comparisons between objects. We bound the finite sample error rates between the scores assumed by the BTL model and those estimated by our algorithm. This, in essence, leads to order-optimal dependence on the number of samples required to learn the scores well by our algorithm. Indeed, the experimental evaluation shows that our (model independent) algorithm performs as well as the Maximum Likelihood Estimator of the BTL model and outperforms a recently proposed algorithm by Ammar and Shah [1].

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons reveal which of two objects is preferred, but many applications need an overall ranking and numerical scores. This paper introduces an iterative algorithm that recovers such scores from comparisons without requiring a particular model of how those comparisons were generated.

The method has a random-walk interpretation on a graph whose objects are nodes and whose edges indicate observed comparisons. The estimated scores are the walk's stationary probabilities: its long-run probability distribution over objects. This gives the ranking procedure a graph-based meaning and links the resulting scores to the pattern of comparisons.

They bound finite-sample estimation error and obtain order-optimal dependence on the number of samples. Experiments find performance matching that model's maximum-likelihood estimator and exceeding the compared Ammar-Shah algorithm. The algorithm's model independence thus coexists with guarantees established under a specific probabilistic model.
summary.tldr: An iterative random-walk algorithm turns pairwise comparisons into scores, with sample-efficiency guarantees under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model.

title: Iterative ranking from pair-wise comparisons

abstract: We address the problem of estimating the difference between two probability densities. A naive approach is a two-step procedure of first estimating two densities separately and then computing their difference. However, such a two-step procedure does not necessarily work well because the first step is performed without regard to the second step and thus a small estimation error incurred in the first stage can cause a big error in the second stage. In this paper, we propose a single-shot procedure for directly estimating the density difference without separately estimating two densities. We derive a non-parametric finite-sample error bound for the proposed single-shot density-difference estimator and show that it achieves the optimal convergence rate. We then show how the proposed density-difference estimator can be utilized in L2-distance approximation. Finally, we experimentally demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed method in robust distribution comparison such as class-prior estimation and change-point detection.

paragraphs: Comparing two probability distributions can require estimating where their densities differ and by how much. One approach estimates each density separately and then subtracts the estimates. The paper explains why this can work poorly: each estimation stage ignores the eventual subtraction, and relatively small errors in the individual estimates can produce a large error in the difference.

The proposed method estimates the density difference directly in a single procedure. Its fitting target is therefore the quantity needed for comparison, rather than two intermediate quantities. The authors derive a nonparametric error bound for a finite sample and show that the estimator attains the optimal convergence rate in their analysis.

The paper also connects the estimate to approximation of L2 distance between distributions. Experiments demonstrate its usefulness for robust distribution comparison, including class-prior estimation and change-point detection. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support treating density difference as an estimation problem in its own right, especially when the downstream task depends on differences rather than on recovering each density separately.
summary.tldr: Directly estimating a density difference achieves an optimal convergence rate and supports practical distribution-comparison tasks.

title: Density-Difference Estimation

abstract: In hierarchical classification, the prediction paths may be required to always end at leaf nodes. This is called mandatory leaf node prediction (MLNP) and is particularly useful when the leaf nodes have much stronger semantic meaning than the internal nodes. However, while there have been a lot of MLNP methods in hierarchical multiclass classification, performing MLNP in hierarchical multilabel classification is much more difficult. In this paper, we propose a novel MLNP algorithm that (i) considers the global hierarchy structure; and (ii) can be used on hierarchies of both trees and DAGs. We show that one can efficiently maximize the joint posterior probability of all the node labels by a simple greedy algorithm. Moreover, this can be further extended to the minimization of the expected symmetric loss. Experiments are performed on a number of real-world data sets with tree- and DAG-structured label hierarchies. The proposed method consistently outperforms other hierarchical and flat multilabel classification methods.

In this paper, we propose a novel MLNP algorithm that (i) considers the global hierarchy structure; and (ii) can be used on hierarchies of both trees and DAGs. paragraphs: Hierarchical classification organizes labels into broader and narrower categories. In some applications, predictions must reach the leaf nodes because these most specific categories carry stronger meaning than intermediate ones. Enforcing this requirement becomes harder when an example can receive several labels, since the predicted paths must be considered together.

The paper introduces an algorithm for mandatory leaf node prediction that takes the global hierarchy into account. It handles both trees and directed acyclic graphs, allowing a category structure with more than one route to a node. The authors show that a simple greedy algorithm can efficiently maximize the joint posterior probability of all node labels in their formulation.

They also extend the approach to minimize expected symmetric loss, providing another criterion for choosing predictions. Experiments cover real-world datasets with both kinds of hierarchy. The proposed method consistently outperforms the hierarchical and flat multilabel methods considered, indicating that enforcing specific predictions while accounting for the full label structure can be useful.
summary.tldr: A greedy algorithm supports globally informed leaf-level multilabel predictions on both tree and directed acyclic graph hierarchies.

title: Mandatory Leaf Node Prediction in Hierarchical Multilabel Classification

abstract: Estimating a vector from noisy quadratic observations is a task that arises naturally in many contexts, from dimensionality reduction, to synchronization and phase retrieval problems. It is often the case that additional information is available about the unknown vector (for instance, sparsity, sign or magnitude of its entries). Many authors propose non-convex quadratic optimization problems that aim at exploiting optimally this information. However, solving these problems is typically NP-hard. We consider a simple model for noisy quadratic observation of an unknown vector $\bvz$. The unknown vector is constrained to belong to a cone $\Cone \ni \bvz$. While optimal estimation appears to be intractable for the general problems in this class, we provide evidence that it is tractable when $\Cone$ is a convex cone with an efficient projection. This is surprising, since the corresponding optimization problem is non-convex and --from a worst case perspective-- often NP hard. We characterize the resulting minimax risk in terms of the statistical dimension of the cone $\delta(\Cone)$. This quantity is already known to control the risk of estimation from gaussian observations and random linear measurements. It is rather surprising that the same quantity plays a role in the estimation risk from quadratic measurements.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover an unknown vector from noisy quadratic observations when additional information restricts its possible values. Such information might concern sparsity, signs, or entry magnitudes. The authors express the restriction through a cone containing the vector, connecting the problem to tasks such as dimensionality reduction, synchronization, and phase retrieval.

Using this information can lead to nonconvex quadratic optimization problems that are difficult in the worst case. The paper nevertheless provides evidence for tractable estimation when the cone is convex and projection onto it can be computed efficiently. This is a qualified claim about the observation model and favorable constraint geometry, not a general solution to hard quadratic optimization.

The authors characterize minimax estimation risk through the cone's statistical dimension, a quantity describing its effective geometric complexity. The same quantity already governs estimation risk in Gaussian observation and random linear measurement settings. Its appearance here links quadratic measurements to those other problems: the geometry of the allowed vectors helps explain achievable accuracy despite the different observation mechanism.
summary.tldr: For noisy quadratic observations, convex cones with efficient projections offer evidence of tractable estimation, with minimax risk characterized by statistical dimension.

title: Cone-Constrained Principal Component Analysis

abstract: We provide a general mechanism to design online learning algorithms based on a minimax analysis within a drifting-games framework. Different online learning settings (Hedge, multi-armed bandit problems and online convex optimization) are studied by converting into various kinds of drifting games. The original minimax analysis for drifting games is then used and generalized by applying a series of relaxations, starting from choosing a convex surrogate of the 0-1 loss function. With different choices of surrogates, we not only recover existing algorithms, but also propose new algorithms that are totally parameter-free and enjoy other useful properties. Moreover, our drifting-games framework naturally allows us to study high probability bounds without resorting to any concentration results, and also a generalized notion of regret that measures how good the algorithm is compared to all but the top small fraction of candidates. Finally, we translate our new Hedge algorithm into a new adaptive boosting algorithm that is computationally faster as shown in experiments, since it ignores a large number of examples on each round.

paragraphs: The paper develops a shared way to design algorithms that learn through a sequence of decisions. It translates several settings, including learning from expert advice, multi-armed bandits, and online convex optimization, into drifting games. This translation lets the authors use a minimax analysis, which considers performance against unfavorable choices, across otherwise different learning problems.

The design process starts by replacing the zero-one loss with a convex surrogate and then applying further relaxations. Different surrogate choices recover existing algorithms or produce new, fully parameter-free algorithms. The framework also supports high-probability bounds without invoking concentration results. It accommodates a broader comparison criterion that measures performance against candidates outside a small top-performing fraction.

The authors additionally turn their new expert-advice algorithm into an adaptive boosting method. In the reported experiments, this method runs faster because it ignores many training examples during each round. The contribution therefore connects a general theoretical design framework with a concrete computational improvement for boosting.
summary.tldr: A drifting-games framework unifies online algorithm design and yields parameter-free methods plus an empirically faster adaptive boosting algorithm.

title: A Drifting-Games Analysis for Online Learning and Applications to Boosting

abstract: A major challenge in scaling object detection is the difficulty of obtaining labeled images for large numbers of categories. Recently, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as clear winners on object classification benchmarks, in part due to training with 1.2M+ labeled classification images. Unfortunately, only a small fraction of those labels are available for the detection task. It is much cheaper and easier to collect large quantities of image-level labels from search engines than it is to collect detection data and label it with precise bounding boxes. In this paper, we propose Large Scale Detection through Adaptation (LSDA), an algorithm which learns the difference between the two tasks and transfers this knowledge to classifiers for categories without bounding box annotated data, turning them into detectors. Our method has the potential to enable detection for the tens of thousands of categories that lack bounding box annotations, yet have plenty of classification data. Evaluation on the ImageNet LSVRC-2013 detection challenge demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. This algorithm enables us to produce a >7.6K detector by using available classification data from leaf nodes in the ImageNet tree. We additionally demonstrate how to modify our architecture to produce a fast detector (running at 2fps for the 7.6K detector). Models and software are available at

paragraphs: Object detection is difficult to scale because precise bounding-box annotations are expensive to collect. Image-level category labels are much easier to obtain, but a classifier trained on those labels does not directly supply a detector. LSDA addresses this mismatch by transferring knowledge about the difference between classification and detection.

The algorithm learns how the two tasks differ and applies that knowledge to category classifiers without bounding-box training annotations. It thereby converts those classifiers into detectors. The intended benefit is to extend detection to categories with abundant classification data but no corresponding box labels, reducing dependence on category-specific detection annotations.

Evaluation on the ImageNet LSVRC-2013 detection challenge supports the approach's effectiveness. Using classification data from ImageNet leaf categories, the authors produce a detector covering more than 7,600 categories. They also modify the architecture to run the 7,600-category detector at two frames per second. Detection for tens of thousands of categories is presented as a potential future reach of the method; the demonstrated scale is the reported 7,600-plus-category system.
summary.tldr: LSDA transfers knowledge from classification to detection, enabling a demonstrated detector for more than 7,600 categories using available classification data.

title: LSDA: Large Scale Detection through Adaptation

abstract: We propose a deep feed-forward neural network architecture for pixel-wise semantic scene labeling. It uses a novel recursive neural network architecture for context propagation, referred to as rCPN. It first maps the local visual features into a semantic space followed by a bottom-up aggregation of local information into a global representation of the entire image. Then a top-down propagation of the aggregated information takes place that enhances the contextual information of each local feature. Therefore, the information from every location in the image is propagated to every other location. Experimental results on Stanford background and SIFT Flow datasets show that the proposed method outperforms previous approaches. It is also orders of magnitude faster than previous methods and takes only 0.07 seconds on a GPU for pixel-wise labeling of a 256x256 image starting from raw RGB pixel values, given the super-pixel mask that takes an additional 0.3 seconds using an off-the-shelf implementation.

It first maps the local visual features into a semantic space followed by a bottom-up aggregation of local information into a global representation of the entire image. Then a top-down propagation of the aggregated information takes place that enhances the contextual information of each local feature. Therefore, the information from every location in the image is propagated to every other location. paragraphs: Assigning a semantic label to every pixel can benefit from information elsewhere in the image. This paper proposes a deep feed-forward architecture called the recursive context propagation network, or rCPN. Its purpose is to enrich local visual information with an interpretation of the entire scene before producing pixel-wise labels.

The network first maps local visual features into a semantic space. It then aggregates those features from the bottom up into a global image representation. A top-down pass sends the aggregated information back to local features. Through these two directions of propagation, information from every image location reaches every other location.

Experiments on Stanford Background and SIFT Flow outperform previous approaches, with reported speed improvements of orders of magnitude. For a 256-by-256 image, GPU labeling from raw RGB values takes 0.07 seconds when a superpixel mask is already available. Producing that mask adds 0.3 seconds with the off-the-shelf implementation used. The timing distinction matters when interpreting the speed of the full procedure, while the accuracy results support the value of scene-wide context.
summary.tldr: rCPN distributes global image context back to local features, improving scene labeling accuracy and speed in the reported evaluations.

title: Recursive Context Propagation Network for Semantic Scene Labeling

abstract: Bayesian networks are a popular representation of asymmetric (for example causal) relationships between random variables. Markov random fields (MRFs) are a complementary model of symmetric relationships used in computer vision, spatial modeling, and social and gene expression networks. A chain graph model under the Lauritzen-Wermuth-Frydenberg interpretation (hereafter a chain graph model) generalizes both Bayesian networks and MRFs, and can represent asymmetric and symmetric relationships together.As in other graphical models, the set of marginals from distributions in a chain graph model induced by the presence of hidden variables forms a complex model. One recent approach to the study of marginal graphical models is to consider a well-behaved supermodel. Such a supermodel of marginals of Bayesian networks, defined only by conditional independences, and termed the ordinary Markov model, was studied at length in (Evans and Richardson, 2014).In this paper, we show that special mixed graphs which we call segregated graphs can be associated, via a Markov property, with supermodels of a marginal of chain graphs defined only by conditional independences. Special features of segregated graphs imply the existence of a very natural factorization for these supermodels, and imply many existing results on the chain graph model, and ordinary Markov model carry over. Our results suggest that segregated graphs define an analogue of the ordinary Markov model for marginals of chain graph models.

paragraphs: Chain graphs under the interpretation studied here combine asymmetric relationships, as in Bayesian networks, with symmetric relationships, as in Markov random fields. When some variables are hidden, the distributions over the remaining variables can form a complicated model. This paper seeks a more manageable graphical description of those observable distributions.

The authors introduce mixed graphs called segregated graphs and associate them with models through a Markov property. These models are supermodels of chain-graph marginals: they contain the marginal distributions and are defined using conditional-independence restrictions. This makes the representation a structured enlargement of the marginal model rather than a claim to capture all of its possible constraints exactly.

Special properties of segregated graphs yield a natural factorization and allow many results from chain graphs and ordinary Markov models to carry over. The authors interpret this as evidence that segregated graphs provide an analogue of the ordinary Markov model for chain-graph marginals. The contribution supplies mathematical structure for reasoning about hidden variables in models that mix symmetric and asymmetric relationships.
summary.tldr: Segregated graphs provide factorized conditional-independence supermodels for chain-graph distributions with hidden variables.

title: Segregated Graphs and Marginals of Chain Graph Models

abstract: We develop a new bidirectional algorithm for estimating Markov chain multi-step transition probabilities: given a Markov chain, we want to estimate the probability of hitting a given target state in $\ell$ steps after starting from a given source distribution. Given the target state $t$, we use a (reverse) local power iteration to construct an `expanded target distribution', which has the same mean as the quantity we want to estimate, but a smaller variance -- this can then be sampled efficiently by a Monte Carlo algorithm. Our method extends to any Markov chain on a discrete (finite or countable) state-space, and can be extended to compute functions of multi-step transition probabilities such as PageRank, graph diffusions, hitting/return times, etc. Our main result is that in `sparse' Markov Chains -- wherein the number of transitions between states is comparable to the number of states -- the running time of our algorithm for a uniform-random target node is order-wise smaller than Monte Carlo and power iteration based algorithms; in particular, our method can estimate a probability $p$ using only $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ running time.

paragraphs: The task is to estimate a multi-step transition probability in a Markov chain: starting from a specified distribution, how likely is the chain to reach a particular target after a given number of steps? The paper develops a bidirectional method that combines computation working backward from the target with Monte Carlo sampling.

The backward stage uses local power iteration to construct an expanded target distribution. This construction preserves the mean of the quantity being estimated while reducing its variance. The sampling stage can therefore estimate the desired probability more efficiently. The method applies to Markov chains with finite or countably infinite discrete state spaces, and the authors describe extensions to quantities including PageRank, graph diffusions, and hitting or return times.

The main runtime result concerns sparse chains, where the number of transitions is comparable to the number of states, and a uniformly random target. In that setting, the algorithm improves the runtime order over Monte Carlo and power iteration approaches, including an O(1/√p) runtime for estimating probability p.
summary.tldr: A backward computation reduces variance before Monte Carlo sampling, enabling faster transition-probability estimation under stated sparsity and target conditions.

title: Fast Bidirectional Probability Estimation in Markov Models

abstract: Expectation propagation (EP) is a deterministic approximation algorithm that is often used to perform approximate Bayesian parameter learning. EP approximates the full intractable posterior distribution through a set of local-approximations that are iteratively refined for each datapoint. EP can offer analytic and computational advantages over other approximations, such as Variational Inference (VI), and is the method of choice for a number of models. The local nature of EP appears to make it an ideal candidate for performing Bayesian learning on large models in large-scale datasets settings. However, EP has a crucial limitation in this context: the number approximating factors needs to increase with the number of data-points, N, which often entails a prohibitively large memory overhead. This paper presents an extension to EP, called stochastic expectation propagation (SEP), that maintains a global posterior approximation (like VI) but updates it in a local way (like EP). Experiments on a number of canonical learning problems using synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that SEP performs almost as well as full EP, but reduces the memory consumption by a factor of N. SEP is therefore ideally suited to performing approximate Bayesian learning in the large model, large dataset setting.

paragraphs: Expectation propagation approximates a difficult Bayesian posterior through local approximations refined for individual data points. This local structure offers useful analytic and computational properties, but it also creates a memory problem. As the dataset grows, the number of approximating factors grows with it, which can make large-model, large-dataset applications expensive.

The method therefore preserves a local update approach without storing a separate collection of approximating factors that expands with every data point.

The near-match in approximation quality is an empirical finding. Its practical significance is the possibility of retaining much of EP's performance while removing the dataset-sized factor storage that limits scalability.
summary.tldr: Stochastic expectation propagation locally updates a global posterior approximation, approaching full EP's empirical performance with much lower memory use.

title: Stochastic Expectation Propagation

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating a function defined over $n$ locations on a $d$-dimensional grid (having all side lengths equal to $n^{1/d}$). When the function is constrained to have discrete total variation bounded by $C_n$, we derive the minimax optimal (squared) $\ell_2$ estimation error rate, parametrized by $n, C_n$. Total variation denoising, also known as the fused lasso, is seen to be rate optimal. Several simpler estimators exist, such as Laplacian smoothing and Laplacian eigenmaps. A natural question is: can these simpler estimators perform just as well? We prove that these estimators, and more broadly all estimators given by linear transformations of the input data, are suboptimal over the class of functions with bounded variation. This extends fundamental findings of Donoho and Johnstone (1998) on 1-dimensional total variation spaces to higher dimensions. The implication is that the computationally simpler methods cannot be used for such sophisticated denoising tasks, without sacrificing statistical accuracy. We also derive minimax rates for discrete Sobolev spaces over $d$-dimensional grids, which are, in some sense, smaller than the total variation function spaces. Indeed, these are small enough spaces that linear estimators can be optimal---and a few well-known ones are, such as Laplacian smoothing and Laplacian eigenmaps, as we show. Lastly, we investigate the adaptivity of the total variation denoiser to these smaller Sobolev function spaces.

It assumes the function's discrete total variation is bounded and derives the minimax squared-error rate in terms of the number of locations and that bound. This rate describes the best achievable worst-case accuracy over the specified function class.

By contrast, the authors prove that every estimator formed as a linear transformation of the observations is suboptimal over the bounded-variation class. This includes Laplacian smoothing and Laplacian eigenmaps, showing a statistical cost to using these simpler methods for this class of denoising problems.

The authors derive minimax rates there and show that linear estimators, including those same Laplacian methods, can be optimal. They also investigate how total variation denoising adapts to these smaller spaces, making the assumed function class central to comparing methods.
summary.tldr: Total variation denoising achieves optimal grid-estimation rates where linear smoothers fall short, although linear methods can be optimal on smaller Sobolev classes.

title: Total Variation Classes Beyond 1d: Minimax Rates, and the Limitations of Linear Smoothers

abstract: Given a matrix of observed data, Principal Components Analysis (PCA) computes a small number of orthogonal directions that contain most of its variability. Provably accurate solutions for PCA have been in use for a long time. However, to the best of our knowledge, all existing theoretical guarantees for it assume that the data and the corrupting noise are mutually independent, or at least uncorrelated. This is valid in practice often, but not always. In this paper, we study the PCA problem in the setting where the data and noise can be correlated. Such noise is often also referred to as ``data-dependent noise". We obtain a correctness result for the standard eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) based solution to PCA under simple assumptions on the data-noise correlation. We also develop and analyze a generalization of EVD, cluster-EVD, that improves upon EVD in certain regimes.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis finds a small set of perpendicular directions that capture much of the variation in observed data. Its accuracy becomes harder to reason about when the noise depends on the underlying data. The authors identify this as a gap in existing guarantees, which, to their knowledge, assume independence or at least an absence of correlation.

The paper analyzes PCA with correlated, or data-dependent, noise. Under assumptions controlling the relationship between data and noise, it proves correctness for the standard solution based on eigenvalue decomposition. This matters because it gives theoretical support to an existing, familiar procedure in a setting outside the usual uncorrelated-noise framework.

The authors also introduce and analyze cluster-EVD, a generalization of eigenvalue decomposition. It improves on the standard method in certain regimes, providing a reason to go beyond ordinary PCA when the problem has suitable structure. Both contributions are conditional: the analysis permits correlation under specified assumptions, and the improvement from cluster-EVD is not asserted for every correlated-noise problem.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes PCA guarantees with data-dependent noise and introduces cluster-EVD, which improves on standard eigenvalue decomposition in certain regimes.

title: Correlated-PCA: Principal Components' Analysis when Data and Noise are Correlated

abstract: For sophisticated reinforcement learning (RL) systems to interact usefully with real-world environments, we need to communicate complex goals to these systems. In this work, we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments. Our approach separates learning the goal from learning the behavior to achieve it. We show that this approach can effectively solve complex RL tasks without access to the reward function, including Atari games and simulated robot locomotion, while providing feedback on about 0.1% of our agent's interactions with the environment. This reduces the cost of human oversight far enough that it can be practically applied to state-of-the-art RL systems. To demonstrate the flexibility of our approach, we show that we can successfully train complex novel behaviors with about an hour of human time. These behaviors and environments are considerably more complex than any which have been previously learned from human feedback.

paragraphs: Complex goals can be difficult to communicate as an explicit reward function. This paper instead asks nonexpert humans to compare pairs of short trajectory segments. It separates learning what behavior people prefer from learning a policy that achieves the inferred goal.

The approach is tested on Atari games and simulated robot locomotion without giving the learner access to the task’s reward function. Human feedback covers about 0.1% of the agent’s interactions with its environment, showing that direct supervision of every action is unnecessary in these experiments.

The authors also report training complex novel behaviors with about an hour of human time. This supports the flexibility and practical feasibility of preference-based goal learning in the evaluated environments. It does not mean all real-world goals can be inferred from that amount of feedback; the abstract’s evidence is tied to these demonstrations and their particular human-comparison setup.
summary.tldr: Human comparisons of short behavior segments can train reinforcement-learning goals with sparse feedback.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences

abstract: Computable Stein discrepancies have been deployed for a variety of applications, ranging from sampler selection in posterior inference to approximate Bayesian inference to goodness-of-fit testing. Existing convergence-determining Stein discrepancies admit strong theoretical guarantees but suffer from a computational cost that grows quadratically in the sample size. While linear-time Stein discrepancies have been proposed for goodness-of-fit testing, they exhibit avoidable degradations in testing power—even when power is explicitly optimized. To address these shortcomings, we introduce feature Stein discrepancies (ΦSDs), a new family of quality measures that can be cheaply approximated using importance sampling. We show how to construct ΦSDs that provably determine the convergence of a sample to its target and develop high-accuracy approximations—random ΦSDs (RΦSDs)—which are computable in near-linear time. In our experiments with sampler selection for approximate posterior inference and goodness-of-fit testing, RΦSDs perform as well or better than quadratic-time KSDs while being orders of magnitude faster to compute.

paragraphs: Stein discrepancies measure how well a sample matches a target distribution and can support sampler selection or goodness-of-fit testing. Existing convergence-determining versions have strong guarantees but require computation that grows quadratically with sample size. Faster testing methods can lose statistical power. This paper seeks a better balance between computational cost and assessment quality.

The authors introduce feature Stein discrepancies, a family of measures that can be approximated cheaply through importance sampling. They show how to construct members of this family that provably determine convergence to a target distribution. They then develop high-accuracy randomized approximations that can be computed in near-linear time.

Experiments evaluate these random feature measures for selecting samplers in approximate posterior inference and for goodness-of-fit testing. They perform as well as or better than quadratic-time kernel Stein discrepancies while taking orders of magnitude less computation. The contribution pairs theoretical convergence-detection properties with empirical evidence that substantial speed gains can preserve useful sample-quality assessments in the tested applications.
summary.tldr: Random feature Stein discrepancies provide near-linear-time sample-quality assessments with strong theory and favorable empirical performance.

title: Random Feature Stein Discrepancies

abstract: The most widely used technology to identify the proteins present in a complex biological sample is tandem mass spectrometry, which quickly produces a large collection of spectra representative of the peptides (i.e., protein subsequences) present in the original sample. In this work, we greatly expand the parameter learning capabilities of a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) peptide-scoring algorithm, Didea, by deriving emission distributions for which its conditional log-likelihood scoring function remains concave. We show that this class of emission distributions, called Convex Virtual Emissions (CVEs), naturally generalizes the log-sum-exp function while rendering both maximum likelihood estimation and conditional maximum likelihood estimation concave for a wide range of Bayesian networks. Utilizing CVEs in Didea allows efficient learning of a large number of parameters while ensuring global convergence, in stark contrast to Didea’s previous parameter learning framework (which could only learn a single parameter using a costly grid search) and other trainable models (which only ensure convergence to local optima). The newly trained scoring function substantially outperforms the state-of-the-art in both scoring function accuracy and downstream Fisher kernel analysis. Furthermore, we significantly improve Didea’s runtime performance through successive optimizations to its message passing schedule and derive explicit connections between Didea’s new concave score and related MS/MS scoring functions.

This paper improves Didea, a dynamic Bayesian network algorithm that scores candidate peptides. Its central challenge is to expand how many parameters can be learned while retaining an optimization objective with reliable convergence properties.

summary.tldr: New emission distributions let Didea learn many peptide-scoring parameters with global convergence while improving accuracy and runtime.

title: Learning Concave Conditional Likelihood Models for Improved Analysis of Tandem Mass Spectra

abstract: For MCMC methods like Metropolis-Hastings, tuning the proposal distribution is important in practice for effective sampling from the target distribution \pi. In this paper, we present Sample Adaptive MCMC (SA-MCMC), a MCMC method based on a reversible Markov chain for \pi^{\otimes N} that uses an adaptive proposal distribution based on the current state of N points and a sequential substitution procedure with one new likelihood evaluation per iteration and at most one updated point each iteration. The SA-MCMC proposal distribution automatically adapts within its parametric family to best approximate the target distribution, so in contrast to many existing MCMC methods, SA-MCMC does not require any tuning of the proposal distribution. Instead, SA-MCMC only requires specifying the initial state of N points, which can often be chosen a priori, thereby automating the entire sampling procedure with no tuning required. Experimental results demonstrate the fast adaptation and effective sampling of SA-MCMC.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo methods depend heavily on how they propose new points. A poorly chosen proposal can make sampling ineffective, so methods such as Metropolis–Hastings often require practical tuning. Sample Adaptive MCMC addresses this burden by constructing its proposal from a current collection of N points.

The method uses a reversible Markov chain whose target is the N-fold product of the desired distribution. A sequential substitution procedure requires one new likelihood evaluation per iteration and updates at most one point. The proposal adapts automatically within its chosen parametric family to approximate the target distribution, connecting adaptation to the chain's current state.

According to the authors, users need only specify the initial collection of points, which can often be chosen in advance, without tuning the proposal distribution. Experiments demonstrate rapid adaptation and effective sampling. The key distinction is that adaptation occurs within the proposal family: the automation concerns selecting its parameters through the method, while initialization still supplies the starting state.
summary.tldr: Sample Adaptive MCMC automatically adapts its proposal from a collection of points, requiring one new likelihood evaluation and at most one point update per iteration.

title: Sample Adaptive MCMC

abstract: In the contextual linear bandit setting, algorithms built on the optimism principle fail to exploit the structure of the problem and have been shown to be asymptotically suboptimal. In this paper, we follow recent approaches of deriving asymptotically optimal algorithms from problem-dependent regret lower bounds and we introduce a novel algorithm improving over the state-of-the-art along multiple dimensions. We build on a reformulation of the lower bound, where context distribution and exploration policy are decoupled, and we obtain an algorithm robust to unbalanced context distributions. Then, using an incremental primal-dual approach to solve the Lagrangian relaxation of the lower bound, we obtain a scalable and computationally efficient algorithm. Finally, we remove forced exploration and build on confidence intervals of the optimization problem to encourage a minimum level of exploration that is better adapted to the problem structure. We demonstrate the asymptotic optimality of our algorithm, while providing both problem-dependent and worst-case finite-time regret guarantees. Our bounds scale with the logarithm of the number of arms, thus avoiding the linear dependence common in all related prior works. Notably, we establish minimax optimality for any learning horizon in the special case of non-contextual linear bandits. Finally, we verify that our algorithm obtains better empirical performance than state-of-the-art baselines.

The paper starts from the observation that optimism-based approaches can miss useful problem structure and be asymptotically suboptimal. It instead designs an algorithm around problem-dependent lower bounds on regret, the loss associated with learning rather than always choosing optimally.

summary.tldr: An incremental primal-dual bandit algorithm achieves asymptotic optimality while adapting exploration to context frequencies and problem structure.

title: An Asymptotically Optimal Primal-Dual Incremental Algorithm for Contextual Linear Bandits

abstract: Binary Neural Network (BNN) shows its predominance in reducing the complexity of deep neural networks. However, it suffers severe performance degradation. One of the major impediments is the large quantization error between the full-precision weight vector and its binary vector. Previous works focus on compensating for the norm gap while leaving the angular bias hardly touched. In this paper, for the first time, we explore the influence of angular bias on the quantization error and then introduce a Rotated Binary Neural Network (RBNN), which considers the angle alignment between the full-precision weight vector and its binarized version. At the beginning of each training epoch, we propose to rotate the full-precision weight vector to its binary vector to reduce the angular bias. To avoid the high complexity of learning a large rotation matrix, we further introduce a bi-rotation formulation that learns two smaller rotation matrices. In the training stage, we devise an adjustable rotated weight vector for binarization to escape the potential local optimum. Our rotation leads to around 50% weight flips which maximize the information gain. Finally, we propose a training-aware approximation of the sign function for the gradient backward. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate the superiorities of RBNN over many state-of-the-arts. Our source code, experimental settings, training logs and binary models are available at https://github.com/lmbxmu/RBNN.

title: Rotated Binary Neural Network

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for learning software engineering tasks including code completion, bug finding, and program repair. They benefit from leveraging program structure like control flow graphs, but they are not well-suited to tasks like program execution that require far more sequential reasoning steps than number of GNN propagation steps. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), on the other hand, are well-suited to long sequential chains of reasoning, but they do not naturally incorporate program structure and generally perform worse on the above tasks. Our aim is to achieve the best of both worlds, and we do so by introducing a novel GNN architecture, the Instruction Pointer Attention Graph Neural Networks (IPA-GNN), which achieves improved systematic generalization on the task of learning to execute programs using control flow graphs. The model arises by considering RNNs operating on program traces with branch decisions as latent variables. The IPA-GNN can be seen either as a continuous relaxation of the RNN model or as a GNN variant more tailored to execution. To test the models, we propose evaluating systematic generalization on learning to execute using control flow graphs, which tests sequential reasoning and use of program structure. More practically, we evaluate these models on the task of learning to execute partial programs, as might arise if using the model as a heuristic function in program synthesis. Results show that the IPA-GNN outperforms a variety of RNN and GNN baselines on both tasks.

Graph neural networks can use control flow graphs, but execution may require many more sequential steps than their propagation supports. Recurrent networks handle long sequences more naturally, yet do not inherently incorporate the same program structure.

Instruction Pointer Attention Graph Neural Networks combine these strengths.
