The results support aligning a learned model's computation with the sequential and structural demands of the program it is trying to execute.
summary.tldr: IPA-GNN combines control-flow structure with sequential reasoning, improving learned execution of complete and partial programs in the reported evaluations.

title: Learning to Execute Programs with Instruction Pointer Attention Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In recent years, artificial neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance for predicting the responses of neurons in the visual cortex to natural stimuli. However, they require a time consuming parameter optimization process for accurately modeling the tuning function of newly observed neurons, which prohibits many applications including real-time, closed-loop experiments. We overcome this limitation by formulating the problem as $K$-shot prediction to directly infer a neuron's tuning function from a small set of stimulus-response pairs using a Neural Process. This required us to developed a Factorized Neural Process, which embeds the observed set into a latent space partitioned into the receptive field location and the tuning function properties. We show on simulated responses that the predictions and reconstructed receptive fields from the Factorized Neural Process approach ground truth with increasing number of trials. Critically, the latent representation that summarizes the tuning function of a neuron is inferred in a quick, single forward pass through the network. Finally, we validate this approach on real neural data from visual cortex and find that the predictive accuracy is comparable to --- and for small $K$ even greater than --- optimization based approaches, while being substantially faster. We believe this novel deep learning systems identification framework will facilitate better real-time integration of artificial neural network modeling into neuroscience experiments.
originalAbstract: In recent years, artificial neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance for predicting the responses of neurons in the visual cortex to natural stimuli. However, they require a time consuming parameter optimization process for accurately modeling the tuning function of newly observed neurons, which prohibits many applications including real-time, closed-loop experiments. We overcome this limitation by formulating the problem as $K$-shot prediction to directly infer a neuron's tuning function from a small set of stimulus-response pairs using a Neural Process. This required us to developed a Factorized Neural Process, which embeds the observed set into a latent space partitioned into the receptive field location and the tuning function properties. We show on simulated responses that the predictions and reconstructed receptive fields from the Factorized Neural Process approach ground truth with increasing number of trials. Critically, the latent representation that summarizes the tuning function of a neuron is inferred in a quick, single forward pass through the network. Finally, we validate this approach on real neural data from visual cortex and find that the predictive accuracy is comparable to --- and for small $K$ even greater than --- optimization based approaches, while being substantially faster. We believe this novel deep learning systems identification framework will facilitate better real-time integration of artificial neural network modeling into neuroscience experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting how a visual-cortex neuron responds to stimuli usually requires fitting a model to that neuron. Repeating this optimization for newly observed neurons takes time and can obstruct real-time experiments. This paper reframes the task as K-shot prediction: infer a neuron’s response properties directly from a small collection of stimulus–response observations.

The authors develop a Factorized Neural Process that converts those observations into a latent representation with two parts. One represents receptive-field location, and the other represents properties of the neuron’s tuning function. The representation is inferred in a single forward pass through the network, avoiding the time-consuming parameter optimization otherwise needed to model each newly observed neuron.

On simulated responses, predictions and reconstructed receptive fields approach the true values as more trials become available. On real visual-cortex data, predictive accuracy is comparable to optimization-based methods and better when K is small, while inference is substantially faster. These findings support the authors’ expectation that rapid response modeling could make neural-network models easier to integrate into real-time neuroscience experiments.
summary.tldr: A Factorized Neural Process predicts a neuron’s responses from a few observations in one forward pass, matching or exceeding optimization-based accuracy in reported settings.

title: Factorized Neural Processes for Neural Processes: K-Shot Prediction of Neural Responses

abstract: De novo molecular design attempts to search over the chemical space for molecules with the desired property. Recently, deep learning has gained considerable attention as a promising approach to solve the problem. In this paper, we propose genetic expert-guided learning (GEGL), a simple yet novel framework for training a deep neural network (DNN) to generate highly-rewarding molecules. Our main idea is to design a "genetic expert improvement" procedure, which generates high-quality targets for imitation learning of the DNN. Extensive experiments show that GEGL significantly improves over state-of-the-art methods. For example, GEGL manages to solve the penalized octanol-water partition coefficient optimization with a score of 31.40, while the best-known score in the literature is 27.22. Besides, for the GuacaMol benchmark with 20 tasks, our method achieves the highest score for 19 tasks, in comparison with state-of-the-art methods, and newly obtains the perfect score for three tasks. Our training code is available at https://github.com/sungsoo-ahn/genetic-expert-guided-learning.

Its central idea connects a genetic improvement procedure with imitation learning.

The genetic expert produces high-quality molecular targets for the network to imitate. This makes the quality of the training targets a direct part of the optimization strategy: the network learns from candidates supplied by an improvement process. The framework combines molecular exploration with the training of a generative model rather than treating those as unrelated activities.

The reported experiments show substantial gains over the compared methods. summary.tldr: GEGL trains a molecular generator to imitate genetically improved candidates, achieving strong results across molecular optimization benchmarks.

title: Guiding Deep Molecular Optimization with Genetic Exploration

abstract: Many computer vision tasks rely on labeled data. Rapid progress in generative modeling has led to the ability to synthesize photorealistic images. However, controlling specific aspects of the generation process such that the data can be used for supervision of downstream tasks remains challenging. In this paper we propose a novel generative model for images of faces, that is capable of producing high-quality images under fine-grained control over eye gaze and head orientation angles. This requires the disentangling of many appearance related factors including gaze and head orientation but also lighting, hue etc. We propose a novel architecture which learns to discover, disentangle and encode these extraneous variations in a self-learned manner. We further show that explicitly disentangling task-irrelevant factors results in more accurate modelling of gaze and head orientation. A novel evaluation scheme shows that our method improves upon the state-of-the-art in redirection accuracy and disentanglement between gaze direction and head orientation changes. Furthermore, we show that in the presence of limited amounts of real-world training data, our method allows for improvements in the downstream task of semi-supervised cross-dataset gaze estimation. Please check our project page at: https://ait.ethz.ch/projects/2020/STED-gaze/

paragraphs: Realistic generated faces are useful for supervision only if the relevant properties can be controlled accurately. For gaze-related tasks, this means changing eye direction and head orientation without confusing those changes with lighting, hue, or other appearance variation. The paper develops a face generator designed for this fine-grained control.

Its architecture learns to discover, separate, and encode additional appearance factors without requiring them all to be specified in advance. Explicitly separating these task-irrelevant variations improves the modeling of gaze and head angles. This makes the treatment of background appearance variation part of the solution to controlling the target properties.

Using a new evaluation scheme, the authors report improved redirection accuracy and better separation between gaze changes and head-orientation changes compared with the state of the art. They also show improvements in semi-supervised gaze estimation across datasets when real training data is limited. The findings connect more precise control of generated faces with a benefit for a downstream prediction task under that limited-data condition.
summary.tldr: Separating learned appearance factors improves control of generated gaze and head orientation and helps gaze estimation when real data is limited.

title: Self-Learning Transformations for Improving Gaze and Head Redirection

abstract: One paradigm for learning from few labeled examples while making best use of a large amount of unlabeled data is unsupervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Although this paradigm uses unlabeled data in a task-agnostic way, in contrast to common approaches to semi-supervised learning for computer vision, we show that it is surprisingly effective for semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A key ingredient of our approach is the use of big (deep and wide) networks during pretraining and fine-tuning. We find that, the fewer the labels, the more this approach (task-agnostic use of unlabeled data) benefits from a bigger network. After fine-tuning, the big network can be further improved and distilled into a much smaller one with little loss in classification accuracy by using the unlabeled examples for a second time, but in a task-specific way. The proposed semi-supervised learning algorithm can be summarized in three steps: unsupervised pretraining of a big ResNet model using SimCLRv2, supervised fine-tuning on a few labeled examples, and distillation with unlabeled examples for refining and transferring the task-specific knowledge. This procedure achieves 73.9% ImageNet top-1 accuracy with just 1% of the labels ($\le$13 labeled images per class) using ResNet-50, a 10X improvement in label efficiency over the previous state-of-the-art. With 10% of labels, ResNet-50 trained with our method achieves 77.5% top-1 accuracy, outperforming standard supervised training with all of the labels.

Unlabeled data thus supports both general representation learning and later task-specific learning.

With 1% of ImageNet labels, the resulting ResNet-50 achieves 73.9% top-1 accuracy, reported as a tenfold improvement in label efficiency over the previous state of the art. With 10% of labels, it reaches 77.5%, exceeding standard supervised training using all labels. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the full training procedure in the reported setting.
summary.tldr: Large self-supervised models, followed by fine-tuning and distillation, achieve strong ImageNet classification with very few labels.

title: Big Self-Supervised Models are Strong Semi-Supervised Learners

abstract: Psychological research shows that enjoyment of many goods is subject to satiation, with short-term satisfaction declining after repeated exposures to the same item. Nevertheless, proposed algorithms for powering recommender systems seldom model these dynamics, instead proceeding as though user preferences were fixed in time. In this work, we introduce rebounding bandits, a multi-armed bandit setup, where satiation dynamics are modeled as time-invariant linear dynamical systems. Expected rewards for each arm decline monotonically with consecutive exposures and rebound towards the initial reward whenever that arm is not pulled. Unlike classical bandit algorithms, methods for tackling rebounding bandits must plan ahead and model-based methods rely on estimating the parameters of the satiation dynamics. We characterize the planning problem, showing that the greedy policy is optimal when the arms exhibit identical deterministic dynamics. To address stochastic satiation dynamics with unknown parameters, we propose Explore-Estimate-Plan, an algorithm that pulls arms methodically, estimates the system dynamics, and then plans accordingly.

paragraphs: Repeated exposure to the same item can make it less enjoyable, while time away can restore its appeal. Rebounding bandits incorporate this satiation pattern into a sequential choice problem. Each option has an expected reward that decreases with consecutive selections and moves back toward its initial level when the option is left unselected.

The authors model these changes using time-invariant linear dynamical systems. Because a choice changes future rewards, deciding what to select requires planning beyond the immediate payoff. They analyze this planning problem and show that a greedy policy is optimal when all options have identical deterministic dynamics. That conclusion is tied to this particular condition.

For stochastic dynamics with unknown parameters, the paper proposes Explore-Estimate-Plan. The algorithm selects options methodically, estimates how their rewards decline and recover, and then plans using those estimates. The contribution is a framework in which changing enjoyment is explicitly part of the decision problem, together with a conditional planning result and an algorithm for learning the underlying dynamics.
summary.tldr: Rebounding bandits model rewards that decline with repeated use and recover with rest, motivating an exploration, estimation, and planning algorithm.

title: Rebounding Bandits for Modeling Satiation Effects

abstract: Transformer architectures have become very popular yet the original implementation requires $O(L^2)$ in serial time and memory as functions of input length $L$. Recent works proposed various linear self-attention mechanisms, scaling only as $O(L)$ for serial computation. We conduct a thorough complexity analysis of Performers, a class which includes most recent linear Transformer mechanisms. We note a remarkable computational flexibility: the gradient computation can be performed with no approximations using sublinear memory as a function of $L$ (in addition to negligible storage for the input sequence), at a cost of greater time complexity in the parallel setting. In the extreme case, a Performer consumes only $O(1)$ memory, and still requires $O(L)$ time. Due to complete backward-compatibility, this discovered time-memory tradeoff can be used for fine-tuning on low-memory devices in a decentralized fashion without any server computations.

paragraphs: Standard Transformer attention has quadratic time and memory costs in sequence length, while linear-attention mechanisms reduce serial computation to linear cost. This paper studies the computational flexibility of Performers, a class encompassing many such mechanisms. Its focus is the memory needed to compute gradients, which matters when training or fine-tuning on constrained devices.

The analysis shows that Performer gradients can be computed without adding approximations while using memory that grows sublinearly with sequence length. At the extreme, the computation uses constant memory and linear time, with input-sequence storage accounted for separately. The tradeoff is increased time complexity in the parallel setting, so memory savings change the available balance between storage and parallel computation.

The approach is fully backward-compatible, making the tradeoff applicable to existing Performer models. The authors identify decentralized fine-tuning on low-memory devices without server computation as a use case. The contribution shows that linear attention offers flexibility in gradient computation beyond its already reduced forward-computation complexity.
summary.tldr: Performer gradients can be computed exactly with sublinear or constant working memory by trading away parallel-time efficiency.

title: Sub-Linear Memory: How to Make Performers SLiM

abstract: We propose a general method to construct centroid approximation for the distribution of maximum points of a random function (a.k.a. argmax distribution), which finds broad applications in machine learning. Our method optimizes a set of centroid points to compactly approximate the argmax distribution with a simple objective function, without explicitly drawing exact samples from the argmax distribution. Theoretically, the argmax centroid method can be shown to minimize a surrogate of Wasserstein distance between the ground-truth argmax distribution and the centroid approximation under proper conditions. We demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of our method on a variety of real-world multi-task learning applications, including few-shot image classification, personalized dialogue systems and multi-target domain adaptation.

paragraphs: When a function is random, the location of its maximum is also uncertain. The resulting distribution describes where the best point might be, rather than simply providing one optimum. This paper develops a general way to represent that distribution compactly through a set of optimized representative points, called centroids.

The method uses a simple objective to adjust those centroids without explicitly drawing exact samples from the distribution of maximizers. This matters because the desired representation can be constructed without making exact sampling an intermediate requirement. Under appropriate conditions, the authors show that the objective minimizes a surrogate for Wasserstein distance between the true distribution and its centroid approximation.

That theoretical result connects the optimization procedure to a measure of how closely two distributions match, while retaining the qualification that it concerns a surrogate under stated conditions. The paper demonstrates applications in few-shot image classification, personalized dialogue, and multi-target domain adaptation. These examples support the usefulness of the same compact distributional representation across several real-world multi-task learning settings.
summary.tldr: Argmax centroid approximates a random function's distribution of maximizers with optimized representative points, without requiring exact samples from that distribution.

title: argmax centroid

abstract: Contrastive self-supervised learning has outperformed supervised pretraining on many downstream tasks like segmentation and object detection. However, current methods are still primarily applied to curated datasets like ImageNet. In this paper, we first study how biases in the dataset affect existing methods. Our results show that an approach like MoCo works surprisingly well across: (i) object- versus scene-centric, (ii) uniform versus long-tailed and (iii) general versus domain-specific datasets. Second, given the generality of the approach, we try to realize further gains with minor modifications. We show that learning additional invariances - through the use of multi-scale cropping, stronger augmentations and nearest neighbors - improves the representations. Finally, we observe that MoCo learns spatially structured representations when trained with a multi-crop strategy. The representations can be used for semantic segment retrieval and video instance segmentation without finetuning. Moreover, the results are on par with specialized models. We hope this work will serve as a useful study for other researchers.

paragraphs: Contrastive self-supervised learning has produced useful visual representations, but much of its use has centered on curated datasets. This paper investigates how dataset composition affects those methods. It finds that MoCo works well across object-focused and scene-focused data, balanced and long-tailed distributions, and general and domain-specific collections.

Building on that observed flexibility, the authors examine modest changes to the learning procedure. Multi-scale cropping, stronger augmentations, and nearest neighbors introduce additional invariances and improve the learned representations. The study therefore connects broader applicability with adjustments to what the model is encouraged to treat as equivalent.

A further finding concerns spatial information. With a multi-crop training strategy, MoCo learns representations that retain useful spatial structure. Those representations support semantic segment retrieval and video instance segmentation without fine-tuning, with results comparable to specialized models. This shows that the learned features can support region-level uses as well as broader image representation tasks, under the evaluated training strategy and applications.
summary.tldr: MoCo works across varied dataset types, and simple training changes improve representations while enabling spatial tasks without fine-tuning.

title: Revisiting Contrastive Methods for Unsupervised Learning of Visual Representations

abstract: The advancement of generative radiance fields has pushed the boundary of 3D-aware image synthesis. Motivated by the observation that a 3D object should look realistic from multiple viewpoints, these methods introduce a multi-view constraint as regularization to learn valid 3D radiance fields from 2D images. Despite the progress, they often fall short of capturing accurate 3D shapes due to the shape-color ambiguity, limiting their applicability in downstream tasks. In this work, we address this ambiguity by proposing a novel shading-guided generative implicit model that is able to learn a starkly improved shape representation. Our key insight is that an accurate 3D shape should also yield a realistic rendering under different lighting conditions. This multi-lighting constraint is realized by modeling illumination explicitly and performing shading with various lighting conditions. Gradients are derived by feeding the synthesized images to a discriminator. To compensate for the additional computational burden of calculating surface normals, we further devise an efficient volume rendering strategy via surface tracking, reducing the training and inference time by 24% and 48%, respectively. Our experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed approach achieves photorealistic 3D-aware image synthesis while capturing accurate underlying 3D shapes. We demonstrate improved performance of our approach on 3D shape reconstruction against existing methods, and show its applicability on image relighting. Our code is available at https://github.com/XingangPan/ShadeGAN.

paragraphs: Generating convincing views of an object does not necessarily mean recovering its correct three-dimensional shape. The paper addresses ambiguity between shape and color: different combinations can produce realistic images, even when the underlying geometry is inaccurate.

The proposed model adds a lighting requirement to the usual requirement that objects look realistic from multiple viewpoints. It explicitly represents illumination and renders objects under different lighting conditions. A discriminator evaluates the generated images, supplying gradients that guide learning toward shapes whose shading also looks plausible.

Computing surface normals for shading adds work. To offset that cost, the authors introduce a volume-rendering strategy based on tracking the surface. They report reductions of 24% in training time and 48% in inference time.

Experiments across multiple datasets show photorealistic image generation alongside improved underlying shapes. The paper also reports better shape reconstruction than existing methods and demonstrates image relighting. Its central contribution is using appearance under changing illumination as an additional source of guidance for learning geometry.
summary.tldr: Explicitly modeling lighting helps a generative image model learn more accurate 3D shapes while supporting realistic rendering and relighting.

title: A Shading-Guided Generative Implicit Model for Shape-Accurate 3D-Aware Image Synthesis

abstract: In recent years, the Transformer architecture has proven to be very successful in sequence processing, but its application to other data structures, such as graphs, has remained limited due to the difficulty of properly defining positions. Here, we present the \textit{Spectral Attention Network} (SAN), which uses a learned positional encoding (LPE) that can take advantage of the full Laplacian spectrum to learn the position of each node in a given graph.This LPE is then added to the node features of the graph and passed to a fully-connected Transformer.By leveraging the full spectrum of the Laplacian, our model is theoretically powerful in distinguishing graphs, and can better detect similar sub-structures from their resonance.Further, by fully connecting the graph, the Transformer does not suffer from over-squashing, an information bottleneck of most GNNs, and enables better modeling of physical phenomenons such as heat transfer and electric interaction.When tested empirically on a set of 4 standard datasets, our model performs on par or better than state-of-the-art GNNs, and outperforms any attention-based model by a wide margin, becoming the first fully-connected architecture to perform well on graph benchmarks.

paragraphs: Transformers need a useful notion of position, but graph nodes do not have the straightforward ordering of sequence elements. The Spectral Attention Network, or SAN, addresses this by learning positional information from a graph’s Laplacian spectrum. Those learned encodings are added to node features before a fully connected Transformer processes them.

The positional encoding can use the full spectrum, giving the model theoretical power to distinguish graphs and helping it recognize similar substructures through their resonance. Full connectivity also addresses over-squashing, the information bottleneck identified in many graph neural networks. The paper connects this design to better modeling of physical phenomena such as heat transfer and electrical interaction.

Across four standard datasets, SAN performs comparably to or better than state-of-the-art graph neural networks and substantially outperforms the attention-based models in the evaluation. The results support combining spectral position information with fully connected attention. In the authors’ account, this provides a successful way to bring a fully connected architecture to graph benchmarks.
summary.tldr: SAN combines learned spectral node positions with fully connected attention to improve graph representation and benchmark performance.

title: Rethinking Graph Transformers with Spectral Attention

abstract: We study a quadrature, proposed by Ermakov and Zolotukhin in the sixties, through the lens of kernel methods. The nodes of this quadrature rule follow the distribution of a determinantal point process, while the weights are defined through a linear system, similarly to the optimal kernel quadrature. In this work, we show how these two classes of quadrature are related, and we prove a tractable formula of the expected value of the squared worst-case integration error on the unit ball of an RKHS of the former quadrature. In particular, this formula involves the eigenvalues of the corresponding kernel and leads to improving on the existing theoretical guarantees of the optimal kernel quadrature with determinantal point processes.

The nodes of this quadrature rule follow the distribution of a determinantal point process, while the weights are defined through a linear system, similarly to the optimal kernel quadrature. In this work, we show how these two classes of quadrature are related, and we prove a tractable formula of the expected value of the squared worst-case integration error on the unit ball of an RKHS of the former quadrature. In particular, this formula involves the eigenvalues of the corresponding kernel and leads to improving on the existing theoretical guarantees of the optimal kernel quadrature with determinantal point processes.

paragraphs: Numerical integration replaces an integral with a weighted combination of function values at selected locations. This paper revisits the Ermakov–Zolotukhin quadrature rule using kernel methods. Its sampling locations follow a determinantal point process, while its weights come from solving a linear system. That construction resembles optimal kernel quadrature, motivating the authors to investigate the mathematical relationship between them.

The central result is a tractable expression for the expected squared worst-case integration error. Here, worst case refers to the largest error over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. The expectation accounts for the randomness of the sampling locations. The formula expresses this error through the eigenvalues of the associated kernel.

Connecting the two quadrature methods makes the analysis useful beyond the original rule. The authors use it to improve existing theoretical guarantees for optimal kernel quadrature with determinantal sampling. The contribution is therefore a sharper mathematical understanding of integration accuracy under this particular function-space and sampling setup.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based analysis of Ermakov–Zolotukhin quadrature yields an explicit expected-error formula and sharper guarantees for related integration methods.

title: An analysis of Ermakov-Zolotukhin quadrature using kernels

abstract: Recent history has seen a tremendous growth of work exploring implicit representations of geometry and radiance, popularized through Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Such works are fundamentally based on a (implicit) {\em volumetric} representation of occupancy, allowing them to model diverse scene structure including translucent objects and atmospheric obscurants. But because the vast majority of real-world scenes are composed of well-defined surfaces, we introduce a {\em surface} analog of such implicit models called Neural Reflectance Surfaces (NeRS). NeRS learns a neural shape representation of a closed surface that is diffeomorphic to a sphere, guaranteeing water-tight reconstructions. Even more importantly, surface parameterizations allow NeRS to learn (neural) bidirectional surface reflectance functions (BRDFs) that factorize view-dependent appearance into environmental illumination, diffuse color (albedo), and specular “shininess.” Finally, rather than illustrating our results on synthetic scenes or controlled in-the-lab capture, we assemble a novel dataset of multi-view images from online marketplaces for selling goods. Such “in-the-wild” multi-view image sets pose a number of challenges, including a small number of views with unknown/rough camera estimates. We demonstrate that surface-based neural reconstructions enable learning from such data, outperforming volumetric neural rendering-based reconstructions. We hope that NeRS serves as a first step toward building scalable, high-quality libraries of real-world shape, materials, and illumination.

Its learned surface is constrained to be smoothly equivalent to a sphere, guaranteeing a closed, watertight reconstruction within that shape family.

title: NeRS: Neural Reflectance Surfaces for Sparse-view 3D Reconstruction in the Wild

abstract: This paper proposes a new algorithm -- the \underline{S}ingle-timescale Do\underline{u}ble-momentum \underline{St}ochastic \underline{A}pprox\underline{i}matio\underline{n} (SUSTAIN) -- for tackling stochastic unconstrained bilevel optimization problems. We focus on bilevel problems where the lower level subproblem is strongly-convex and the upper level objective function is smooth. Unlike prior works which rely on \emph{two-timescale} or \emph{double loop} techniques, we design a stochastic momentum-assisted gradient estimator for both the upper and lower level updates. The latter allows us to control the error in the stochastic gradient updates due to inaccurate solution to both subproblems. If the upper objective function is smooth but possibly non-convex, we show that {SUSTAIN}~requires $O(\epsilon^{-3/2})$ iterations (each using $O(1)$ samples) to find an $\epsilon$-stationary solution. The $\epsilon$-stationary solution is defined as the point whose squared norm of the gradient of the outer function is less than or equal to $\epsilon$. The total number of stochastic gradient samples required for the upper and lower level objective functions matches the best-known complexity for single-level stochastic gradient algorithms. We also analyze the case when the upper level objective function is strongly-convex.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves two linked optimization problems: the upper problem depends on the solution of the lower one. When both use random samples, inaccurate lower-level solutions can also distort upper-level updates. This paper introduces SUSTAIN for unconstrained stochastic bilevel problems whose lower objective is strongly convex and whose upper objective is smooth.

SUSTAIN uses momentum-assisted gradient estimates at both levels. These estimates control errors arising from imperfect solutions of the coupled problems. The method operates on a single timescale, avoiding the two-timescale or nested-loop approaches used in prior work. Its central contribution is therefore a way to coordinate both updates while managing the errors they introduce into one another.

For a potentially nonconvex upper objective, the authors prove an iteration requirement of O(ε^−3/2), with a constant-order number of samples per iteration. Here, success means the outer gradient’s squared norm is at most ε, rather than reaching a global optimum. The resulting sample complexity matches the best known for single-level stochastic gradient methods. The paper also analyzes strongly convex upper objectives.
summary.tldr: SUSTAIN uses momentum at both levels to solve a class of stochastic bilevel problems with sample complexity matching the best-known single-level rate.

title: A Near-Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization via Double-Momentum

abstract: Discovering cause and effect variables from observational data is an important but challenging problem in science and engineering. In this work, a recently proposed brain inspired learning algorithm namely-\emph{Neurochaos Learning} (NL) is used for the classification of cause and effect time series generated using coupled autoregressive processes, coupled 1D chaotic skew tent maps, coupled 1D chaotic logistic maps and a real-world prey-predator system. In the case of coupled skew tent maps, the proposed method consistently outperforms a five layer Deep Neural Network (DNN) and Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for unidirectional coupling coefficient values ranging from $0.1$ to $0.7$. Further, we investigate the preservation of causality in the feature extracted space of NL using Granger Causality for coupled autoregressive processes and Compression-Complexity Causality for coupled chaotic systems and real-world prey-predator dataset. Unlike DNN, LSTM and 1D Convolutional Neural Network, it is found that NL preserves the inherent causal structures present in the input timeseries data. These findings are promising for the theory and applications of causal machine learning and open up the possibility to explore the potential of NL for more sophisticated causal learning tasks.

paragraphs: Learning from time series can involve two distinct goals: classifying cause and effect, and preserving causal relationships when transforming the data into features. This paper investigates both using Neurochaos Learning, a brain-inspired learning algorithm. Its examples include coupled autoregressive processes, two kinds of coupled chaotic maps, and a real-world prey-predator system.

For classification with coupled skew tent maps, Neurochaos Learning consistently outperforms a five-layer deep neural network and an LSTM over unidirectional coupling coefficients from 0.1 to 0.7. The authors separately examine the extracted features using Granger Causality for autoregressive processes and Compression-Complexity Causality for the chaotic systems and prey-predator data.

In these investigations, Neurochaos Learning preserves the causal structure present in the input time series, unlike the tested deep neural network, LSTM, and one-dimensional convolutional network. This suggests that useful classification features can also retain information about causal relationships. The findings motivate exploring more sophisticated causal learning tasks, rather than establishing performance on those tasks already.
summary.tldr: Neurochaos Learning preserves causal structure in the studied time-series transformations and improves classification in a specified chaotic-system setting.

title: Causality Preserving Chaotic Transformation and Classification using Neurochaos Learning

abstract: Despite the rapid advance of unsupervised anomaly detection, existing methods require to train separate models for different objects. In this work, we present UniAD that accomplishes anomaly detection for multiple classes with a unified framework. Under such a challenging setting, popular reconstruction networks may fall into an "identical shortcut", where both normal and anomalous samples can be well recovered, and hence fail to spot outliers. To tackle this obstacle, we make three improvements. First, we revisit the formulations of fully-connected layer, convolutional layer, as well as attention layer, and confirm the important role of query embedding (i.e., within attention layer) in preventing the network from learning the shortcut. We therefore come up with a layer-wise query decoder to help model the multi-class distribution. Second, we employ a neighbor masked attention module to further avoid the information leak from the input feature to the reconstructed output feature. Third, we propose a feature jittering strategy that urges the model to recover the correct message even with noisy inputs. We evaluate our algorithm on MVTec-AD and CIFAR-10 datasets, where we surpass the state-of-the-art alternatives by a sufficiently large margin. For example, when learning a unified model for 15 categories in MVTec-AD, we surpass the second competitor on the tasks of both anomaly detection (from 88.1% to 96.5%) and anomaly localization (from 89.5% to 96.8%). Code is available at https://github.com/zhiyuanyou/UniAD.

paragraphs: UniAD addresses anomaly detection across several object categories using one model. This setting exposes a weakness in reconstruction approaches: a network may reproduce unusual inputs just as successfully as normal ones. If both are reconstructed well, reconstruction quality stops being useful for distinguishing anomalies. The paper calls this failure an identical shortcut.

The authors introduce three changes to discourage that shortcut. A decoder with query embeddings at each layer helps represent the distribution across categories. Neighbor masked attention restricts information passing directly from input features into their reconstructed counterparts. Feature jittering adds noise to the inputs and asks the model to recover the correct information, encouraging recovery beyond straightforward copying.

Experiments on MVTec-AD and CIFAR-10 report improvements over the evaluated alternatives. For a single model covering 15 MVTec-AD categories, the reported detection result increases from 88.1% to 96.5%, and localization from 89.5% to 96.8%, relative to the second competitor. These findings support the combination of shared modeling and measures that prevent reconstruction shortcuts.
summary.tldr: UniAD detects anomalies across multiple object categories with one reconstruction model designed to resist copying anomalous inputs.

title: A Unified Model for Multi-class Anomaly Detection

abstract: Dynamic graph neural networks (DyGNNs) have demonstrated powerful predictive abilities by exploiting graph structural and temporal dynamics. However, the existing DyGNNs fail to handle distribution shifts, which naturally exist in dynamic graphs, mainly because the patterns exploited by DyGNNs may be variant with respect to labels under distribution shifts. In this paper, we propose to handle spatio-temporal distribution shifts in dynamic graphs by discovering and utilizing {\it invariant patterns}, i.e., structures and features whose predictive abilities are stable across distribution shifts, which faces two key challenges: 1) How to discover the complex variant and invariant spatio-temporal patterns in dynamic graphs, which involve both time-varying graph structures and node features. 2) How to handle spatio-temporal distribution shifts with the discovered variant and invariant patterns. To tackle these challenges, we propose the Disentangled Intervention-based Dynamic graph Attention networks (DIDA). Our proposed method can effectively handle spatio-temporal distribution shifts in dynamic graphs by discovering and fully utilizing invariant spatio-temporal patterns. Specifically, we first propose a disentangled spatio-temporal attention network to capture the variant and invariant patterns. Then, we design a spatio-temporal intervention mechanism to create multiple interventional distributions by sampling and reassembling variant patterns across neighborhoods and time stamps to eliminate the spurious impacts of variant patterns. Lastly, we propose an invariance regularization term to minimize the variance of predictions in intervened distributions so that our model can make predictions based on invariant patterns with stable predictive abilities and therefore handle distribution shifts. Experiments on three real-world datasets and one synthetic dataset demonstrate the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts. Our work is the first study of spatio-temporal distribution shifts in dynamic graphs, to the best of our knowledge.

paragraphs: Dynamic graph models learn from both changing connections and changing node features. A pattern that predicts labels during training can become unreliable when those relationships shift. This paper addresses that problem by seeking spatio-temporal patterns whose predictive usefulness remains stable across changes in the data distribution.

The proposed DIDA model first uses disentangled spatio-temporal attention to capture stable and variable patterns separately. It then samples and recombines variable patterns across neighborhoods and time points, creating multiple intervened distributions. These interventions are designed to remove the misleading influence of patterns whose association with the prediction target can change.

An invariance regularizer penalizes variation in predictions across those intervened distributions. This encourages the model to rely on the stable patterns it has identified. Experiments on three real-world datasets and one synthetic dataset show better performance than leading baselines under distribution shifts. The approach matters because it treats robustness as a training objective involving both graph structure and time, rather than relying only on predictive fit to the observed distribution.
summary.tldr: DIDA separates stable and variable graph patterns and trains predictions to remain consistent when variable patterns are rearranged.

title: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks Under Spatio-Temporal Distribution Shift

abstract: Humans have the remarkable ability to recognize and acquire novel visual concepts in a zero-shot manner. Given a high-level, symbolic description of a novel concept in terms of previously learned visual concepts and their relations, humans can recognize novel concepts without seeing any examples. Moreover, they can acquire new concepts by parsing and communicating symbolic structures using learned visual concepts and relations. Endowing these capabilities in machines is pivotal in improving their generalization capability at inference time. In this work, we introduce Zero-shot Concept Recognition and Acquisition (ZeroC), a neuro-symbolic architecture that can recognize and acquire novel concepts in a zero-shot way. ZeroC represents concepts as graphs of constituent concept models (as nodes) and their relations (as edges). To allow inference time composition, we employ energy-based models (EBMs) to model concepts and relations. We design ZeroC architecture so that it allows a one-to-one mapping between a symbolic graph structure of a concept and its corresponding EBM, which for the first time, allows acquiring new concepts, communicating its graph structure, and applying it to classification and detection tasks (even across domains) at inference time. We introduce algorithms for learning and inference with ZeroC. We evaluate ZeroC on a challenging grid-world dataset which is designed to probe zero-shot concept recognition and acquisition, and demonstrate its capability.

ZeroC aims to give machines this ability at inference time. It supports both recognizing concepts from symbolic descriptions and acquiring new concepts whose structure can then be communicated and reused.

The architecture represents a concept as a graph: nodes correspond to constituent concept models, and edges encode relationships. Energy-based models represent both concepts and relations, enabling composition during inference. A one-to-one mapping connects each symbolic graph to its corresponding energy-based model, linking an explicit description of a concept with a model usable for recognition.

The paper introduces learning and inference algorithms and demonstrates ZeroC on a challenging grid-world dataset designed to test zero-shot recognition and acquisition. The architecture supports applying communicated structures to classification and detection, including across domains. The contribution is a concrete mechanism for assembling and sharing new concepts from learned components, with its demonstrated capability evaluated in the stated grid-world setting.
summary.tldr: ZeroC composes learned concepts and relations into symbolic graphs and energy-based models to recognize and acquire new concepts at inference time.

title: ZeroC: A Neuro-Symbolic Model for Zero-shot Concept Recognition and Acquisition at Inference Time

abstract: Collaborations among multiple organizations, such as financial institutions, medical centers, and retail markets in decentralized settings are crucial to providing improved service and performance. However, the underlying organizations may have little interest in sharing their local data, models, and objective functions. These requirements have created new challenges for multi-organization collaboration. In this work, we propose Gradient Assisted Learning (GAL), a new method for multiple organizations to assist each other in supervised learning tasks without sharing local data, models, and objective functions. In this framework, all participants collaboratively optimize the aggregate of local loss functions, and each participant autonomously builds its own model by iteratively fitting the gradients of the overarching objective function. We also provide asymptotic convergence analysis and practical case studies of GAL. Experimental studies demonstrate that GAL can achieve performance close to centralized learning when all data, models, and objective functions are fully disclosed.

paragraphs: Organizations may benefit from learning together while remaining unwilling to share their local datasets, models, or objective functions. Gradient Assisted Learning, or GAL, addresses this collaboration problem for supervised learning. It provides a framework in which participants assist one another while continuing to build their own models autonomously.

The shared learning goal is the aggregate of the participants’ local loss functions. Each organization iteratively fits gradients of this overarching objective, allowing its local learning process to contribute to the collaborative objective. This connects separate model-building efforts through optimization information while keeping the specified local data, models, and objectives undisclosed.

The paper provides an asymptotic convergence analysis and practical case studies. Its experimental results show that GAL can approach the performance of centralized learning in which all data, models, and objective functions are fully disclosed. The significance is that useful coordination can occur under the stated sharing constraints. The performance claim concerns closeness to centralized learning in the experiments, while the convergence analysis supplies a theoretical account of the collaborative optimization process.
summary.tldr: GAL coordinates organizations through gradient-based learning without sharing their local data, models, or objectives.

title: GAL: Gradient Assisted Learning for Decentralized Multi-Organization Collaborations

abstract: Autonomous agents have made great strides in specialist domains like Atari games and Go. However, they typically learn tabula rasa in isolated environments with limited and manually conceived objectives, thus failing to generalize across a wide spectrum of tasks and capabilities. Inspired by how humans continually learn and adapt in the open world, we advocate a trinity of ingredients for building generalist agents: 1) an environment that supports a multitude of tasks and goals, 2) a large-scale database of multimodal knowledge, and 3) a flexible and scalable agent architecture. We introduce MineDojo, a new framework built on the popular Minecraft game that features a simulation suite with thousands of diverse open-ended tasks and an internet-scale knowledge base with Minecraft videos, tutorials, wiki pages, and forum discussions. Using MineDojo's data, we propose a novel agent learning algorithm that leverages large pre-trained video-language models as a learned reward function. Our agent is able to solve a variety of open-ended tasks specified in free-form language without any manually designed dense shaping reward. We open-source the simulation suite, knowledge bases, algorithm implementation, and pretrained models (https://minedojo.org) to promote research towards the goal of generally capable embodied agents.

paragraphs: Agents that excel at a specialized game often learn in isolated environments with a narrow set of manually chosen goals. MineDojo addresses the broader challenge of learning many capabilities in an open-ended setting. The paper argues for combining a varied environment, extensive multimodal knowledge, and an agent architecture that can use both.

The framework is built around Minecraft and includes thousands of diverse tasks. Its knowledge base gathers Minecraft videos, tutorials, wiki material, and forum discussions. MineDojo thus contributes both an agent-learning approach and shared infrastructure for research toward broader embodied capabilities.
summary.tldr: MineDojo combines Minecraft tasks, internet-scale knowledge, and video-language reward models to train agents on free-form language goals.

title: MineDojo: Building Open-Ended Embodied Agents with Internet-Scale Knowledge

abstract: We introduce a new intrinsic measure of local curvature on point-cloud data called diffusion curvature. Our measure uses the framework of diffusion maps, including the data diffusion operator, to structure point cloud data and define local curvature based on the laziness of a random walk starting at a point or region of the data. We show that this laziness directly relates to volume comparison results from Riemannian geometry. We then extend this scalar curvature notion to an entire quadratic form using neural network estimations based on the diffusion map of point-cloud data. We show applications of both estimations on toy data, single-cell data, and on estimating local Hessian matrices of neural network loss landscapes.

paragraphs: A point cloud supplies samples of a shape or data geometry without directly describing its local curvature. This paper introduces diffusion curvature, an intrinsic measure intended to recover that local geometric information. It builds on diffusion maps, using a diffusion operator to organize the relationships among sampled points.

The central idea is to examine the laziness of a random walk starting at a point or region. How that walk remains concentrated provides a basis for defining local curvature. The authors connect this behavior directly to volume-comparison results from Riemannian geometry, giving the measure a geometric foundation rather than treating diffusion behavior only as a descriptive statistic.

The paper then extends the scalar measure to a quadratic form through neural-network estimates based on the diffusion map. This richer representation goes beyond assigning one curvature value to each location. The authors demonstrate both kinds of estimates on toy data and single-cell data, and use them to estimate local Hessian matrices in neural-network loss landscapes. Together, these applications connect sampled-data geometry to both biological data analysis and optimization.
summary.tldr: Diffusion curvature estimates local point-cloud geometry from random-walk behavior and extends it to richer neural-network-based curvature estimates.

title: Diffusion Curvature for Estimating Local Curvature in High Dimensional Data

abstract: We present a new implicit warping framework for image animation using sets of source images through the transfer of motion of a driving video. A single cross-modal attention layer is used to find correspondences between the source images and the driving image, choose the most appropriate features from different source images, and warp the selected features. This is in contrast to the existing methods that use explicit flow-based warping, which is designed for animation using a single source and does not extend well to multiple sources. The pick-and-choose capability of our framework helps it achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets for image animation using both single and multiple source images.

paragraphs: Image animation transfers motion from a driving video to the appearance supplied by source images. This paper develops a framework that can use a set of source images, allowing the animation process to draw on different available features. The challenge is to determine which source information corresponds to the current driving image and how to place it.

The proposed method handles these operations with a single cross-modal attention layer. It finds correspondences, selects suitable features from different source images, and warps those selected features. Feature selection and motion transfer are therefore combined within the same implicit warping mechanism.

The authors contrast this with explicit flow-based warping, which was designed around a single source and does not extend well to multiple sources. Their framework’s ability to choose among source features helps it achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple animation datasets, using either one source image or several. The stated findings show that a mechanism built to exploit image sets can also perform strongly in the single-source setting.
summary.tldr: A single attention layer selects and warps features from source image sets to animate them using motion from a driving video.

title: Implicit Warping for Animation with Image Sets

abstract: In accelerated MRI reconstruction, the anatomy of a patient is recovered from a set of undersampled and noisy measurements. Deep learning approaches have been proven to be successful in solving this ill-posed inverse problem and are capable of producing very high quality reconstructions. However, current architectures heavily rely on convolutions, that are content-independent and have difficulties modeling long-range dependencies in images. Recently, Transformers, the workhorse of contemporary natural language processing, have emerged as powerful building blocks for a multitude of vision tasks. These models split input images into non-overlapping patches, embed the patches into lower-dimensional tokens and utilize a self-attention mechanism that does not suffer from the aforementioned weaknesses of convolutional architectures. However, Transformers incur extremely high compute and memory cost when 1) the input image resolution is high and 2) when the image needs to be split into a large number of patches to preserve fine detail information, both of which are typical in low-level vision problems such as MRI reconstruction, having a compounding effect. To tackle these challenges, we propose HUMUS-Net, a hybrid architecture that combines the beneficial implicit bias and efficiency of convolutions with the power of Transformer blocks in an unrolled and multi-scale network. HUMUS-Net extracts high-resolution features via convolutional blocks and refines low-resolution features via a novel Transformer-based multi-scale feature extractor. Features from both levels are then synthesized into a high-resolution output reconstruction. Our network establishes new state of the art on the largest publicly available MRI dataset, the fastMRI dataset. We further demonstrate the performance of HUMUS-Net on two other popular MRI datasets and perform fine-grained ablation studies to validate our design.

title: HUMUS-Net: Hybrid Unrolled Multi-scale Network Architecture for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction

abstract: Social media platforms were conceived to act as online `town squares' where people could get together, share information and communicate with each other peacefully. However, harmful content borne out of bad actors are constantly plaguing these platforms slowly converting them into `mosh pits' where the bad actors take the liberty to extensively abuse various marginalised groups. Accurate and timely detection of abusive content on social media platforms is therefore very important for facilitating safe interactions between users. However, due to the small scale and sparse linguistic coverage of Indic abusive speech datasets, development of such algorithms for Indic social media users (one-sixth of global population) is severely impeded.To facilitate and encourage research in this important direction, we contribute for the first time MACD - a large-scale (150K), human-annotated, multilingual (5 languages), balanced (49\% abusive content) and diverse (70K users) abuse detection dataset of user comments, sourced from a popular social media platform - ShareChat. We also release AbuseXLMR, an abusive content detection model pretrained on large number of social media comments in 15+ Indic languages which outperforms XLM-R and MuRIL on multiple Indic datasets. Along with the annotations, we also release the mapping between comment, post and user id's to facilitate modelling the relationship between them. We share competitive monolingual, cross-lingual and few-shot baselines so that MACD can be used as a dataset benchmark for future research.

This paper contributes both a larger annotated resource and a pretrained detection model. The aim is to support research on identifying harmful comments across languages used by a substantial population of social media users.

In addition to annotations, the release includes mappings among comment, post, and user identifiers. Those links make it possible to study relationships among comments, their surrounding posts, and users rather than relying only on isolated comment text.

Monolingual, cross-lingual, and few-shot baselines accompany the release, giving researchers comparison points for studying learning within a language, transfer across languages, and settings with limited labeled examples.
summary.tldr: MACD and AbuseXLMR provide multilingual data, pretrained modeling, and comparison baselines for abusive-comment detection in Indic languages.

title: Multilingual Abusive Comment Detection at Scale for Indic Languages

abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are a tractable representation of probability distributions allowing for exact and efficient computation of likelihoods and marginals. There has been significant recent progress on improving the scale and expressiveness of PCs. However, PC training performance plateaus as model size increases. We discover that most capacity in existing large PC structures is wasted: fully-connected parameter layers are only sparsely used. We propose two operations: pruning and growing, that exploit the sparsity of PC structures. Specifically, the pruning operation removes unimportant sub-networks of the PC for model compression and comes with theoretical guarantees. The growing operation increases model capacity by increasing the dimensions of latent states. By alternatingly applying pruning and growing, we increase the capacity that is meaningfully used, allowing us to significantly scale up PC learning. Empirically, our learner achieves state-of-the-art likelihoods on MNIST-family image datasets and an Penn Tree Bank language data compared to other PC learners and less tractable deep generative models such as flow-based models and variational autoencoders (VAEs).

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits represent distributions while supporting exact, efficient likelihood and marginal calculations. Yet simply making these models larger does not keep improving training performance. The authors find that much of the capacity in existing large circuits is unused: layers with fully connected parameters are used only sparsely.

They propose alternating two structural operations. Pruning removes unimportant subnetworks to compress the circuit and comes with theoretical guarantees. Growing expands the dimensions of latent states to add capacity. By repeatedly removing weakly used structure and expanding the model, the learner increases the capacity that is meaningfully used rather than relying on size alone.

These results support pruning and growing as a way to scale circuit learning while retaining the representation's appeal for exact probabilistic computations.
summary.tldr: Alternating pruning and latent-state growth makes probabilistic-circuit capacity more useful and achieves strong likelihood results on image and language datasets.

title: Sparse Probabilistic Circuits via Pruning and Growing

abstract: Episodic count has been widely used to design a simple yet effective intrinsic motivation for reinforcement learning with a sparse reward. However, the use of episodic count in a high-dimensional state space as well as over a long episode time requires a thorough state compression and fast hashing, which hinders rigorous exploitation of it in such hard and complex exploration environments. Moreover, the interference from task-irrelevant observations in the episodic count may cause its intrinsic motivation to overlook task-related important changes of states, and the novelty in an episodic manner can lead to repeatedly revisit the familiar states across episodes. In order to resolve these issues, in this paper, we propose a learnable hash-based episodic count, which we name LECO, that efficiently performs as a task-specific intrinsic reward in hard exploration problems. In particular, the proposed intrinsic reward consists of the episodic novelty and the task-specific modulation where the former employs a vector quantized variational autoencoder to automatically obtain the discrete state codes for fast counting while the latter regulates the episodic novelty by learning a modulator to optimize the task-specific extrinsic reward. The proposed LECO specifically enables the automatic transition from exploration to exploitation during reinforcement learning. We experimentally show that in contrast to the previous exploration methods LECO successfully solves hard exploration problems and also scales to large state spaces through the most difficult tasks in MiniGrid and DMLab environments.

paragraphs: Counting visits to states within an episode can encourage exploration when external rewards are sparse. However, large observations make counting difficult, irrelevant visual changes can distract the count, and resetting novelty each episode can encourage repeated visits to already familiar states. LECO makes this exploration signal both learnable and sensitive to the task.

Its intrinsic reward combines episodic novelty with a task-specific modulator. A vector-quantized variational autoencoder learns discrete state codes that support fast counting. The modulator then adjusts the novelty reward through learning aimed at improving the task's external reward. This gives the exploration mechanism a way to account for which novelty contributes to the objective.

The authors state that LECO enables an automatic transition from exploration to exploitation during learning. Experiments on difficult MiniGrid and DMLab tasks show successful exploration and scaling to large state spaces relative to previous exploration methods. The contribution connects efficient state counting with learned task relevance, addressing both the computational burden of novelty tracking and its usefulness for completing the task.
summary.tldr: LECO combines learned discrete state counting with task-specific reward modulation to guide exploration and its transition toward exploitation.

title: LECO: Learnable Episodic Count for Task-Specific Intrinsic Reward

abstract: The large pre-trained vision transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on various visual tasks, but suffer from expensive computational and memory cost problems when deployed on resource-constrained devices. Among the powerful compression approaches, quantization extremely reduces the computation and memory consumption by low-bit parameters and bit-wise operations. However, low-bit ViTs remain largely unexplored and usually suffer from a significant performance drop compared with the real-valued counterparts. In this work, through extensive empirical analysis, we first identify the bottleneck for severe performance drop comes from the information distortion of the low-bit quantized self-attention map. We then develop an information rectification module (IRM) and a distribution guided distillation (DGD) scheme for fully quantized vision transformers (Q-ViT) to effectively eliminate such distortion, leading to a fully quantized ViTs. We evaluate our methods on popular DeiT and Swin backbones. Extensive experimental results show that our method achieves a much better performance than the prior arts. For example, our Q-ViT can theoretically accelerates the ViT-S by 6.14x and achieves about 80.9% Top-1 accuracy, even surpassing the full-precision counterpart by 1.0% on ImageNet dataset. Our codes and models are attached on https://github.com/YanjingLi0202/Q-ViT

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be expensive to deploy on devices with limited memory and computation. Quantization reduces the precision used to represent and process values, but low-bit versions can lose substantial accuracy. This paper investigates where that loss comes from and identifies distorted information in quantized self-attention maps as a central bottleneck.

Q-ViT addresses that distortion with an information rectification module and a distribution-guided distillation scheme. These components are designed to preserve the information needed by attention despite the reduced numerical precision. The resulting approach produces fully quantized Vision Transformers, connecting the compression method to the specific internal computation found to cause difficulty.

Experiments on DeiT and Swin backbones report substantially better performance than prior approaches. One example reaches about 80.9% ImageNet Top-1 accuracy and exceeds its full-precision counterpart by a reported 1.0%. The same example has a theoretical 6.14-fold acceleration for ViT-S; this is a theoretical speedup rather than a stated device measurement. The results show that carefully addressing attention distortion can make aggressive quantization compatible with strong accuracy.
summary.tldr: Q-ViT targets distortion in quantized attention to produce accurate, fully quantized low-bit Vision Transformers.

title: Q-ViT: Accurate and Fully Quantized Low-bit Vision Transformer

abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. paragraphs: Transformers can draw on information stored during training while also adapting to information in their current context. This paper investigates how those two abilities develop together. The authors use a synthetic task in which token transitions come from either a global bigram distribution or a context-specific one. A bigram describes a relationship between successive tokens, giving the study a controlled way to separate the two information sources.

Through empirical analysis of a simplified two-layer transformer, the authors find that global bigram relationships are learned quickly. A mechanism called an induction head develops more slowly and supports the use of context-specific bigrams. The training process therefore reveals different learning timescales for information shared across examples and information supplied within the current context.

The paper interprets weight matrices as associative memories and gives theoretical insights into how gradients build those memories. It also studies how properties of the data distribution affect learning. These results offer a mechanistic account within the synthetic setup, helping explain how stored associations and contextual adaptation can emerge during transformer training.
summary.tldr: A controlled two-layer transformer study finds that global token associations develop before the induction-head mechanism for context-specific associations.

title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint

abstract: The goal of zero-shot human-AI coordination is to develop an agent that can collaborate with humans without relying on human data. Prevailing two-stage population-based methods require a diverse population of mutually distinct policies to simulate diverse human behaviors. The necessity of such populations severely limits their computational efficiency. To address this issue, we propose E3T, an **E**fficient **E**nd-to-**E**nd **T**raining approach for zero-shot human-AI coordination. E3T employs a mixture of ego policy and random policy to construct the partner policy, making it both coordination-skilled and diverse. In this way, the ego agent is end-to-end trained with this mixture policy without the need of a pre-trained population, thus significantly improving the training efficiency. In addition, a partner modeling module is proposed to predict the partner's action from historical information. With the predicted partner's action, the ego policy is able to adapt its policy and take actions accordingly when collaborating with humans of different behavior patterns. Empirical results on the Overcooked environment show that our method significantly improves the training efficiency while preserving comparable or superior performance than the population-based baselines. Demo videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/e3t-overcooked.

paragraphs: Training an AI to cooperate with unfamiliar humans without human training data requires exposing it to different partner behaviors. Existing population-based approaches do this by first building a collection of distinct policies. E3T addresses the computational expense of that preparation by training the cooperating agent directly with a partner policy constructed during the learning process.

That partner combines the agent's own policy with a random policy. The mixture supplies both coordination ability and behavioral variety without requiring a separately pretrained population. E3T also includes a partner-modeling component that predicts the partner's next action using historical information. The agent can use this prediction to adjust its actions when facing different patterns of human behavior.

Experiments in Overcooked show substantially improved training efficiency while maintaining performance comparable to or better than the population-based baselines. The result supports the use of a simple mixture as a practical source of partner diversity in this setting. Partner prediction adds a complementary mechanism for responding to the particular collaborator encountered during execution.
summary.tldr: E3T trains agents with mixed self-and-random partners, improving training efficiency for human–AI coordination in Overcooked.

title: An Efficient End-to-End Training Approach for Zero-Shot Human-AI Coordination

abstract: Previous endeavors in self-supervised learning have enlightened the research of deep clustering from an instance discrimination perspective. Built upon this foundation, recent studies further highlight the importance of grouping semantically similar instances. One effective method to achieve this is by promoting the semantic structure preserved by neighborhood consistency. However, the samples in the local neighborhood may be limited due to their close proximity to each other, which may not provide substantial and diverse supervision signals. Inspired by the versatile re-ranking methods in the context of image retrieval, we propose to employ an efficient online re-ranking process to mine more informative neighbors in a Contextually Affinitive (ConAff) Neighborhood, and then encourage the cross-view neighborhood consistency. To further mitigate the intrinsic neighborhood noises near cluster boundaries, we propose a progressively relaxed boundary filtering strategy to circumvent the issues brought by noisy neighbors. Our method can be easily integrated into the generic self-supervised frameworks and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on several popular benchmarks.

paragraphs: Deep clustering seeks meaningful groups using learned representations. Recent approaches encourage nearby examples to have consistent semantic structure, building on self-supervised methods that distinguish individual instances. However, an immediate neighborhood can contain closely similar examples that offer limited diversity. The paper asks how to obtain more informative supervision from the choice of neighbors.

The proposed Contextually Affinitive Neighborhood uses an efficient online re-ranking procedure inspired by image retrieval. It mines informative neighbors and encourages neighborhood consistency across different views. This changes which relationships guide representation learning, rather than relying exclusively on the closest examples in the current representation.

Neighbors near cluster boundaries can also be misleading. A progressively relaxed boundary filter addresses this noise while the neighborhood-based learning proceeds. The method integrates into general self-supervised frameworks and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several evaluated benchmarks. Its contribution combines two complementary adjustments: making neighborhoods more informative and reducing the influence of unreliable relationships around group boundaries.
summary.tldr: The method improves deep clustering by re-ranking informative neighbors and filtering noisy relationships near cluster boundaries.

title: Contextually Affinitive Neighborhood Refinery for Deep Clustering

abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) methods such as approximate Bayesian computation (ABC), synthetic likelihood, and neural posterior estimation (NPE) rely on simulating statistics to infer parameters of intractable likelihood models. However, such methods are known to yield untrustworthy and misleading inference outcomes under model misspecification, thus hindering their widespread applicability. In this work, we propose the first general approach to handle model misspecification that works across different classes of SBI methods. Leveraging the fact that the choice of statistics determines the degree of misspecification in SBI, we introduce a regularized loss function that penalizes those statistics that increase the mismatch between the data and the model. Taking NPE and ABC as use cases, we demonstrate the superior performance of our method on high-dimensional time-series models that are artificially misspecified. We also apply our method to real data from the field of radio propagation where the model is known to be misspecified. We show empirically that the method yields robust inference in misspecified scenarios, whilst still being accurate when the model is well-specified.

Leveraging the fact that the choice of statistics determines the degree of misspecification in SBI, we introduce a regularized loss function that penalizes those statistics that increase the mismatch between the data and the model. Taking NPE and ABC as use cases, we demonstrate the superior performance of our method on high-dimensional time-series models that are artificially misspecified.
