paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates model parameters by comparing observed data with simulated information when likelihood calculations are intractable. If the simulator is misspecified, those comparisons can lead to misleading conclusions. This paper focuses on the statistics used for comparison, because their choice affects how strongly the mismatch between the simulator and observations appears in inference.

The proposed approach learns statistics with a regularized loss that penalizes statistics contributing to greater data-model mismatch. This makes robustness part of the representation-learning objective. The method is intended to work across different classes of simulation-based inference, and the authors demonstrate it using neural posterior estimation and approximate Bayesian computation as two distinct use cases.

Experiments involve high-dimensional time-series models with deliberately introduced misspecification, along with real radio-propagation data whose model is known to be misspecified. The authors report superior performance on the artificial cases and robust inference across the studied misspecified settings. They also find that accuracy is maintained when the model is well specified, supporting the value of learning statistics that are less sensitive to model mismatch.
summary.tldr: Learning statistics with a mismatch penalty improves empirical robustness of simulation-based inference when the simulator does not accurately represent the data.

title: Learning Robust Statistics for Simulation-based Inference under Model Misspecification

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have recently emerged as promising models of the ventral visual stream, despite their lack of biological specificity.While current state-of-the-art models of the primary visual cortex (V1) have surfaced from training with adversarial examples and extensively augmented data, these models are still unable to explain key neural properties observed in V1 that arise from biological circuitry.To address this gap, we systematically incorporated neuroscience-derived architectural components into CNNs to identify a set of mechanisms and architectures that more comprehensively explain V1 activity.Upon enhancing task-driven CNNs with architectural components that simulate center-surround antagonism, local receptive fields, tuned normalization, and cortical magnification, we uncover models with latent representations that yield state-of-the-art explanation of V1 neural activity and tuning properties.Moreover, analyses of the learned parameters of these components and stimuli that maximally activate neurons of the evaluated networks provide support for their role in explaining neural properties of V1.Our results highlight an important advancement in the field of NeuroAI, as we systematically establish a set of architectural components that contribute to unprecedented explanation of V1.The neuroscience insights that could be gleaned from increasingly accurate in-silico models of the brain have the potential to greatly advance the fields of both neuroscience and artificial intelligence.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can model aspects of the visual system, yet strong task performance does not automatically explain properties of the primary visual cortex, V1. The paper focuses on neural properties associated with biological circuitry that remain inadequately explained by models trained with adversarial examples or extensive data augmentation.

The authors systematically add neuroscience-inspired architectural components to task-trained CNNs. These components simulate center-surround antagonism, local receptive fields, tuned normalization, and cortical magnification. The aim is to determine which mechanisms help the networks’ internal representations account for V1 activity and tuning, making biological structure part of the model design.

The resulting models achieve state-of-the-art explanation of V1 neural activity and tuning properties in the reported evaluation. Analyses of learned component parameters and stimuli that maximally activate network neurons provide additional support for the components’ explanatory roles. The findings establish a useful set of architectural mechanisms for modeling V1, while the broader prospect of advancing neuroscience and AI through increasingly accurate computational brain models remains a potential implication.
summary.tldr: Adding specific biologically inspired components to CNNs improves their explanation of V1 neural activity and tuning properties.

title: Explaining V1 Properties with a Biologically Constrained Deep Learning Architecture

abstract: Neural posterior estimation methods based on discrete normalizing flows have become established tools for simulation-based inference (SBI), but scaling them to high-dimensional problems can be challenging. Building on recent advances in generative modeling, we here present flow matching posterior estimation (FMPE), a technique for SBI using continuous normalizing flows. Like diffusion models, and in contrast to discrete flows, flow matching allows for unconstrained architectures, providing enhanced flexibility for complex data modalities. Flow matching, therefore, enables exact density evaluation, fast training, and seamless scalability to large architectures---making it ideal for SBI. We show that FMPE achieves competitive performance on an established SBI benchmark, and then demonstrate its improved scalability on a challenging scientific problem: for gravitational-wave inference, FMPE outperforms methods based on comparable discrete flows, reducing training time by 30\% with substantially improved accuracy. Our work underscores the potential of FMPE to enhance performance in challenging inference scenarios, thereby paving the way for more advanced applications to scientific problems.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses simulated data to infer which underlying parameters could explain observations. Neural posterior estimation with discrete normalizing flows is an established approach, but scaling these models to high-dimensional problems can be difficult. This paper introduces flow matching posterior estimation, or FMPE, using continuous normalizing flows.

The approach draws on advances in generative modeling to allow more flexible architectures. Like diffusion models, flow matching avoids the architectural restrictions associated with discrete flows. The authors emphasize the combination of exact density evaluation, fast training, and compatibility with large architectures, which makes the approach attractive for complex scientific data.

FMPE performs competitively on an established simulation-based inference benchmark. In a more demanding gravitational-wave inference application, it outperforms comparable discrete-flow methods, reducing training time by 30% while substantially improving accuracy. This application provides evidence for improved scalability in a challenging scientific setting. The broader significance is the potential to expand neural posterior estimation to harder inference problems through a more flexible model family.
summary.tldr: FMPE uses continuous flows for scalable posterior estimation, improving accuracy and cutting training time by 30% in gravitational-wave inference.

title: Flow Matching for Scalable Simulation-Based Inference

abstract: Feature selection (FS) plays an important role in machine learning, which extracts important features and accelerates the learning process. In this paper, we propose a deep FS method that simultaneously conducts feature selection and differentiable $ k $-NN graph learning based on the Dirichlet Energy. The Dirichlet Energy identifies important features by measuring their smoothness on the graph structure, and facilitates the learning of a new graph that reflects the inherent structure in new feature subspace. We employ Optimal Transport theory to address the non-differentiability issue of learning $ k $-NN graphs in neural networks, which theoretically makes our method applicable to other graph neural networks for dynamic graph learning. Furthermore, the proposed framework is interpretable, since all modules are designed algorithmically. We validate the effectiveness of our model with extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We employ Optimal Transport theory to address the non-differentiability issue of learning $ k $-NN graphs in neural networks, which theoretically makes our method applicable to other graph neural networks for dynamic graph learning. Furthermore, the proposed framework is interpretable, since all modules are designed algorithmically. We validate the effectiveness of our model with extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Feature selection aims to retain useful input properties and make learning more efficient. This paper couples that selection with learning a nearest-neighbor graph. The two decisions are connected: the chosen features affect which samples appear similar, while the graph provides structure for judging which features are informative.

Dirichlet energy links the two parts by measuring how smoothly feature values vary over the graph. The method uses this measure to identify important features and to learn a graph that reflects relationships in the resulting feature subspace. Because constructing a nearest-neighbor graph creates a nondifferentiability problem, the authors use optimal transport theory to make graph learning compatible with neural-network training.

The paper states that this construction is theoretically applicable to dynamic graph learning in other graph neural networks. It also describes the framework as interpretable because its modules are designed algorithmically. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate its effectiveness. The central contribution is a coordinated procedure in which feature selection and graph construction can improve together during learning.
summary.tldr: The method jointly selects features and learns a differentiable nearest-neighbor graph using Dirichlet energy and optimal transport.

title: Joint Feature and Differentiable $ k $-NN Graph Learning using Dirichlet Energy

abstract: Given a set of $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the goal of the \emph{determinant maximization} problem is to pick $k$ vectors with the maximum volume. Determinant maximization is the MAP-inference task for determinantal point processes (DPP) and has recently received considerable attention for modeling diversity. As most applications for the problem use large amounts of data, this problem has been studied in the relevant \textit{composable coreset} setting.In particular, [Indyk-Mahabadi-OveisGharan-Rezaei--SODA'20, ICML'19] showed that one can get composable coresets with optimal approximation factor of $\tilde O(k)^k$ for the problem, and that a local search algorithm achieves an almost optimal approximation guarantee of $O(k)^{2k}$.In this work, we show that the widely-used Greedy algorithm also provides composable coresets with an almost optimal approximation factor of $O(k)^{3k}$, which improves over the previously known guarantee of $C^{k^2}$, and supports the prior experimental results showing the practicality of the greedy algorithm as a coreset.Our main result follows by showing a local optimality property for Greedy:swapping a single point from the greedy solution with a vector that was not picked by the greedy algorithm can increase the volume by a factor of at most $(1+\sqrt{k})$. This is tight up to the additive constant $1$. Finally, our experiments show that the local optimality of the greedy algorithm is even lower than the theoretical bound on real data sets.

paragraphs: Determinant maximization selects k vectors whose associated volume is as large as possible. It provides a mathematical way to model diversity and is also the maximum-probability inference problem for determinantal point processes. For large datasets, the paper studies composable coresets: smaller selections that can be combined while retaining an approximation guarantee.

The main result strengthens the theoretical case for the widely used greedy algorithm. Its composable coreset approximation factor improves from the previously established C^(k²) guarantee to O(k)^(3k). The authors describe this as almost optimal relative to the known optimal scale of Õ(k)^k. This supports earlier experimental evidence that greedy selection is practical in this setting.

The proof centers on a local property: replacing one selected vector with an unselected vector can increase volume by at most a factor of 1 + √k. This bound is tight apart from the additive one. On real datasets, the experiments find smaller local improvement factors than the worst-case bound allows. The theoretical and empirical findings together explain why a simple greedy construction can produce useful summaries for diversity selection.
summary.tldr: A sharper analysis shows that greedy selection yields almost-optimal composable coresets for determinant maximization.

title: Composable Coresets for Determinant Maximization: Greedy is Almost Optimal

abstract: We present a discretization-free scalable framework for solving a large class of mass-conserving partial differential equations (PDEs), including the time-dependent Fokker-Planck equation and the Wasserstein gradient flow. The main observation is that the time-varying velocity field of the PDE solution needs to be self-consistent: it must satisfy a fixed-point equation involving the probability flow characterized by the same velocity field. Instead of directly minimizing the residual of the fixed-point equation with neural parameterization, we use an iterative formulation with a biased gradient estimator that bypasses significant computational obstacles with strong empirical performance. Compared to existing approaches, our method does not suffer from temporal or spatial discretization, covers a wider range of PDEs, and scales to high dimensions. Experimentally, our method recovers analytical solutions accurately when they are available and achieves superior performance in high dimensions with less training time compared to alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper tackles mass-conserving partial differential equations by viewing their solutions as evolving probability distributions. Its scope includes time-dependent Fokker-Planck equations and Wasserstein gradient flows. The aim is a scalable method that avoids temporal and spatial discretization, which can make solving these equations difficult in high dimensions.

The key idea is self-consistency: a velocity field moves a probability distribution, and that resulting probability flow must agree with the equation defining the same velocity field. This produces a fixed-point condition. Rather than directly minimizing its residual with a neural representation, the authors develop an iterative formulation using a biased gradient estimator.

That choice bypasses substantial computational obstacles and performs strongly in the reported experiments. The method accurately recovers analytical solutions where these are available and outperforms alternatives in high-dimensional problems with less training time. Its significance lies in replacing a direct residual-minimization problem with a practical self-consistency iteration. The empirical success does not change the explicitly stated fact that the gradient estimator is biased.
summary.tldr: Self-consistent velocity matching solves a broad class of mass-conserving PDEs through scalable probability-flow iterations without spatial or temporal discretization.

title: Self-Consistent Velocity Matching of Probability Flows

abstract: A growing line of work shows how learned predictions can be used to break through worst-case barriers to improve the running time of an algorithm. However, incorporating predictions into data structures with strong theoretical guarantees remains underdeveloped. This paper takes a step in this direction by showing that predictions can be leveraged in the fundamental online list labeling problem. In the problem, $n$ items arrive over time and must be stored in sorted order in an array of size $\Theta(n)$. The array slot of an element is its label and the goal is to maintain sorted order while minimizing the total number of elements moved (i.e., relabeled). We design a new list labeling data structure and bound its performance in two models. In the worst-case learning-augmented model, we give guarantees in terms of the error in the predictions. Our data structure provides strong guarantees: it is optimal for any prediction error and guarantees the best-known worst-case bound even when the predictions are entirely erroneous. We also consider a stochastic error model and bound the performance in terms of the expectation and variance of the error. Finally, the theoretical results are demonstrated empirically. In particular, we show that our data structure has strong performance on real temporal data sets where predictions are constructed from elements that arrived in the past, as is typically done in a practical use case.

paragraphs: Online list labeling stores arriving items in sorted order inside an array whose size is proportional to the number of items. An item's array position serves as its label. Inserting new items can require moving existing ones, so the goal is to minimize those moves while continuously maintaining sorted order.

This paper designs a data structure that uses predictions and analyzes how its performance depends on their errors. In a worst-case model, it provides guarantees optimal for any prediction error while retaining the best-known worst-case bound even when predictions are entirely wrong. This combines the possibility of gains from useful forecasts with a stated fallback guarantee under unreliable ones.

Empirical results support the theoretical analysis on real temporal datasets, where predictions are built from previously arrived elements. That setup connects the analysis to a practical forecasting pattern: past arrivals supply information for future insertions without requiring predictions to be perfect.
summary.tldr: A prediction-aware sorted-array data structure gains error-dependent guarantees while retaining the best-known worst-case bound when predictions fail.

title: Online List Labeling with Predictions

abstract: Histology imaging is an important tool in medical diagnosis and research, enabling the examination of tissue structure and composition at the microscopic level. Understanding the underlying molecular mechanisms of tissue architecture is critical in uncovering disease mechanisms and developing effective treatments.Gene expression profiling provides insight into the molecular processes underlying tissue architecture, but the process can be time-consuming and expensive. We present BLEEP (Bi-modaL Embedding for Expression Prediction), a bi-modal embedding framework capable of generating spatially resolved gene expression profiles of whole-slide Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained histology images. BLEEP uses contrastive learning to construct a low-dimensional joint embedding space from a reference dataset using paired image and expression profiles at micrometer resolution. With this approach, the gene expression of any query image patch can be imputed using the expression profiles from the reference dataset. We demonstrate BLEEP’s effectiveness in gene expression prediction by benchmarking its performance on a human liver tissue dataset captured using the 10x Visium platform, where it achieves significant improvements over existing methods. Our results demonstrate the potential of BLEEP to provide insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying tissue architecture, with important implications in diagnosis and research of various diseases. The proposed approach can significantly reduce the time and cost associated with gene expression profiling, opening up new avenues for high-throughput analysis of histology images for both research and clinical applications.

paragraphs: Histology images reveal tissue structure, while gene-expression measurements provide information about the molecular processes associated with that structure. Collecting expression profiles can be costly and time-consuming. BLEEP aims to predict spatially resolved expression from whole-slide H&E-stained tissue images by learning the relationship between these two forms of evidence.

The framework trains on a reference dataset containing paired image patches and expression profiles at micrometer resolution. Contrastive learning places both modalities in a shared, low-dimensional representation space. For a new image patch, expression is imputed using profiles from the reference dataset, connecting visible tissue appearance to previously measured molecular information.

The authors evaluate BLEEP on human liver tissue data collected with the 10x Visium platform and report significant improvements over existing prediction methods. These results support the potential for image-based expression prediction to make molecular analysis more accessible and less expensive. The reported evaluation establishes performance in that tissue dataset, while broader diagnostic and research applications are presented as opportunities enabled by the approach.
summary.tldr: BLEEP learns a shared representation of tissue images and gene-expression profiles to predict spatial expression from histology.

title: Spatially Resolved Gene Expression Prediction from Histology Images via Bi-modal Contrastive Learning

abstract: In this paper, we introduce Randomized Q-learning (RandQL), a novel randomized model-free algorithm for regret minimization in episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). To the best of our knowledge, RandQL is the first tractable model-free posterior sampling-based algorithm. We analyze the performance of RandQL in both tabular and non-tabular metric space settings. In tabular MDPs, RandQL achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^{5}SAT})$, where $H$ is the planning horizon, $S$ is the number of states, $A$ is the number of actions, and $T$ is the number of episodes. For a metric state-action space, RandQL enjoys a regret bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(H^{5/2} T^{(d_z+1)/(d_z+2)})$, where $d_z$ denotes the zooming dimension. Notably, RandQL achieves optimistic exploration without using bonuses, relying instead on a novel idea of learning rate randomization. Our empirical study shows that RandQL outperforms existing approaches on baseline exploration environments.

In tabular MDPs, RandQL achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^{5}SAT})$, where $H$ is the planning horizon, $S$ is the number of states, $A$ is the number of actions, and $T$ is the number of episodes. paragraphs: Randomized Q-learning, or RandQL, is a model-free algorithm for learning through repeated episodes while limiting regret. The authors present it as, to their knowledge, the first tractable model-free algorithm based on posterior sampling. Its defining mechanism is to randomize learning rates, creating optimistic exploration without adding explicit exploration bonuses.

The paper analyzes both tabular environments and settings with a metric state-action space. In the tabular case, the regret bound is approximately the square root of H⁵SAT, up to logarithmic factors. H is the planning horizon, S and A count states and actions, and T counts episodes. This expresses how the guarantee depends on both problem size and accumulated experience.

For metric spaces, the bound is approximately H^(5/2) T^((d_z+1)/(d_z+2)), again suppressing logarithmic factors, where d_z is the zooming dimension. Thus, the analysis extends beyond finite lookup-table representations and relates performance to the metric setting’s complexity. Experiments on baseline exploration environments show RandQL outperforming existing approaches, supporting learning-rate randomization as a practical exploration mechanism.
summary.tldr: RandQL randomizes learning rates to achieve bonus-free optimistic exploration, with regret guarantees in tabular and metric-space environments.

title: Model-free Posterior Sampling via Learning Rate Randomization

abstract: We derive upper bounds for random design linear regression with dependent ($\beta$-mixing) data absent any realizability assumptions. In contrast to the strictly realizable martingale noise regime, no sharp \emph{instance-optimal} non-asymptotics are available in the literature. Up to constant factors, our analysis correctly recovers the variance term predicted by the Central Limit Theorem---the noise level of the problem---and thus exhibits graceful degradation as we introduce misspecification. Past a burn-in, our result is sharp in the moderate deviations regime, and in particular does not inflate the leading order term by mixing time factors.
originalAbstract: We derive upper bounds for random design linear regression with dependent ($\beta$-mixing) data absent any realizability assumptions. In contrast to the strictly realizable martingale noise regime, no sharp \emph{instance-optimal} non-asymptotics are available in the literature. Up to constant factors, our analysis correctly recovers the variance term predicted by the Central Limit Theorem---the noise level of the problem---and thus exhibits graceful degradation as we introduce misspecification. paragraphs: This paper analyzes linear regression when observations are dependent and a linear model need not exactly describe the data. It studies random-design regression under beta-mixing dependence and derives finite-sample upper bounds. Allowing misspecification matters because the analysis must accommodate errors beyond the strictly realizable martingale-noise setting.

The main result recovers, up to constant factors, the variance term predicted by the Central Limit Theorem. That term represents the problem's noise level. Matching it gives the bound a connection to the particular statistical instance, and the analysis degrades gracefully as misspecification is introduced into the regression problem.

The sharpness claim applies after a burn-in and in the moderate-deviations regime. Within that regime, the leading-order term is not inflated by mixing-time factors. These qualifications define where the result is strongest. The contribution is a more precise account of regression error with dependent data, showing that the leading noise term can retain the appropriate scale even without assuming that the linear model is exactly correct.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sharp regression bounds for dependent, potentially misspecified data that recover the appropriate leading noise term after a burn-in.

title: The noise level in linear regression with dependent data

abstract: Sign language translation (SLT) aims to convert a continuous sign language video clip into a spoken language. Considering different geographic regions generally have their own native sign languages, it is valuable to establish corresponding SLT datasets to support related communication and research. Auslan, as a sign language specific to Australia, still lacks a dedicated large-scale dataset for SLT.To fill this gap, we curate an Australian Sign Language translation dataset, dubbed Auslan-Daily, which is collected from the Auslan educational TV series and Auslan TV programs. The former involves daily communications among multiple signers in the wild, while the latter comprises sign language videos for up-to-date news, weather forecasts, and documentaries. In particular, Auslan-Daily has two main features: (1) the topics are diverse and signed by multiple signers, and (2) the scenes in our dataset are more complex, e.g., captured in various environments, gesture interference during multi-signers' interactions and various camera positions. With a collection of more than 45 hours of high-quality Auslan video materials, we invite Auslan experts to align different fine-grained visual and language pairs, including video $\leftrightarrow$ fingerspelling, video $\leftrightarrow$ gloss, and video $\leftrightarrow$ sentence. As a result, Auslan-Daily contains multi-grained annotations that can be utilized to accomplish various fundamental sign language tasks, such as signer detection, sign spotting, fingerspelling detection, isolated sign language recognition, sign language translation and alignment. Moreover, we benchmark results with state-of-the-art models for each task in Auslan-Daily. Experiments indicate that Auslan-Daily is a highly challenging SLT dataset, and we hope this dataset will contribute to the development of Auslan and the advancement of sign languages worldwide in a broader context. All datasets and benchmarks are available at Auslan-Daily.

paragraphs: Sign language translation requires interpreting continuous signing and connecting it to spoken language. Because sign languages differ across geographic regions, progress depends on datasets for the particular language being studied. This paper introduces Auslan-Daily to address the lack of a dedicated large-scale translation dataset for Australian Sign Language.

The collection contains more than 45 hours of video from educational television and Auslan television programs. It spans everyday interactions, news, weather, and documentaries, with multiple signers and varied environments. Camera positions and interference from gestures during interactions add complexity. Auslan experts align video with fingerspelling, gloss annotations, and sentences, providing several levels of language supervision.

Those annotations support tasks ranging from detecting signers and locating signs to recognizing isolated signs and translating continuous sequences. The authors benchmark state-of-the-art models for the different tasks and find the dataset highly challenging. Its contribution is therefore both a substantial Auslan resource and a shared evaluation setting, allowing researchers to study related visual and language problems using coordinated annotations.
summary.tldr: Auslan-Daily provides over 45 hours of diverse, expert-annotated Australian Sign Language video and challenging benchmarks for multiple signing tasks.

title: Auslan-Daily: Australian Sign Language Translation for Daily Communication and News

abstract: Recently, Deep Image Prior (DIP) has emerged as an effective unsupervised one-shot learner, delivering competitive results across various image recovery problems. This method only requires the noisy measurements and a forward operator, relying solely on deep networks initialized with random noise to learn and restore the structure of the data. However, DIP is notorious for its vulnerability to overfitting due to the overparameterization of the network. This method progressively denoises and reconstructs the image through a sequential optimization of network weights. This is achieved using an input-adaptive DIP objective, combined with an autoencoding regularization term. Compared to diffusion models, our method does not require training data and outperforms other DIP-based methods in mitigating noise overfitting while maintaining a similar number of parameter updates as Vanilla DIP. Through extensive experiments, we validate the effectiveness of our method in various image reconstruction tasks, such as MRI and CT reconstruction, as well as in image restoration tasks like image denoising, inpainting, and non-linear deblurring.

abstract: The lack of transparency in the decision-making processes of deep learning systems presents a significant challenge in modern artificial intelligence (AI), as it impairs users’ ability to rely on and verify these systems. To address this challenge, Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) have made significant progress by incorporating human-interpretable concepts into deep learning architectures. This approach allows predictions to be traced back to specific concept patterns that users can understand and potentially intervene on. However, existing CBMs’ task predictors are not fully interpretable, preventing a thorough analysis and any form of formal verification of their decision-making process prior to deployment, thereby raising significant reliability concerns. To bridge this gap, we introduce Concept-based Memory Reasoner (CMR), a novel CBM designed to provide a human-understandable and provably-verifiable task prediction process. Our approach is to model each task prediction as a neural selection mechanism over a memory of learnable logic rules, followed by a symbolic evaluation of the selected rule. The presence of an explicit memory and the symbolic evaluation allow domain experts to inspect and formally verify the validity of certain global properties of interest for the task prediction process. Experimental results demonstrate that CMR achieves better accuracy-interpretability trade-offs to state-of-the-art CBMs, discovers logic rules consistent with ground truths, allows for rule interventions, and allows pre-deployment verification.

The model also discovers rules consistent with ground truths and permits rule interventions and verification before deployment. The contribution is an architecture that makes the rule-based prediction process inspectable and supports checking specified properties; the abstract’s verification claim concerns those properties rather than an unrestricted guarantee about every aspect of the system.
summary.tldr: A memory of learned logical rules makes concept-based predictions inspectable, editable, and amenable to formal verification of specified properties.

title: Interpretable Concept-Based Memory Reasoning

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the dynamics in the topology of time-evolving point clouds, the prevalent spatiotemporal model for systems exhibiting collective behavior, such as swarms of insects and birds or particles in physics. In such systems, patterns emerge from (local) interactions among self-propelled entities. While several well-understood governing equations for motion and interaction exist, they are notoriously difficult to fit to data, as most prior work requires knowledge about individual motion trajectories, i.e., a requirement that is challenging to satisfy with an increasing number of entities. To evade such confounding factors, we investigate collective behavior from a _topological perspective_, but instead of summarizing entire observation sequences (as done previously), we propose learning a latent dynamical model from topological features _per time point_. The latter is then used to formulate a downstream regression task to predict the parametrization of some a priori specified governing equation. We implement this idea based on a latent ODE learned from vectorized (static) persistence diagrams and show that a combination of recent stability results for persistent homology justifies this modeling choice. Various (ablation) experiments not only demonstrate the relevance of each model component but provide compelling empirical evidence that our proposed model -- _Neural Persistence Dynamics_ -- substantially outperforms the state-of-the-art across a diverse set of parameter regression tasks.

paragraphs: Collective systems such as swarms and interacting particles can be observed as point clouds changing over time. Inferring the parameters of their governing equations is difficult when methods require tracking every individual trajectory. Neural Persistence Dynamics instead studies how the topology of the whole point cloud evolves.

The method extracts topological features separately at each observation time, using vectorized persistence diagrams. It then learns a latent ordinary differential equation describing their temporal evolution. This preserves a time-resolved account of collective structure rather than compressing an entire sequence into a single summary. The learned dynamics feed a regression task that predicts parameters of a governing equation specified in advance.

The authors connect their modeling choice to stability results for persistent homology and evaluate its components through ablation experiments. Across diverse parameter-regression tasks, they report substantial improvements over the state of the art. The approach offers a route from changing group structure to physical parameters without relying on individual motion trajectories, while retaining the requirement that the family of governing equations be chosen beforehand.
summary.tldr: Neural Persistence Dynamics learns evolving topological structure to estimate collective-motion parameters without tracking individual trajectories.

title: Neural Persistence Dynamics

abstract: The problem of benign overfitting asks whether it is possible for a model to perfectly fit noisy training data and still generalize well. We study benign overfitting in two-layer leaky ReLU networks trained with the hinge loss on a binary classification task. We consider input data which can be decomposed into the sum of a common signal and a random noise component, which lie on subspaces orthogonal to one another. We characterize conditions on the signal to noise ratio (SNR) of the model parameters giving rise to benign versus non-benign, or harmful, overfitting: in particular, if the SNR is high then benign overfitting occurs, conversely if the SNR is low then harmful overfitting occurs. We attribute both benign and non-benign overfitting to an approximate margin maximization property and show that leaky ReLU networks trained on hinge loss with gradient descent (GD) satisfy this property. In contrast to prior work we do not require the training data to be nearly orthogonal. Notably, for input dimension $d$ and training sample size $n$, while results in prior work require $d = \Omega(n^2 \log n)$, here we require only $d = \Omega(n)$.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting occurs when a model fits noisy training data perfectly yet still predicts well on new data. This paper studies when that can happen in two-layer leaky ReLU networks trained for binary classification with hinge loss. Its data model separates each input into a shared signal and random noise occupying orthogonal subspaces.

Within this setting, the authors characterize conditions on the signal-to-noise ratio of the model parameters that distinguish benign from harmful overfitting. A sufficiently high ratio leads to benign overfitting, whereas a low ratio leads to harmful overfitting. They connect both outcomes to approximate margin maximization and show that gradient descent training with hinge loss has this property.

The analysis does not require the training examples to be nearly orthogonal. In particular, its input-dimension requirement grows linearly with the number of samples, rather than the quadratic-times-logarithmic requirement described for prior results. This extends the theory to more moderate dimensions while retaining the stated signal-and-noise structure, clarifying when fitting noise can coexist with useful generalization.
summary.tldr: Under a structured signal-and-noise model, leaky ReLU networks can overfit benignly at input dimensions that grow only linearly with sample size.

title: Benign overfitting in leaky ReLU networks with moderate input dimension

abstract: Recent analysis on the training dynamics of Transformers has unveiled an interesting characteristic: the training loss plateaus for a significant number of training steps, and then suddenly (and sharply) drops to near--optimal values. To understand this phenomenon in depth, we formulate the low-rank matrix completion problem as a masked language modeling (MLM) task, and show that it is possible to train a BERT model to solve this task to low error. Furthermore, the loss curve shows a plateau early in training followed by a sudden drop to near-optimal values, despite no changes in the training procedure or hyper-parameters. To gain interpretability insights into this sudden drop, we examine the model's predictions, attention heads, and hidden states before and after this transition. Concretely, we observe that (a) the model transitions from simply copying the masked input to accurately predicting the masked entries; (b) the attention heads transition to interpretable patterns relevant to the task; and (c) the embeddings and hidden states encode information relevant to the problem. We also analyze the training dynamics of individual model components to understand the sudden drop in loss.

paragraphs: Transformer training can appear stalled for many steps before its loss suddenly falls. This paper investigates that behavior through low-rank matrix completion: predicting missing entries in a matrix with underlying structure. The researchers express the problem as masked language modeling and show that a BERT model can learn to complete the matrix with low error.

The resulting training curve contains an early plateau followed by a sharp improvement, even though the training procedure and hyperparameters remain unchanged. This creates a concrete setting for examining what changes inside the model when performance improves abruptly. The analysis compares predictions, attention heads, embeddings, and hidden states on either side of the transition.

Before the transition, the model largely copies its masked input; afterward, it accurately predicts missing entries. Attention develops interpretable patterns relevant to matrix completion, while internal representations encode information useful for the task. The authors also examine individual components during training. Together, these observations connect the sudden loss drop to changes in task-relevant behavior within this case study.
summary.tldr: A matrix-completion case study links abrupt improvement in BERT training to emerging task-relevant attention and internal representations.

title: Abrupt Learning in Transformers: A Case Study on Matrix Completion

abstract: Recent advancements have shown promise in applying traditional Semi-Supervised Learning strategies to the task of Generalized Category Discovery (GCD). Typically, this involves a teacher-student framework in which the teacher imparts knowledge to the student to classify categories, even in the absence of explicit labels. Nevertheless, GCD presents unique challenges, particularly the absence of priors for new classes, which can lead to the teacher's misguidance and unsynchronized learning with the student, culminating in suboptimal outcomes. In our work, we delve into why traditional teacher-student designs falter in generalized category discovery as compared to their success in closed-world semi-supervised learning. We identify inconsistent pattern learning as the crux of this issue and introduce FlipClass—a method that dynamically updates the teacher to align with the student's attention, instead of maintaining a static teacher reference. Our teacher-attention-update strategy refines the teacher's focus based on student feedback, promoting consistent pattern recognition and synchronized learning across old and new classes. Extensive experiments on a spectrum of benchmarks affirm that FlipClass significantly surpasses contemporary GCD methods, establishing new standards for the field.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery requires learning about both familiar categories and new categories without explicit labels for all of them. Teacher-student methods can provide guidance in this setting, but the teacher lacks prior information about new classes. Its guidance can therefore become misaligned with what the student is learning, reducing the effectiveness of the training process.

The paper identifies inconsistent pattern learning as a central reason conventional teacher-student designs struggle here. Its proposed method, FlipClass, dynamically adjusts the teacher's attention using feedback from the student. This changes the relationship between the two models: the teacher's focus is updated to help them recognize patterns consistently across old and new categories.

Experiments across a range of benchmarks show that FlipClass significantly outperforms contemporary generalized category discovery methods. The findings support adapting the source of supervision as discovery proceeds. In a setting where the teacher has incomplete knowledge of the categories, synchronizing what teacher and student attend to can make their interaction more effective.
summary.tldr: FlipClass improves generalized category discovery by updating the teacher's attention to align with the student's learning.

title: Flipped Classroom: Aligning Teacher Attention with Student in Generalized Category Discovery

abstract: Rendering and reconstruction are long-standing topics in computer vision and graphics. Achieving both high rendering quality and accurate geometry is a challenge. Recent advancements in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled high-fidelity novel view synthesis at real-time speeds. However, the noisy and discrete nature of 3D Gaussian primitives hinders accurate surface estimation. Previous attempts to regularize 3D Gaussian normals often degrade rendering quality due to the fundamental disconnect between normal vectors and the rendering pipeline in 3DGS-based methods. Therefore, we introduce Normal-GS, a novel approach that integrates normal vectors into the 3DGS rendering pipeline. The core idea is to model the interaction between normals and incident lighting using the physically-based rendering equation. Our approach re-parameterizes surface colors as the product of normals and a designed Integrated Directional Illumination Vector (IDIV). To optimize memory usage and simplify optimization, we employ an anchor-based 3DGS to implicitly encode locally-shared IDIVs. Additionally, Normal-GS leverages optimized normals and Integrated Directional Encoding (IDE) to accurately model specular effects, enhancing both rendering quality and surface normal precision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Normal-GS achieves near state-of-the-art visual quality while obtaining accurate surface normals and preserving real-time rendering performance.

summary.tldr: Normal-GS integrates surface normals into Gaussian rendering to improve normal accuracy while retaining strong visual quality and real-time performance.

title: Normal-GS: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Normal-Involved Rendering

abstract: We introduce motion graph, a novel approach to address the video prediction problem, i.e., predicting future video frames from limited past data. The motion graph transforms patches of video frames into interconnected graph nodes, to comprehensively describe the spatial-temporal relationships among them. This representation overcomes the limitations of existing motion representations such as image differences, optical flow, and motion matrix that either fall short in capturing complex motion patterns or suffer from excessive memory consumption. We further present a video prediction pipeline empowered by motion graph, exhibiting substantial performance improvements and cost reductions. Extensive experiments on various datasets, including UCF Sports, KITTI and Cityscapes, highlight the strong representative ability of motion graph. Especially on UCF Sports, our method matches and outperforms the SOTA methods with a significant reduction in model size by 78% and a substantial decrease in GPU memory utilization by 47%.

paragraphs: Video prediction asks a model to generate future frames from a limited set of earlier observations. The representation of movement is central to that task: it must capture relationships across space and time without becoming too expensive to store or process. This paper introduces a motion graph to address that balance.

The method turns patches of video frames into connected graph nodes. Their connections describe spatial and temporal relationships among patches, providing a representation for the prediction pipeline. The authors position this approach against motion representations such as image differences, optical flow, and motion matrices, which can struggle with complex movement or require excessive memory.

Experiments on UCF Sports, KITTI, and Cityscapes support the graph representation’s ability to describe motion and improve prediction. On UCF Sports, the method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art results while reducing model size by 78% and GPU memory use by 47%. Those figures show that the reported prediction gains can accompany substantial resource savings, rather than requiring a larger model.
summary.tldr: Motion graphs represent relationships between video patches to improve future-frame prediction while reducing reported model size and memory use.

title: Motion Graph Unleashed: A Novel Approach to Video Prediction

abstract: We propose a new method named LoD-Loc for visual localization in the air. Unlike existing localization algorithms, LoD-Loc does not rely on complex 3D representations and can estimate the pose of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) using a Level-of-Detail (LoD) 3D map. LoD-Loc mainly achieves this goal by aligning the wireframe derived from the LoD projected model with that predicted by the neural network. Specifically, given a coarse pose provided by the UAV sensor, LoD-Loc hierarchically builds a cost volume for uniformly sampled pose hypotheses to describe pose probability distribution and select a pose with maximum probability. Each cost within this volume measures the degree of line alignment between projected and predicted wireframes. LoD-Loc also devises a 6-DoF pose optimization algorithm to refine the previous result with a differentiable Gaussian-Newton method. As no public dataset exists for the studied problem, we collect two datasets with map levels of LoD3.0 and LoD2.0, along with real RGB queries and ground-truth pose annotations. We benchmark our method and demonstrate that LoD-Loc achieves excellent performance, even surpassing current state-of-the-art methods that use textured 3D models for localization. The code and dataset will be made available upon publication.

paragraphs: LoD-Loc estimates a drone’s position and orientation using a Level-of-Detail 3D map. Its central idea is to compare geometric outlines: a wireframe projected from the map is aligned with a wireframe predicted from the camera image by a neural network. This allows localization without relying on a complex textured representation of the scene.

The method starts with a coarse pose supplied by the drone’s sensor. It hierarchically evaluates uniformly sampled candidate poses, assigning costs according to how well their projected lines align with the predicted image wireframe. The resulting cost volume represents pose probabilities. After choosing the most probable pose, a differentiable optimization procedure refines all six position-and-orientation degrees of freedom.

The researchers collect two datasets with LoD3.0 and LoD2.0 maps, real RGB images, and reference poses because no public dataset covered this problem. Their benchmark results show strong localization performance, including improvements over leading methods using textured 3D models. The findings support geometric line alignment as an effective basis for aerial localization given a coarse starting pose.
summary.tldr: LoD-Loc refines a drone’s coarse pose by aligning image-predicted wireframes with projections from a simplified 3D map.

title: LoD-Loc: Aerial Visual Localization using LoD 3D Map with Neural Wireframe Alignment

abstract: Genetic variants (GVs) are defined as differences in the DNA sequences among individuals and play a crucial role in diagnosing and treating genetic diseases. The rapid decrease in next generation sequencing cost, analogous to Moore’s Law, has led to an exponential increase in the availability of patient-level GV data. This growth poses a challenge for clinicians who must efficiently prioritize patient-specific GVs and integrate them with existing genomic databases to inform patient management. To addressing the interpretation of GVs, genomic foundation models (GFMs) have emerged. However, these models lack standardized performance assessments, leading to considerable variability in model evaluations. This poses the question: *How effectively do deep learning methods classify unknown GVs and align them with clinically-verified GVs?* We argue that representation learning, which transforms raw data into meaningful feature spaces, is an effective approach for addressing both indexing and classification challenges. We introduce a large-scale Genetic Variant dataset, named $\textsf{GV-Rep}$, featuring variable-length contexts and detailed annotations, designed for deep learning models to learn GV representations across various traits, diseases, tissue types, and experimental contexts. Our contributions are three-fold: (i) $\textbf{Construction}$ of a comprehensive dataset with 7 million records, each labeled with characteristics of the corresponding variants, alongside additional data from 17,548 gene knockout tests across 1,107 cell types, 1,808 variant combinations, and 156 unique clinically-verified GVs from real-world patients. (ii) $\textbf{Analysis}$ of the structure and properties of the dataset. (iii) $\textbf{Experimentation}$ of the dataset with pre-trained genomic foundation models (GFMs). The results highlight a significant disparity between the current capabilities of GFMs and the accurate representation of GVs. We hope this dataset will advance genomic deep learning to bridge this gap.

Genomic foundation models are being developed for this purpose, but inconsistent evaluation makes their capabilities difficult to assess. GV-Rep introduces a large dataset focused on learning useful representations for variant indexing and classification.

The dataset contains seven million annotated records with variable-length contexts spanning traits, diseases, tissues, and experimental settings. Additional data include 17,548 gene knockout tests across 1,107 cell types, 1,808 variant combinations, and 156 distinct clinically verified variants from patients. This collection brings several kinds of information into the study of how variants are represented.

The authors analyze the dataset’s structure and evaluate pretrained genomic foundation models on it. Their results reveal a substantial gap between current model capabilities and accurate genetic-variant representation. The contribution is therefore both a resource and an assessment: it supplies material for developing representations while showing that existing models have significant room to improve on the intended task.
summary.tldr: GV-Rep provides seven million annotated genetic-variant records and exposes substantial gaps in existing genomic foundation models’ representations.

title: GV-Rep: A Large-Scale Dataset for Genetic Variant Representation Learning

abstract: Remote physiological sensing is an evolving area of research. As systems approach clinical precision, there is increasing focus on complex applications such as cognitive state estimation. Hence, there is a need for large datasets that facilitate research into complex downstream tasks such as remote cognitive load estimation. A first-of-its-kind, our paper introduces an open-source multimodal multi-vital sign dataset consisting of concurrent recordings from RGB, NIR (near-infrared), thermal, and RF (radio-frequency) sensors alongside contact-based physiological signals, such as pulse oximeter and chest bands, providing a benchmark for cognitive state assessment. By adopting a multimodal approach to remote health sensing, our dataset and its associated hardware system excel at modeling the complexities of cognitive load. Here, cognitive load is defined as the mental effort exerted during tasks such as reading, memorizing, and solving math problems. By using the NASA-TLX survey, we set personalized thresholds for defining high/low cognitive levels, enabling a more reliable benchmark. Our benchmarking scheme bridges the gap between existing remote sensing strategies and cognitive load estimation techniques by using vital signs (such as photoplethysmography (PPG) and respiratory waveforms) and physiological signals (blink waveforms) as an intermediary. Through this paper, we focus on replacing the need for intrusive contact-based physiological measurements with more user-friendly remote sensors. Our benchmarking demonstrates that multimodal fusion significantly improves remote vital sign estimation, with our fusion model achieving $<3~BPM$ (beats per minute) error for vital sign estimation. For cognitive load classification, the combination of remote PPG, remote respiratory signals, and blink markers achieves $86.49$% accuracy, approaching the performance of contact-based sensing ($87.5$%) and validating the feasibility of non-intrusive cognitive monitoring.

title: CogPhys: Assessing Cognitive Load via Multimodal Remote and Contact-based Physiological Sensing

abstract: Image restoration is a fundamental task in computer vision and machine learning, which learns a mapping between the clear images and the degraded images under various conditions (e.g., blur, low-light, haze). Yet, most existing image restoration methods are highly restricted by the requirement of degraded and clear image pairs, which limits the generalization and feasibility to enormous real-world scenarios without paired images. To address this bottleneck, we propose a Degradation-aware Dynamic Schr\"{o}dinger Bridge (DDSB) for unpaired image restoration. Its general idea is to learn a Schr\"{o}dinger Bridge between clear and degraded image distribution, while at the same time emphasizing the physical degradation priors to reduce the accumulation of errors during the restoration process. A Degradation-aware Optimal Transport (DOT) learning scheme is accordingly devised. Training a degradation model to learn the inverse restoration process is particularly challenging, as it must be applicable across different stages of the iterative restoration process. A Dynamic Transport with Consistency (DTC) learning objective is further proposed to reduce the loss of image details in the early iterations and therefore refine the degradation model. Extensive experiments on multiple image degradation tasks show its state-of-the-art performance over the prior arts.

paragraphs: Training image restoration systems often requires a damaged image and its corresponding clear version. That pairing can be difficult to obtain in real settings involving blur, low light, or haze. This paper introduces DDSB, which learns a connection between clear and degraded image distributions without requiring matched image pairs.

The approach uses a Schrödinger bridge to describe the transformation between those distributions. Its Degradation-aware Optimal Transport learning scheme incorporates physical knowledge about image degradation to reduce errors accumulating during restoration. Experiments across multiple degradation tasks report state-of-the-art performance. These findings support combining distribution-level learning with degradation knowledge when paired restoration data are unavailable.
summary.tldr: DDSB combines unpaired distribution learning with physical degradation knowledge to improve iterative image restoration.

title: Degradation-Aware Dynamic Schrödinger Bridge for Unpaired Image Restoration

abstract: Existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods primarily focus on scenarios involving domain shifts in a single modality. However, they often prove ineffective when multiple modalities simultaneously undergo domain shifts, as they struggle to identify and utilize reliable samples within testing batches amid severe prediction bias. To address this problem, we propose Partition-Then-Adapt (PTA), a novel approach combating prediction bias for TTA with multi-modal domain shifts. PTA comprises two key components: Partition and Debiased Reweighting (PDR) and multi-modal Attention-Guided Alignment (AGA). Specifically, PDR evaluates each sample’s predicted label frequency relative to the batch average, partitioning the batch into potential reliable and unreliable subsets. It then reweights each sample by jointly assessing its bias and confidence levels through a quantile-based approach. By applying weighted entropy loss, PTA simultaneously promotes learning from reliable subsets and discourages reliance on unreliable ones. Moreover, AGA regularizes PDR to focus on semantically meaningful multi-modal cues. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of PTA, surpassing state-of-the-art method by 6.1\% on Kinetics50-MC and 5.8\% on VGGSound-MC, respectively. Code of this paper is available at https://github.com/MPI-Lab/PTA.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using the data it encounters during deployment. When several input modalities shift simultaneously, prediction bias can make it difficult to identify trustworthy examples within a batch. Partition-Then-Adapt tackles this problem by considering both confidence and bias before deciding how strongly each example should influence adaptation.

Its Partition and Debiased Reweighting component compares the frequency of each sample's predicted label with the batch average. It uses this information to form potentially reliable and unreliable subsets, then assigns weights through a quantile-based assessment of bias and confidence. A weighted entropy loss encourages learning from the reliable subset while discouraging dependence on the unreliable one.

Experiments report improvements of 6.1% on Kinetics50-MC and 5.8% on VGGSound-MC over the state-of-the-art method. The findings support treating apparent confidence cautiously when predictions themselves are biased, and combining sample selection with guidance about which multimodal information deserves attention.
summary.tldr: Partition-Then-Adapt combines bias-aware sample weighting with multimodal alignment to improve adaptation when multiple modalities shift together.

title: Partition-Then-Adapt: Combating Prediction Bias for Reliable Multi-Modal Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: We study a relaxation of the problem of coupling probability distributions — a list of samples is generated from one distribution and an *accept* is declared if any one of these samples is identical to the sample generated from the other distribution. We propose a novel method for generating samples, which extends the Gumbel-max sampling suggested in Daliri et al. (2025) for coupling probability distributions. We also establish a corresponding lower bound on the acceptance probability, which we call the \emph{list matching lemma}. We next discuss two applications of our setup. First, we develop a new mechanism for multi-draft speculative sampling that is simple to implement and achieves performance competitive with baselines such as SpecTr and SpecInfer across a range of language tasks. Our method also guarantees a certain degree of *drafter invariance* with respect to the output tokens which is not supported by existing schemes. We also provide a theoretical lower bound on the token level acceptance probability. As our second application, we consider distributed lossy compression with side information in a setting where a source sample is compressed and available to multiple decoders, each with independent side information. We propose a compression technique that is based on our generalization of Gumbel-max sampling and show that it provides significant gains in experiments involving synthetic Gaussian sources and the MNIST image dataset.

paragraphs: This paper studies a relaxed form of coupling probability distributions. One distribution supplies a list of samples, and a match succeeds if any list entry equals the sample drawn from the other distribution. Allowing several candidates changes the matching problem and creates opportunities in both language generation and compression.

The authors extend Gumbel-max sampling to this setting and derive a lower bound on the probability of acceptance, called the list matching lemma. They use the construction for multi-draft speculative sampling, where several draft candidates can contribute to token generation. The resulting mechanism is simple to implement, performs competitively with SpecTr and SpecInfer across language tasks, and provides both a token-acceptance bound and a qualified guarantee of drafter invariance.

A compression method based on the same sampling generalization yields significant experimental gains on synthetic Gaussian sources and MNIST images. The contribution connects one probabilistic matching construction to two distinct computational uses.
summary.tldr: A list-based distribution-coupling method supplies acceptance guarantees and practical applications in speculative decoding and distributed lossy compression.

title: List-Level Distribution Coupling with Applications to Speculative Decoding and Lossy Compression

abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to identify abnormal frames from discrete events within video sequences. Existing VAD methods suffer from heavy annotation burdens in fully-supervised paradigm, insensitivity to subtle anomalies in semi-supervised paradigm, and vulnerability to noise in weakly-supervised paradigm. To address these limitations, we propose a novel paradigm: Single-Frame supervised VAD (SF-VAD), which uses a single annotated abnormal frame per abnormal video. SF-VAD ensures annotation efficiency while offering precise anomaly reference, facilitating robust anomaly modeling, and enhancing the detection of subtle anomalies in complex visual contexts. To validate its effectiveness, we construct three SF-VAD benchmarks by manually re-annotating the ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence datasets in a practical procedure. Further, we devise Frame-guided Progressive Learning (FPL), to generalize sparse frame supervision to event-level anomaly understanding. FPL first leverages evidential learning to estimate anomaly relevance guided by annotated frames. Then it extends anomaly supervision by mining discrete abnormal events based on anomaly relevance and feature similarity. Meanwhile, FPL decouples normal patterns by isolating distinct normal frames outside abnormal events, reducing false alarms. Extensive experiments show SF-VAD achieves state-of-the-art detection results while offering a favorable trade-off between performance and annotation cost.

paragraphs: Video anomaly detection needs to identify abnormal moments, but detailed annotations are expensive and weaker labels can be noisy or imprecise. This paper proposes supervising each abnormal video with just one annotated abnormal frame. That frame provides a precise reference while keeping annotation demands low, creating a starting point for learning the broader abnormal event.

The accompanying Frame-guided Progressive Learning method first estimates how strongly other video content relates to the annotated anomaly using evidential learning. It then expands supervision by finding discrete abnormal events through those relevance estimates and feature similarity. The method also separates distinct normal frames outside abnormal events, helping it model normal behavior and reduce false alarms.

The authors manually re-annotate ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence to create three benchmarks for this supervision setting. Experiments report state-of-the-art detection results and a favorable balance between performance and annotation cost. The central finding is that a small amount of precise frame-level supervision can support learning that extends to complete events.
summary.tldr: A single labeled abnormal frame guides progressive learning of whole anomalous events, delivering strong detection with limited annotation.

title: Generalizing Single-Frame Supervision to Event-Level Understanding for Video Anomaly Detection

abstract: For communication-efficient decentralized learning, it is essential to employ dynamic graphs designed to improve the expected spectral gap by reducing deviations from global averaging. The $1$-peer exponential graph demonstrates its finite-time convergence property--achieved by maximizing the expected spectral gap--but only when the number of nodes $n$ is a power of two. However, its efficiency across any $n$ and the commutativity of mixing matrices remain unexplored. We delve into the principles underlying the $1$-peer exponential graph to explain its efficiency across any $n$ and leverage them to develop new dynamic graphs. We propose two new dynamic graphs: the $k$-peer exponential graph and the null-cascade graph. Notably, the null-cascade graph achieves finite-time convergence for any $n$ while ensuring commutativity. Our experiments confirm the effectiveness of these new graphs, particularly the null-cascade graph, in most test settings.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, communication patterns influence how efficiently participating nodes approach global averaging. Dynamic graphs change those communication connections over time. This paper revisits the one-peer exponential graph, whose known finite-time convergence property applies when the number of nodes is a power of two, and studies its efficiency for arbitrary node counts.

The analysis examines principles behind the graph's behavior, including the expected spectral gap and whether mixing matrices commute. These matrices describe the averaging operations associated with communication, and commutativity concerns whether their order changes their combined effect. The authors use the resulting understanding to construct two alternatives: the k-peer exponential graph and the null-cascade graph.

The null-cascade graph achieves finite-time convergence for any number of nodes while preserving commutativity. This removes the power-of-two restriction attached to the stated finite-time property of the one-peer design. Experiments confirm the effectiveness of the new graphs, especially null-cascade, in most tested settings. The empirical qualification matters: the reported advantage spans most settings examined, rather than establishing superiority for every decentralized-learning configuration.
summary.tldr: New communication graphs improve decentralized learning, with null-cascade achieving finite-time averaging convergence for any node count and commuting mixing matrices.

title: Revisiting 1-peer exponential graph for enhancing decentralized learning efficiency

abstract: Generative modeling of non-negative, discrete data, such as symbolic music, remains challenging due to two persistent limitations in existing methods. Firstly, many approaches rely on modeling continuous embeddings, which is suboptimal for inherently discrete data distributions. Secondly, most models optimize variational bounds rather than exact data likelihood, resulting in inaccurate likelihood estimates and degraded sampling quality. While recent diffusion-based models have addressed these issues separately, we tackle them jointly. In this work, we introduce the Information-Theoretic Discrete Poisson Diffusion Model (ItDPDM), inspired by photon arrival process, which combines exact likelihood estimation with fully discrete-state modeling. Central to our approach is an information-theoretic Poisson Reconstruction Loss (PRL) that has a provable exact relationship with the true data likelihood. ItDPDM achieves improved likelihood and sampling performance over prior discrete and continuous diffusion models on a variety of synthetic discrete datasets. Furthermore, on real-world datasets such as symbolic music and images, ItDPDM attains superior likelihood estimates and competitive generation quality—demonstrating a proof of concept for distribution-robust discrete generative modeling.

paragraphs: Generating nonnegative discrete data presents two linked challenges: representing discrete values faithfully and accurately measuring the probability assigned to data. The paper argues that continuous embeddings can be poorly matched to these distributions, while training against variational bounds can give inaccurate likelihood estimates. ItDPDM addresses both issues within one diffusion model.

Inspired by photon arrival processes, the method keeps its modeled states discrete. Its central training quantity is a Poisson Reconstruction Loss with a provable exact relationship to the true data likelihood. This relationship provides a principled connection between reconstruction training and probability estimation, rather than relying only on a variational approximation.

On synthetic discrete datasets, ItDPDM improves both likelihood and sampling performance over the discrete and continuous diffusion models compared. On real-world symbolic music and image datasets, it produces superior likelihood estimates and competitive generation quality. Those two findings have different strengths: the abstract claims improved probability estimates but competitive, rather than universally superior, real-world generation. The authors present the results as a proof of concept for robust generative modeling across discrete distributions.
summary.tldr: ItDPDM combines discrete-state diffusion with a reconstruction loss exactly related to likelihood, improving probability estimation and supporting competitive generation.

title: ItDPDM: Information-Theoretic Discrete Poisson Diffusion Model

abstract: Human social interactions depend on the ability to infer others' unspoken intentions, emotions, and beliefs—a cognitive skill grounded in the psychological concept of Theory of Mind (ToM). While large language models (LLMs) excel in semantic understanding tasks, they struggle with the ambiguity and contextual nuance inherent in human communication. To bridge this gap, we introduce **MetaMind**, a multi-agent framework inspired by psychological theories of metacognition, designed to emulate human-like social reasoning. MetaMind decomposes social understanding into three collaborative stages: (1) a *Theory-of-Mind Agent* generates hypotheses about user mental states (e.g., intent, emotion), (2) a *Moral Agent* refines these hypotheses using cultural norms and ethical constraints, and (3) a *Response Agent* generates contextually appropriate responses while validating alignment with inferred intent. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance across three challenging benchmarks, with 35.7% improvement in real-world social scenarios and 6.2% gain in ToM reasoning. Notably, it enables LLMs to match human-level performance on key ToM tasks for the first time. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of all components, which showcase the framework’s ability to balance contextual plausibility, social appropriateness, and user adaptation. This work advances AI systems toward human-like social intelligence, with applications in empathetic dialogue and culturally sensitive interactions. Code is available at https://github.com/XMZhangAI/MetaMind.

paragraphs: MetaMind addresses social understanding: interpreting intentions, emotions, and beliefs that people leave unstated. The paper connects this challenge to Theory of Mind and argues that strong language comprehension alone does not resolve the ambiguity of human interaction. Its proposed solution distributes social reasoning across agents with distinct responsibilities.

A Theory-of-Mind agent proposes interpretations of a user's mental state. A Moral agent revises these interpretations using cultural norms and ethical constraints. A Response agent then produces an appropriate reply and checks whether it fits the inferred intent. This staged process makes interpretation, social evaluation, and response checking explicit parts of generating an answer.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across three benchmarks, including a 35.7% improvement in real-world social scenarios and a 6.2% gain in Theory-of-Mind reasoning. They also report human-level performance on key Theory-of-Mind tasks. Ablation studies support the importance of all components in their evaluations. Together, these findings suggest that structured collaboration among specialized reasoning roles can improve contextual plausibility, social appropriateness, and adaptation to users on the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: MetaMind uses three collaborating agents to interpret mental states, apply social constraints, and check responses, improving tested social-reasoning performance.

title: MetaMind: Modeling Human Social Thoughts with Metacognitive Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Multimodal federated learning in real-world settings often encounters incomplete and heterogeneous data across clients. This results in misaligned local feature representations that limit the effectiveness of model aggregation. Unlike prior work that assumes either differing modality sets without missing input features or a shared modality set with missing features across clients, we consider a more general and realistic setting where each client observes a different subset of modalities and might also have missing input features within each modality. To address the resulting misalignment in learned representations, we propose a new federated learning framework featuring locally adaptive representations based on learnable client-side embedding controls that encode each client’s data-missing patterns. These embeddings serve as reconfiguration signals that align the globally aggregated representation with each client's local context, enabling more effective use of shared information. Furthermore, the embedding controls can be algorithmically aggregated across clients with similar data-missing patterns to enhance the robustness of reconfiguration signals in adapting the global representation. Empirical results on multiple federated multimodal benchmarks with diverse data-missing patterns across clients demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, achieving up to 36.45\% performance improvement under severe data incompleteness. The method is also supported by a theoretical analysis with an explicit performance bound that matches our empirical observations. Our source codes are provided at [https://github.com/nmduonggg/PEPSY](https://github.com/nmduonggg/PEPSY)
