paragraphs: Multimodal federated learning becomes difficult when clients have different kinds of data and missing features within the kinds they possess. These differences can make locally learned representations incompatible, reducing the usefulness of combining them into a shared model. The paper considers both forms of missingness together in a single framework.

Each client learns embedding controls that encode its pattern of missing data. These controls act as signals for adapting the globally aggregated representation to the client's local circumstances. The approach aims to make shared information useful without requiring every client to observe the same inputs. Controls can also be aggregated among clients with similar missingness patterns to strengthen these adaptation signals.

Across multimodal federated benchmarks, the method reports improvements of up to 36.45% under severe data incompleteness. A theoretical analysis supplies an explicit performance bound consistent with the empirical observations. The contribution is a mechanism for making representation sharing sensitive to how data are missing, addressing misalignment at the point where global information meets each client's available inputs.
summary.tldr: Learned client-specific controls adapt shared multimodal representations to missing-data patterns, improving federated learning under severe incompleteness.

title: Learning Reconfigurable Representations for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Data

abstract: Modeling interactive driving behaviors in complex scenarios remains a fundamental challenge for autonomous driving planning. Learning-based approaches attempt to address this challenge with advanced generative models, removing the dependency on over-engineered architectures for representation fusion. However, brute-force implementation by simply stacking transformer blocks lacks a dedicated mechanism for modeling interactive behaviors that is common in real driving scenarios. The scarcity of interactive driving data further exacerbates this problem, leaving conventional imitation learning methods ill-equipped to capture high-value interactive behaviors. We propose Flow Planner, which tackles these problems through coordinated innovations in data modeling, model architecture, and learning scheme. Specifically, we first introduce fine-grained trajectory tokenization, which decomposes the trajectory into overlapping segments to decrease the complexity of whole trajectory modeling. With a sophisticatedly designed architecture, we achieve efficient temporal and spatial fusion of planning and scene information, to better capture interactive behaviors. In addition, the framework incorporates flow matching with classifier-free guidance for multi-modal behavior generation, which dynamically reweights agent interactions during inference to maintain coherent response strategies, providing a critical boost for interactive scenario understanding. Experimental results on the large-scale nuPlan dataset demonstrate that Flow Planner achieves state-of-the-art performance among learning-based approaches while effectively modeling interactive behaviors in complex driving scenarios.

paragraphs: Flow Planner targets the interactions that make autonomous driving difficult: a planned trajectory must account for the behavior of other agents in a changing scene. The paper argues that simply stacking transformer blocks does not supply a dedicated mechanism for these interactions. Scarce examples of interactive driving further complicate learning them through imitation.

The method coordinates changes to trajectory representation, architecture, and generation. It breaks trajectories into overlapping segments, reducing the complexity of modeling an entire trajectory at once. Its architecture combines planning and scene information across time and space. Flow matching with classifier-free guidance supports multiple possible behaviors and dynamically reweights agent interactions during inference to maintain coherent responses.

On the large-scale nuPlan dataset, Flow Planner achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated learning-based approaches and effectively models complex interactions. The significance is the coordinated treatment of interaction throughout the planning pipeline. The reported gains support designing representations and inference mechanisms specifically around interactive behavior, alongside the use of a generative model.
summary.tldr: Flow Planner combines segmented trajectories, scene fusion, and guided flow matching to improve interactive autonomous-driving planning on nuPlan.

title: Flow Matching-Based Autonomous Driving Planning with Advanced Interactive Behavior Modeling

abstract: Learning effective visuomotor policies for robotic manipulation is challenging, as it requires generating precise actions while maintaining computational efficiency. Existing methods remain unsatisfactory due to inherent limitations in the essential action representation and the basic network architectures. We observe that representing actions in the frequency domain captures the structured nature of motion more effectively: low-frequency components reflect global movement patterns, while high-frequency components encode fine local details. Additionally, robotic manipulation tasks of varying complexity demand different levels of modeling precision across these frequency bands. Motivated by this, we propose a novel paradigm for visuomotor policy learning that progressively models hierarchical frequency components. To further enhance precision, we introduce continuous latent representations that maintain smoothness and continuity in the action space. Extensive experiments across diverse 2D and 3D robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency, showcasing the potential of a frequency-domain autoregressive framework with continuous tokens for generalized robotic manipulation.Code is available at https://github.com/4DVLab/Freqpolicy

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation requires visually guided actions that are both precise and efficient to compute. FreqPolicy approaches this challenge through the representation of motion. The authors observe that frequency components separate broad movement patterns from finer local details, creating a structured way to model the actions a robot should take.

Low-frequency components describe the overall movement, while high-frequency components capture finer variations. Because manipulation tasks differ in complexity, they can require different levels of precision across these components. FreqPolicy progressively models this frequency hierarchy using an autoregressive framework. It also introduces continuous latent representations to preserve smoothness and continuity in the action space while improving precision.

Experiments across diverse two-dimensional and three-dimensional manipulation benchmarks show better accuracy and efficiency than the existing methods evaluated. These findings support frequency-based action modeling as a useful design for visuomotor policies. The contribution brings together a hierarchical description of motion and continuous action representations, with the reported results indicating benefits for both precise control and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: FreqPolicy progressively models robot actions across frequency bands with continuous representations, improving accuracy and efficiency on evaluated manipulation benchmarks.

title: FreqPolicy: Frequency Autoregressive Visuomotor Policy with Continuous Tokens

abstract: Recently, leveraging pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for building vision-language-action (VLA) models has emerged as a promising approach to effective robot manipulation learning. However, only few methods incorporate 3D signals into VLMs for action prediction, and they do not fully leverage the spatial structure inherent in 3D data, leading to low data efficiency. In this paper, we introduce a new paradigm for constructing 3D VLAs. Specifically, we first pre-train the VLM backbone to take 2D images as input and produce 2D heatmaps as output. Using this pre-trained VLM as the backbone, we then fine-tune the entire VLA model while maintaining alignment between inputs and outputs by: (1) projecting raw point cloud inputs into multi-view images, and (2) predicting heatmaps before generating the final action. Extensive experiments show that the resulting model, BridgeVLA, can learn 3D manipulation both efficiently and effectively. BridgeVLA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three simulation benchmarks. In RLBench, it improves the average success rate from 81.4\% to 88.2\%. In COLOSSEUM, it demonstrates significantly better performance in challenging generalization settings, boosting the average success rate from 56.7\% to 64.0\%. In GemBench, it surpasses all the comparing baseline methods in terms of average success rate. In real-robot experiments, BridgeVLA outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline method by 32\% on average. It generalizes robustly in multiple out-of-distribution settings, including visual disturbances and unseen instructions. Remarkably, it is able to achieve a success rate of 95.4\% on 10+ tasks with only 3 trajectories per task, while other VLA methods such as $\pi_{0}$ fail completely. Project Website: https://bridgevla.github.io/.

paragraphs: BridgeVLA investigates how a pretrained vision-language model can learn robot manipulation while making better use of three-dimensional spatial information. Its central idea is to keep the model’s input and output representations aligned across pretraining and robot learning. This addresses the limited data efficiency of approaches that do not fully exploit 3D structure.

The backbone first learns to map two-dimensional images to two-dimensional heatmaps. During robot training, point clouds are projected into images from multiple viewpoints, and the model continues to predict heatmaps before producing actions. Fine-tuning therefore preserves the image-to-heatmap structure established during pretraining while incorporating spatial information from the robot’s environment.

The reported results include improvements over leading baselines on three simulation benchmarks and stronger real-robot performance. RLBench success rises from 81.4% to 88.2%, and COLOSSEUM success rises from 56.7% to 64.0%. The model also handles tested visual disturbances and unseen instructions. With three trajectories per task, it achieves 95.4% success across more than ten tasks, providing particularly strong evidence of learning efficiency in that evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: BridgeVLA aligns image inputs and heatmap outputs across training stages to learn 3D robot manipulation efficiently.

title: BridgeVLA: Input-Output Alignment for Efficient 3D Manipulation Learning with Vision-Language Models

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely adopted parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique for adapting large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks. While prior work has explored strategies for integrating LLM training and serving, there still remains a gap in unifying fine-tuning and inference for LoRA-based models. We present **Loquetier**, a virtualized multi-LoRA framework that seamlessly integrates LoRA fine-tuning and serving within a single runtime. Loquetier introduces two key components: (1) a Virtualized Module that isolates PEFT-based modifications and supports multiple adapters on a shared base model, and (2) an optimized computation flow with a kernel design that merges fine-tuning and inference paths in forward propagation, enabling efficient batching and minimizing kernel invocation overhead. Extensive experiments across three task settings show that Loquetier consistently outperforms existing baselines in both performance and flexibility, achieving up to $3.0\times$ the throughput of the state-of-the-art co-serving system on inference-only tasks and $46.4\times$ higher SLO attainment than PEFT on unified fine-tuning and inference tasks. The implementation of Loquetier is publicly available at https://github.com/NJUDeepEngine/Loquetier.

paragraphs: LoRA adapts language models through parameter-efficient modifications, but supporting adaptation and inference together presents a runtime challenge. Loquetier addresses this by unifying LoRA fine-tuning and serving within one framework. The aim is to support multiple adapters on a shared base model while making their different computational workloads work efficiently together.

The framework has two main components. A Virtualized Module isolates the adapter-specific modifications, allowing multiple adapters to coexist around the common model. An optimized computation flow and kernel design merge fine-tuning and inference paths during forward propagation. This makes batching more efficient and reduces kernel invocation overhead, directly targeting the runtime cost of handling these workloads together.

Across three task settings, the authors report gains in performance and flexibility over existing baselines. For inference-only workloads, throughput reaches up to three times that of the compared state-of-the-art co-serving system. For combined fine-tuning and inference, service-level objective attainment is reported as 46.4 times higher than PEFT. These measurements describe different operational benefits: processing capacity in one setting and meeting service objectives in another.
summary.tldr: Loquetier shares a base model across LoRA adapters and merges computation paths to improve unified fine-tuning and inference.

title: Loquetier: A Virtualized Multi-LoRA Framework for Unified LLM Fine-tuning and Serving

abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to simulate human behavior has gained significant attention, particularly through personas that approximate individual characteristics. Persona-based simulations hold promise for transforming disciplines that rely on population-level feedback, including social science, economic analysis, marketing research, and business operations. Traditional methods to collect realistic persona data face significant challenges. They are prohibitively expensive and logistically challenging due to privacy constraints, and often fail to capture multi-dimensional attributes, particularly subjective qualities. Consequently, synthetic persona generation with LLMs offers a scalable, cost-effective alternative. However, current approaches rely on ad hoc and heuristic generation techniques that do not guarantee methodological rigor or simulation precision, resulting in systematic biases in downstream tasks. Through extensive large-scale experiments including presidential election forecasts and general opinion surveys of the U.S. population, we reveal that these biases can lead to significant deviations from real-world outcomes. Based on the experimental results, this position paper argues that **a rigorous and systematic science of persona generation is needed to ensure the reliability of LLM-driven simulations of human behavior.** We call for not only methodological innovations and empirical foundations but also interdisciplinary organizational and institutional support for the development of this field. To support further research and development in this area, we have open-sourced approximately one million generated personas, available for public access and analysis.

paragraphs: Language models can generate personas intended to approximate individual characteristics and support simulations of human behavior. Such simulations could provide population-level feedback for social science, economics, marketing, and business. Synthetic personas offer an appealing alternative when collecting realistic persona data is expensive, constrained by privacy, or unable to capture multiple attributes and subjective qualities.

The paper examines the reliability of current persona-generation practices, which often use ad hoc heuristics. Large-scale experiments include U.S. presidential election forecasts and general opinion surveys. The results show that systematic biases in generated personas can carry into downstream tasks and produce substantial departures from real-world outcomes. Generating a large population of personas therefore does not itself establish simulation accuracy.

As a position paper, the work argues for a systematic science of persona generation supported by methodological advances, empirical foundations, and interdisciplinary institutions. The authors also release approximately one million generated personas for further study. The contribution combines evidence of consequential bias with a research agenda and a resource for investigating more reliable simulation methods.
summary.tldr: Large-scale experiments reveal consequential biases in LLM-generated personas and motivate a more rigorous science of human-behavior simulation.

title: LLM Generated Persona is a Promise with a Catch

abstract: While deep learning models often achieve high predictive accuracy, their predictions typically do not come with any provable guarantees on risk or reliability, which are critical for deployment in high-stakes applications. The framework of conformal risk control (CRC) provides a distribution-free, finite-sample method for controlling the expected value of any bounded monotone loss function and can be conveniently applied post-hoc to any pre-trained deep learning model. However, many real-world applications are sensitive to tail risks, as opposed to just expected loss. In this work, we develop a method for controlling the general class of Optimized Certainty-Equivalent (OCE) risks, a broad class of risk measures which includes as special cases the expected loss (generalizing the original CRC method) and common tail risks like the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR). Furthermore, standard post-hoc CRC can degrade average-case performance due to its lack of feedback to the model. To address this, we introduce "conformal risk training," an end-to-end approach that differentiates through conformal OCE risk control _during model training or fine-tuning_. Our method achieves provable risk guarantees while demonstrating significantly improved average-case performance over post-hoc approaches on applications to controlling classifiers' false negative rate and controlling financial risk in battery storage operation.

paragraphs: Accurate predictions do not automatically provide guarantees about the losses a system may incur. Conformal risk control addresses this by controlling expected bounded, monotone losses using a finite-sample, distribution-free procedure applied after training. This paper extends that approach to situations where unusually bad outcomes matter, so controlling the average loss alone is insufficient.

The authors develop control for Optimized Certainty-Equivalent risks, a family that includes expected loss and tail-focused measures such as conditional value-at-risk. They also address a separate problem: applying risk control only after training can reduce average performance because the model never receives feedback about that adjustment. Their conformal risk training method differentiates through risk control during training or fine-tuning.

The resulting approach combines provable risk guarantees with a training process that can adapt to the imposed risk requirement. Experiments on controlling classifier false negatives and financial risk in battery storage operation show significantly better average-case performance than post-hoc approaches. The findings suggest that incorporating risk control into learning can improve the performance achieved alongside the stated guarantees.
summary.tldr: Conformal risk training incorporates average and tail-risk control into learning, improving average performance while retaining provable risk guarantees.

title: Conformal Risk Training: End-to-End Optimization of Conformal Risk Control

abstract: Gene expression estimation from pathology images has the potential to reduce the RNA sequencing cost. Point-wise loss functions have been widely used to minimize the discrepancy between predicted and absolute gene expression values. However, due to the complexity of the sequencing techniques and intrinsic variability across cells, the observed gene expression contains stochastic noise and batch effects, and estimating the absolute expression values accurately remains a significant challenge. To mitigate this, we propose a novel objective of learning relative expression patterns rather than absolute levels. We assume that the relative expression levels of genes exhibit consistent patterns across independent experiments, even when absolute expression values are affected by batch effects and stochastic noise in tissue samples. Based on the assumption, we model the relation and propose a novel loss function called STRank that is robust to noise and batch effects. Experiments using synthetic datasets and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code is available at https://github.com/naivete5656/STRank.

paragraphs: Estimating gene expression from pathology images could reduce reliance on costly RNA sequencing. Common training objectives compare each predicted expression value with its measured absolute value. However, sequencing procedures, cell variability, random noise, and batch effects make those absolute measurements difficult targets to predict accurately across tissue samples.

This paper changes the learning objective to relative expression patterns. Its explicit assumption is that relative gene-expression levels exhibit consistent patterns across independent experiments, even when noise and batch effects alter absolute values. Under that assumption, relationships among expression levels can provide a more stable training signal than exact numerical measurements.

The authors model these relationships through a loss function called STRank, designed to resist noise and batch effects. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets support the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a change in what image-based prediction is trained to preserve: the relative structure of expression. Its rationale depends on the stated consistency assumption, which explains why learning trends can help when absolute measurements vary between experiments.
summary.tldr: STRank learns relative gene-expression patterns from pathology images, assuming those relationships remain more consistent across experiments than absolute measurements.

title: Learning Relative Gene Expression Trends from Pathology Images in Spatial Transcriptomics

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides additional contextual knowledge to complement the parametric knowledge in Large Language Models (LLMs). These two knowledge interweave to enhance the accuracy and timeliness of LLM responses. However, the internal mechanisms by which LLMs utilize these knowledge remain unclear. We propose modeling the forward propagation of knowledge as an entity flow, employing this framework to trace LLMs' internal behaviors when processing mixed-source knowledge. Linear probing utilizes a trainable linear classifier to detect specific attributes in hidden layers. However, once trained, a probe cannot adapt to dynamically specified entities. To address this challenge, we construct an entity-aware probe, which introduces special tokens to mark probing targets and employs a small trainable rank-8 lora update to process these special markers. We first verify this approach through an attribution experiment, demonstrating that it can accurately detect information about ad-hoc entities from complex hidden states. Next, we trace entity flows across layers to understand how LLMs reconcile conflicting knowledge internally. Our probing results reveal that contextual and parametric knowledge are routed between tokens through distinct sets of attention heads, supporting attention competition only within knowledge types. While conflicting knowledge maintains a residual presence across layers, aligned knowledge from multiple sources gradually accumulates, with the magnitude of this accumulation directly determining its influence on final outputs.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation combines information stored in model parameters with information supplied in context. This paper studies how those sources interact inside a language model, especially when they conflict. It treats information about entities as a flow through the network, allowing the authors to trace how entity-related content changes across layers.

A conventional trained linear probe cannot adapt to arbitrarily specified entities. The authors introduce an entity-aware probe that marks targets with special tokens and uses a small rank-8 LoRA update to process those markers. An attribution experiment verifies that the probe can detect information about newly specified entities within complex hidden representations.

The probing results indicate that contextual and parametric information travel between tokens through distinct attention-head sets, supporting competition within knowledge types. Conflicting information retains a residual presence across layers, while agreement between sources leads to accumulating information. The authors report that the magnitude of this accumulation determines its influence on final outputs. These observations provide an internal account of how mixed-source knowledge contributes to answers.
summary.tldr: Entity-aware probing traces distinct attention routes for stored and contextual knowledge and reveals how agreement accumulates to influence model outputs.

title: Understanding Parametric and Contextual Knowledge Reconciliation within Large Language Models

abstract: It is commonly believed that scaling language models should commit a significant space or time cost, by increasing the parameters (parameter scaling) or output tokens (inference-time scaling). We introduce another and more inference-efficient scaling paradigm: increasing the model's parallel computation during both training and inference time. We apply $P$ diverse and learnable transformations to the input, execute forward passes of the model in parallel, and dynamically aggregate the $P$ outputs. This method, namely parallel scaling (ParScale), scales parallel computation by reusing existing parameters and can be applied to any model structure, optimization procedure, data, or task. We theoretically propose a new scaling law and validate it through large-scale pre-training, which shows that a model with $P$ parallel streams is similar to scaling the parameters by $\mathcal O(\log P)$ while showing superior inference efficiency. For example, ParScale can use up to 22$\times$ less memory increase and 6$\times$ less latency increase compared to parameter scaling that achieves the same performance improvement. It can also recycle an off-the-shelf pre-trained model into a parallelly scaled one by post-training on a small amount of tokens, further reducing the training budget. The new scaling law we discovered potentially facilitates the deployment of more powerful models in low-resource scenarios, and provides an alternative perspective for the role of computation in machine learning. Our code and 67 trained model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/QwenLM/ParScale and https://huggingface.co/ParScale.

paragraphs: ParScale explores improving language models by increasing parallel computation during training and inference. It applies P different learnable transformations to an input, runs the model on these versions in parallel, and dynamically combines the outputs. The parallel streams reuse existing model parameters, providing another way to allocate computation for improved performance.

The authors propose a scaling law and validate it through large-scale pretraining. Their results relate P parallel streams to parameter scaling of order log P, with better inference efficiency. For equivalent performance improvements, the reported examples require up to 22 times less additional memory and six times less additional latency than parameter scaling.

The method can also adapt an existing pretrained model through post-training on a small quantity of tokens, reducing the training budget needed to introduce parallel scaling. These findings suggest a potential route to stronger models in resource-constrained deployment settings. The central contribution is the demonstrated relationship between shared-parameter parallel computation, predictive performance, and the incremental costs of memory and latency.
summary.tldr: ParScale improves language models through parallel, shared-parameter streams, with reported memory and latency advantages over parameter scaling.

title: Parallel Scaling Law for Language Models

abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a wide range of tasks, growing concerns have emerged over the misuse of sensitive, copyrighted, or harmful data during training. To address these concerns, unlearning techniques have been developed to remove the influence of specific data without retraining from scratch. However, this paper reveals a critical vulnerability in fine-tuning-based unlearning: a malicious user can craft a manipulated forgetting request that stealthily degrades the model’s utility for benign users. We demonstrate this risk through a red-teaming Stealthy Attack (SA), which is inspired by two key limitations of existing unlearning—the inability to constrain the scope of unlearning effect and the failure to distinguish benign tokens from unlearning signals. Prior work has shown that unlearned models tend to memorize forgetting data as unlearning signals, and respond with hallucinations or feigned ignorance when unlearning signals appear in the input. By subtly increasing the presence of common benign tokens in the forgetting data, SA enhances the connection between benign tokens and unlearning signals. As a result, when normal users include such tokens in their prompts, the model exhibits unlearning behaviors, leading to unintended utility degradation. To address this vulnerability, we propose Scope-aware Unlearning (SU), a lightweight enhancement that introduces a scope term into the unlearning objective, encouraging the model to localize the forgetting effect. Our method requires no additional data processing, integrates seamlessly with existing fine-tuning frameworks, and significantly improves robustness against SA. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of both SA and SU.
originalAbstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a wide range of tasks, growing concerns have emerged over the misuse of sensitive, copyrighted, or harmful data during training. To address these concerns, unlearning techniques have been developed to remove the influence of specific data without retraining from scratch. However, this paper reveals a critical vulnerability in fine-tuning-based unlearning: a malicious user can craft a manipulated forgetting request that stealthily degrades the model’s utility for benign users. We demonstrate this risk through a red-teaming Stealthy Attack (SA), which is inspired by two key limitations of existing unlearning—the inability to constrain the scope of unlearning effect and the failure to distinguish benign tokens from unlearning signals. Prior work has shown that unlearned models tend to memorize forgetting data as unlearning signals, and respond with hallucinations or feigned ignorance when unlearning signals appear in the input. By subtly increasing the presence of common benign tokens in the forgetting data, SA enhances the connection between benign tokens and unlearning signals. As a result, when normal users include such tokens in their prompts, the model exhibits unlearning behaviors, leading to unintended utility degradation. To address this vulnerability, we propose Scope-aware Unlearning (SU), a lightweight enhancement that introduces a scope term into the unlearning objective, encouraging the model to localize the forgetting effect. Our method requires no additional data processing, integrates seamlessly with existing fine-tuning frameworks, and significantly improves robustness against SA. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of both SA and SU.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data without rebuilding a language model from scratch. This paper identifies a vulnerability in fine-tuning-based unlearning: a manipulated forgetting request can cause damage to ordinary model use. The problem arises when the effect of forgetting spreads beyond its intended scope.

The authors demonstrate a Stealthy Attack that strengthens associations between common benign tokens and the signals a model learns to forget. As a result, ordinary prompts containing those tokens can trigger hallucinations or apparent ignorance associated with unlearning. This connects unintended utility loss to both weak control over forgetting scope and difficulty separating benign content from forgetting signals.

The proposed remedy, Scope-aware Unlearning, adds a scope term to the training objective to encourage more localized forgetting. It requires no additional data processing and fits into existing fine-tuning workflows. Experiments validate the attack and show that the remedy significantly improves robustness against it, making control of unlearning's reach a concrete design concern.
summary.tldr: Manipulated forgetting requests can harm ordinary language-model use; Scope-aware Unlearning improves robustness by encouraging localized forgetting.

title: Keeping an Eye on LLM Unlearning: The Hidden Risk and Remedy

abstract: Recent advances in Large Multi-modal Models (LMMs) have demonstrated their remarkable success as general-purpose multi-modal assistants, with particular focuses on holistic image- and video-language understanding. Conversely, less attention has been given to scaling fine-grained pixel-level understanding capabilities, where the models are expected to realize pixel-level alignment between visual signals and language semantics. Some previous studies have applied LMMs to related tasks such as region-level captioning and referring expression segmentation. However, these models are limited to performing either referring or segmentation tasks independently and fail to integrate these fine-grained perception capabilities into visual reasoning. To bridge this gap, we propose UniPixel, a large multi-modal model capable of flexibly comprehending visual prompt inputs and generating mask-grounded responses. Our model distinguishes itself by seamlessly integrating pixel-level perception with general visual understanding capabilities. Specifically, UniPixel processes visual prompts and generates relevant masks on demand, and performs subsequent reasoning conditioning on these intermediate pointers during inference, thereby enabling fine-grained pixel-level reasoning. The effectiveness of our approach has been verified on 10 benchmarks across a diverse set of tasks, including pixel-level referring/segmentation and object-centric understanding in images/videos. A novel PixelQA task that jointly requires referring, segmentation, and question answering is also designed to verify the flexibility of our method.

paragraphs: Understanding an image as a whole does not necessarily give a multimodal model precise control over which pixels correspond to an object or phrase. UniPixel targets that finer connection between language and visual content. It brings object referring, segmentation, and broader visual reasoning into a single model.

The model accepts visual prompts and generates relevant masks when needed. These masks identify specific visual regions and can serve as intermediate pointers for subsequent reasoning during inference. This creates a connection between locating an object and reasoning about it: the model can condition later processing on the pixel-level regions it has identified, while retaining general image and video understanding capabilities.

The authors evaluate UniPixel on ten benchmarks covering pixel-level referring and segmentation as well as object-centric understanding in images and videos. They also introduce PixelQA, which requires referring, segmentation, and question answering together. The reported results support the flexibility of integrating these capabilities, with pixel-level outputs participating in the reasoning process rather than remaining isolated task results.
summary.tldr: UniPixel integrates object referring and segmentation with visual reasoning by using generated masks as intermediate pointers.

title: UniPixel: Unified Object Referring and Segmentation for Pixel-Level Visual Reasoning

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities utilizing reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable reward, whether large vision-language models (VLMs) can directly inherit such capabilities through similar post-training strategies remains underexplored. In this work, we conduct a systematic compositional probing study to evaluate whether current VLMs trained with RL or other post-training strategies can compose capabilities across modalities or tasks under out-of-distribution conditions. We design a suite of diagnostic tasks that train models on unimodal tasks or isolated reasoning skills, and evaluate them on multimodal, compositional variants requiring skill integration. Through comparisons between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL-trained models, we identify three key findings: (1) RL-trained models consistently outperform SFT on compositional generalization, demonstrating better integration of learned skills; (2) although VLMs achieve strong performance on individual tasks, they struggle to generalize compositionally under cross-modal and cross-task scenarios, revealing a significant gap in current training strategies; (3) enforcing models to explicitly describe visual content before reasoning (e.g., caption-before-thinking), along with rewarding progressive vision-to-text grounding, yields notable gains. It highlights two essential ingredients for improving compositionality in VLMs: visual-to-text alignment and accurate visual grounding. Our findings shed light on the current limitations of RL-based reasoning VLM training and provide actionable insights toward building models that reason compositionally across modalities and tasks.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may succeed at individual skills yet struggle when a new task requires combining them. This paper studies that gap through diagnostic tasks: models learn unimodal tasks or isolated reasoning skills, then face unfamiliar multimodal problems that require those capabilities to work together. The evaluation focuses on composition beyond the training distribution.

The authors compare reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning and find that reinforcement-trained models consistently generalize better compositionally. However, strong performance on separate tasks still does not reliably translate into successful integration across modalities or tasks. This distinguishes improvement from resolution: reinforcement learning helps in the studied settings, but a substantial compositional gap remains.

Two interventions produce notable gains: requiring a description of visual content before reasoning, and rewarding progressive grounding from vision into text. The findings point to accurate visual grounding and visual-to-text alignment as important ingredients for combining skills. They also provide concrete training directions, linking failures of compositional reasoning to how visual evidence is represented and made available to subsequent reasoning.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning improves compositional vision-language reasoning, but substantial gaps remain and explicit visual grounding yields further gains.

title: Unveiling the Compositional Ability Gap in Vision-Language Reasoning Model

abstract: We present a novel benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in mathematical reasoning and algorithmic code synthesis tasks. The benchmark comprises integer sequence generation tasks sourced from the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), testing LLMs' abilities to accurately and efficiently generate Python code to compute these sequences without using lookup tables. Our comprehensive evaluation includes leading models from OpenAI (including the specialized reasoning-focused o-series), Anthropic, Meta, and Google across a carefully selected set of 1000 OEIS sequences categorized as ``easy'' or ``hard.'' Half of these sequences are classical sequences from the early days of OEIS and half were recently added to avoid contamination with the models' training data. To prevent models from exploiting memorized sequence values, we introduce an automated cheating detection mechanism that flags usage of lookup tables, validated by comparison with human expert evaluations. Experimental results demonstrate that reasoning-specialized models (o3, o3-mini, o4-mini from OpenAI, and Gemini 2.5-pro from Google) achieve substantial improvements in accuracy over non-reasoning models, especially on more complex tasks. However, overall model performance on the hard sequences is poor, highlighting persistent challenges in algorithmic reasoning. Our benchmark provides important insights into the strengths and limitations of state-of-the-art LLMs, particularly emphasizing the necessity for further advancements to reliably solve complex mathematical reasoning tasks algorithmically.

summary.tldr: A benchmark of 1,000 integer sequences tests algorithmic code generation and finds that hard sequences remain challenging even for reasoning-specialized models.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Integer Sequence Generation Tasks

abstract: The coordinated activity of neural populations underlies myriad brain functions. Manipulating this activity using brain stimulation techniques has great potential for scientific and clinical applications, as it provides a tool to causally influence brain function. To improve the accuracy by which one can manipulate neural activity, it is important to (1) take into account the pre-stimulation brain state, which can influence the brain’s response to stimulation, and (2) adaptively update stimulation parameters over time to compensate for changes in the brain’s response to stimulation. In this work, we propose Online MicroStimulation Optimization (OMiSO), a brain stimulation framework that leverages brain state information to find stimulation parameters that can drive neural population activity toward specified states. OMiSO includes two key advances: i) training a stimulation-response model that leverages the pre-stimulation brain state, and inverting this model to choose the stimulation parameters, and ii) updating this inverse model online using newly-observed responses to stimulation. We tested OMiSO using intracortical microstimulation with a ``Utah'' array and found that it outperformed competing methods that do not incorporate these advances. Taken together, OMiSO provides greater accuracy in achieving specified activity states, thereby advancing neuromodulation technologies for understanding the brain and for treating brain disorders.

paragraphs: OMiSO aims to guide the collective activity of neurons toward specified states using brain stimulation. The paper addresses two reasons why selecting stimulation parameters is difficult: the response depends on the brain’s state before stimulation, and the relationship between stimulation and response can change over time. Both factors affect how accurately a desired activity state can be reached.

The framework first trains a stimulation-response model that incorporates the pre-stimulation brain state. It then inverts this model to choose parameters for producing a target response. As new stimulation responses are observed, OMiSO updates the inverse model online. This makes parameter selection responsive to both the current state and newly collected evidence about stimulation effects.

The authors test OMiSO with intracortical microstimulation using a Utah array. It outperforms competing methods that lack these advances in achieving specified neural activity states. The result supports state-aware, adaptive stimulation as a route to more accurate neuromodulation. Scientific and clinical applications motivate the work, while the reported experimental finding concerns control of neural population activity.
summary.tldr: OMiSO uses current brain-state information and online response updates to improve stimulation-driven control of neural population activity.

title: OMiSO: Adaptive optimization of state-dependent brain stimulation to shape neural population states

abstract: Modern Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduce the cost of customizing large language models (LLMs), yet still require a separate optimization run for every downstream dataset. We introduce \textbf{Drag-and-Drop LLMs (\textit{DnD})}, a prompt-conditioned parameter generator that eliminates per-task training by mapping a handful of unlabeled task prompts directly to LoRA weight updates. A lightweight text encoder distills each prompt batch into condition embeddings, which are then transformed by a cascaded hyper-convolutional decoder into the full set of LoRA matrices. Once trained in a diverse collection of prompt-checkpoint pairs, DnD produces task-specific parameters in seconds, yielding i) up to \textbf{12,000$\times$} lower overhead than full fine-tuning, ii) average gains up to \textbf{30\%} in performance over the strongest training LoRAs on unseen common-sense reasoning, math, coding, and multimodal benchmarks, and iii) robust cross-domain generalization improving \textbf{40\%} performance without access to the target data or labels. Our results demonstrate that prompt-conditioned parameter generation is a viable alternative to gradient-based adaptation for rapidly specializing LLMs. We open source \href{https://jerryliang24.github.io/DnD}{our project} in support of future research.

paragraphs: Drag-and-Drop LLMs tackles the repeated training cost of adapting a language model to new tasks. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA reduce the number of parameters that need updating, but still require a separate optimization run for each downstream dataset. DnD instead learns to generate the adaptation parameters directly from a small batch of unlabeled task prompts.

A lightweight text encoder compresses the prompts into conditioning embeddings. A cascaded hyper-convolutional decoder then turns those embeddings into the complete set of LoRA matrices. The parameter generator itself is trained on a diverse collection of prompt-checkpoint pairs. Once that training is complete, it can produce task-specific updates in seconds without a new optimization run for each task.

The reported results include up to 12,000-fold lower overhead than full fine-tuning and average performance gains of up to 30% over the strongest training LoRAs on unseen benchmarks. The authors also report a 40% cross-domain performance improvement without target data or labels. These findings support prompt-conditioned weight generation as an empirical alternative for rapidly specializing language models.
summary.tldr: DnD learns to turn unlabeled task prompts into LoRA weights, enabling rapid adaptation without per-task optimization.

title: Drag-and-Drop LLMs: Zero-Shot Prompt-to-Weights

abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) have achieved widespread empirical success, but their theoretical expressive power remains only partially understood. In this work, we analyze a restricted idealization of fixed-precision transformers with strict future masking, soft attention, and no positional encodings. We establish that this class of models is exactly as expressive as a specific fragment of linear temporal logic that contains only a single temporal operator: the $\texttt{past}$ operator. We further connect this fragment to established classes in formal language theory, automata theory, and algebra, yielding a unified framework for understanding transformer expressivity under this idealization. Finally, we present empirical results that align closely with our theory: transformers trained on languages within their characterized expressive capacity generalize reliably across sequence lengths, while they consistently fail to generalize on languages beyond it.

paragraphs: This paper asks which sequence patterns a particular idealized class of transformers can express. The models use fixed numerical precision, strict future masking, soft attention, and no positional encodings. These restrictions define the scope of the analysis: the result characterizes this model class rather than every transformer-based language model.

The main theorem gives an exact correspondence with a fragment of linear temporal logic containing only the past operator. In practical terms, the authors describe the models’ representational capacity through a precisely specified language for expressing temporal relationships. They also connect that logical fragment to classes from formal language theory, automata theory, and algebra, bringing several mathematical perspectives into one framework.

Experiments examine whether trained transformers generalize to sequence lengths beyond those encountered during training. Models trained on languages within the characterized capacity generalize reliably in the reported tests, whereas those trained on languages outside it consistently fail to do so. This agreement links the theoretical expressivity boundary to observed length generalization under the studied idealization.
summary.tldr: A restricted class of fixed-precision transformers exactly matches a temporal-logic fragment, with experiments supporting the resulting expressivity boundary.

title: Characterizing the Expressivity of Fixed-Precision Transformer Language Models

abstract: We show how to train SVMs with an optimal guarantee on the number of support vectors (up to constants), and with sample complexity and training runtime bounds matching the best known for kernel SVM optimization (i.e. without any additional asymptotic cost beyond standard SVM training). Our method is simple to implement and works well in practice.
originalAbstract: We show how to train SVMs with an optimal guarantee on the number of support vectors (up to constants), and with sample complexity and training runtime bounds matching the best known for kernel SVM optimization (i.e. without any additional asymptotic cost beyond standard SVM training). Our method is simple to implement and works well in practice.

paragraphs: This paper studies training support vector machines with a guarantee on how many support vectors the learned model uses. Its target is sparsity in the support-vector representation. The central claim is that the number of support vectors can be made optimal up to constant factors, giving a formal guarantee on this aspect of the learned model.

The guarantee is paired with bounds on sample complexity and training time that match the best known bounds for kernel SVM optimization. In asymptotic terms, the proposed method achieves its support-vector guarantee without adding cost beyond standard SVM training. This combination matters because a sparse result is obtained together with competitive bounds on the resources needed to learn it.

The authors also describe the method as simple to implement and report that it works well in practice. The main contribution combines three properties: support-vector sparsity with an optimality guarantee up to constants, established learning and runtime bounds, and practical usability. The abstract presents these as compatible features of one training method.
summary.tldr: The method trains SVMs with an optimal support-vector count up to constants without additional asymptotic sample or training cost.

title: Learning Optimally Sparse Support Vector Machines

abstract: A commonly used approach to multiclass classification is to replace the 0-1 loss with a convex surrogate so as to make empirical risk minimization computationally tractable. Previous work has uncovered sufficient and necessary conditions for the consistency of the resulting procedures. In this paper, we strengthen these results by showing how the 0-1 excess loss of a predictor can be upper bounded as a function of the excess loss of the predictor measured using the convex surrogate. The bound is developed for the case of cost-sensitive multiclass classification and a convex surrogate loss that goes back to the work of Lee, Lin and Wahba. The bounds are as easy to calculate as in binary classification. Furthermore, we also show that our analysis extends to the analysis of the recently introduced “Simplex Coding” scheme.

In this paper, we strengthen these results by showing how the 0-1 excess loss of a predictor can be upper bounded as a function of the excess loss of the predictor measured using the convex surrogate. The bound is developed for the case of cost-sensitive multiclass classification and a convex surrogate loss that goes back to the work of Lee, Lin and Wahba. The bounds are as easy to calculate as in binary classification. Furthermore, we also show that our analysis extends to the analysis of the recently introduced “Simplex Coding” scheme.

paragraphs: Multiclass classifiers are often trained using a convex surrogate loss because directly optimizing classification errors is computationally difficult. This creates a translation problem: a training procedure improves the surrogate objective, while the eventual concern is classification performance. Earlier consistency results establish conditions connecting the two, but the paper seeks a quantitative relationship.

The authors derive an upper bound on a predictor's excess classification loss in terms of its excess surrogate loss. Excess loss measures the gap from the best achievable value of the relevant objective. Such a bound explains how progress on the tractable training objective can control the remaining gap in the classification objective.

The analysis covers cost-sensitive multiclass classification with a particular convex surrogate associated with Lee, Lin, and Wahba. The resulting bounds are reported to be as straightforward to calculate as their binary-classification counterparts. The authors also extend their analysis to Simplex Coding, showing that the reasoning applies beyond the initial surrogate formulation.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies how excess convex-surrogate loss bounds excess classification loss in cost-sensitive multiclass learning.

title: Cost-sensitive Multiclass Classification Risk Bounds

abstract: The Nyström method has been one of the most effective techniques for kernel-based approach that scales well to large data sets. Since its introduction, there has been a large body of work that improves the approximation accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. In this paper, we present a novel Nyström method that improves both accuracy and efficiency based on a new theoretical analysis. We first provide a generalized sampling scheme, CAPS, that minimizes a novel error bound based on the subspace distance. We then present our double Nyström method that reduces the size of the decomposition in two stages. We show that our method is highly efficient and accurate compared to other state-of-the-art Nyström methods by evaluating them on a number of real data sets.

Since its introduction, there has been a large body of work that improves the approximation accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. We first provide a generalized sampling scheme, CAPS, that minimizes a novel error bound based on the subspace distance. paragraphs: The Nyström method helps kernel-based learning scale by approximating a computation that would otherwise involve a large matrix. Improving approximation quality without losing computational efficiency is a central challenge. This paper proposes a method intended to improve both aspects through a new theoretical analysis.

The first component is CAPS, a generalized sampling scheme. The authors derive a new error bound based on subspace distance and design CAPS to minimize that bound. This makes the sampling decision part of the approximation analysis: the chosen samples are guided by a geometric measure associated with the resulting error guarantee.

The second component is the double Nyström method, which reduces the size of the decomposition in two stages. The two contributions address complementary parts of the problem: how to sample and how to keep the decomposition manageable. Evaluations on several real datasets show high efficiency and accuracy compared with other leading Nyström methods. These comparisons support the practical value of the theoretically motivated design on the tested data.
summary.tldr: Double Nyström combines theoretically guided sampling with two-stage decomposition reduction to improve observed approximation accuracy and efficiency.

title: Double Nyström Method: An Efficient and Accurate Nyström Scheme for Large-Scale Data Sets

abstract: Rank aggregation systems collect ordinal preferences from individuals to produce a global ranking that represents the social preference. To reduce the computational complexity of learning the global ranking, a common practice is to use rank-breaking. Individuals’ preferences are broken into pairwise comparisons and then applied to efficient algorithms tailored for independent pairwise comparisons. However, due to the ignored dependencies, naive rank-breaking approaches can result in inconsistent estimates. The key idea to produce unbiased and accurate estimates is to treat the paired comparisons outcomes unequally, depending on the topology of the collected data. In this paper, we provide the optimal rank-breaking estimator, which not only achieves consistency but also achieves the best error bound. This allows us to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between accuracy and complexity in some canonical scenarios. Further, we identify how the accuracy depends on the spectral gap of a corresponding comparison graph.

To reduce the computational complexity of learning the global ranking, a common practice is to use rank-breaking. Individuals’ preferences are broken into pairwise comparisons and then applied to efficient algorithms tailored for independent pairwise comparisons. However, due to the ignored dependencies, naive rank-breaking approaches can result in inconsistent estimates. The key idea to produce unbiased and accurate estimates is to treat the paired comparisons outcomes unequally, depending on the topology of the collected data. In this paper, we provide the optimal rank-breaking estimator, which not only achieves consistency but also achieves the best error bound. This allows us to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between accuracy and complexity in some canonical scenarios. Further, we identify how the accuracy depends on the spectral gap of a corresponding comparison graph.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines individual preferences into a shared ordering. A common computational shortcut breaks each preference into comparisons between pairs, then uses methods designed for independent pairwise observations. The problem is that comparisons derived from the same preference can be dependent. Ignoring that structure can produce estimates that remain incorrect even as more data becomes available.

This paper develops a rank-breaking estimator that treats the resulting comparisons differently according to the topology of the collected data. The central idea is that the structure of the observations should influence how much each comparison contributes. Simply converting a ranking into many pairs is therefore insufficient to ensure an accurate aggregate ranking.

The authors establish consistency and an optimal error bound for their rank-breaking estimator. They use these results to characterize accuracy–complexity tradeoffs in canonical scenarios and connect estimation accuracy to the spectral gap of an associated comparison graph. This links computational simplification to the connectivity structure of the evidence, explaining why the arrangement of comparisons matters alongside their availability.
summary.tldr: A topology-aware rank-breaking estimator preserves consistency and achieves an optimal error bound while simplifying rank aggregation.

title: Data-driven Rank Breaking for Efficient Rank Aggregation

abstract: Neural network architectures with memory and attention mechanisms exhibit certain reason- ing capabilities required for question answering. One such architecture, the dynamic memory net- work (DMN), obtained high accuracy on a variety of language tasks. However, it was not shown whether the architecture achieves strong results for question answering when supporting facts are not marked during training or whether it could be applied to other modalities such as images. Based on an analysis of the DMN, we propose several improvements to its memory and input modules. Together with these changes we introduce a novel input module for images in order to be able to answer visual questions. Our new DMN+ model improves the state of the art on both the Visual Question Answering dataset and the bAbI-10k text question-answering dataset without supporting fact supervision.
originalAbstract: Neural network architectures with memory and attention mechanisms exhibit certain reason- ing capabilities required for question answering. One such architecture, the dynamic memory net- work (DMN), obtained high accuracy on a variety of language tasks. However, it was not shown whether the architecture achieves strong results for question answering when supporting facts are not marked during training or whether it could be applied to other modalities such as images. Based on an analysis of the DMN, we propose several improvements to its memory and input modules. Together with these changes we introduce a novel input module for images in order to be able to answer visual questions. Our new DMN+ model improves the state of the art on both the Visual Question Answering dataset and the bAbI-10k text question-answering dataset without supporting fact supervision.

Earlier results showed strong performance on language tasks, but left two questions open: whether the architecture could perform strongly without training annotations identifying supporting facts, and whether it could handle questions about images. This paper addresses both questions through changes to the architecture.

The authors analyze the existing network and improve its memory and input modules. They also introduce an image input module, allowing visual information to enter the question-answering system. The resulting model, DMN+, extends the architecture’s scope while revising the components responsible for receiving information and using memory.

DMN+ improves the state of the art on the Visual Question Answering dataset and the bAbI-10k text question-answering dataset without supporting-fact supervision. This matters because the training process does not require explicit markings of the facts needed to answer each question. The results support the revised architecture across both visual and textual tasks, with the claim grounded in these two benchmark evaluations.
summary.tldr: DMN+ improves memory and input processing to advance visual and textual question answering without supporting-fact supervision.

title: Dynamic Memory Networks for Visual and Textual Question Answering

abstract: Efficient unsupervised training and inference in deep generative models remains a challenging problem. One basic approach, called Helmholtz machine or Variational Autoencoder, involves training a top-down directed generative model together with a bottom-up auxiliary model used for approximate inference. Recent results indicate that better generative models can be obtained with better approximate inference procedures. Instead of improving the inference procedure, we here propose a new model, the bidirectional Helmholtz machine, which guarantees that the top-down and bottom-up distributions can efficiently invert each other. We achieve this by interpreting both the top-down and the bottom-up directed models as approximate inference distributions and by defining the model distribution to be the geometric mean of these two. We present a lower-bound for the likelihood of this model and we show that optimizing this bound regularizes the model so that the Bhattacharyya distance between the bottom-up and top-down approximate distributions is minimized. This approach results in state of the art generative models which prefer significantly deeper architectures while it allows for orders of magnitude more efficient likelihood estimation.

This paper changes how those two directions define the model, motivated by the connection between inference quality and the quality of learned generative models.

The bidirectional Helmholtz machine treats both directed networks as approximate inference distributions. The model distribution is defined through their geometric mean. This construction guarantees efficient inversion between the top-down and bottom-up distributions. The authors also derive a lower bound on likelihood that provides an objective for training the resulting model.

The reported results include state-of-the-art generative performance, a preference for substantially deeper architectures, and likelihood estimation that is orders of magnitude more efficient. The central contribution is to make agreement between the two inference directions part of the generative model itself.
summary.tldr: Bidirectional Helmholtz machines combine top-down and bottom-up distributions through a geometric mean, improving generative modeling and likelihood-estimation efficiency.

title: Bidirectional Helmholtz Machines

abstract: In this paper we develop a new framework that captures the common landscape underlying the common non-convex low-rank matrix problems including matrix sensing, matrix completion and robust PCA. In particular, we show for all above problems (including asymmetric cases): 1) all local minima are also globally optimal; 2) no high-order saddle points exists. These results explain why simple algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent have global converge, and efficiently optimize these non-convex objective functions in practice. Our framework connects and simplifies the existing analyses on optimization landscapes for matrix sensing and symmetric matrix completion. The framework naturally leads to new results for asymmetric matrix completion and robust PCA.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix problems often use nonconvex objectives, making their apparent optimization difficulty hard to reconcile with the success of simple algorithms. This paper develops a common geometric framework for matrix sensing, matrix completion, and robust PCA. It studies the landscape of their objectives to explain what kinds of stationary points optimization can encounter.

For the problems analyzed, including asymmetric cases, the authors show that every local minimum is globally optimal and that there are no high-order saddle points. The first result rules out locally attractive solutions with worse objective values than the global optimum. The second further restricts the kinds of saddle-point geometry present in these landscapes.

These structural results explain why methods such as stochastic gradient descent can converge globally and efficiently optimize the studied nonconvex objectives in practice. The framework connects and simplifies existing analyses for matrix sensing and symmetric matrix completion. It also produces new results for asymmetric matrix completion and robust PCA, giving several problems a shared explanation rather than treating their optimization behavior separately.
summary.tldr: A unified landscape analysis shows that the studied low-rank objectives have globally optimal local minima and no high-order saddle points.

title: No Spurious Local Minima in Nonconvex Low Rank Problems: A Unified Geometric Analysis

abstract: Hidden units can play essential roles in modeling time-series having long-term dependency or on-linearity but make it difficult to learn associated parameters. Here we propose a way to learn such a time-series model by training a backward model for the time-reversed time-series, where the backward model has a common set of parameters as the original (forward) model. Our key observation is that only a subset of the parameters is hard to learn, and that subset is complementary between the forward model and the backward model. By training both of the two models, we can effectively learn the values of the parameters that are hard to learn if only either of the two models is trained. We apply bidirectional learning to a dynamic Boltzmann machine extended with hidden units. Numerical experiments with synthetic and real datasets clearly demonstrate advantages of bidirectional learning.

paragraphs: Hidden units can help time-series models represent long-term dependencies and complex relationships, but they also make parameter learning difficult. This paper asks whether the direction in which a sequence is modeled can help address that difficulty. Its proposal trains both an ordinary forward model and a model of the time-reversed sequence.

The two models share parameters. The central observation is that the parameters that are difficult to learn in one direction form a complementary subset to those that are difficult in the other. Training both directions therefore provides a way to improve estimates of parameters that would be poorly learned from either direction alone.

The authors apply this bidirectional learning procedure to a dynamic Boltzmann machine extended with hidden units. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate advantages for the approach. The contribution is a training strategy that uses complementary information from temporal directions: reversing the sequence becomes a means of learning shared parameters more effectively, rather than merely another way to present the data.
summary.tldr: Training shared-parameter time-series models in both temporal directions helps learn parameters that are difficult to estimate in either direction alone.

title: Bidirectional Learning for Time-series Models with Hidden Units

abstract: We study the parameter tuning problem for the penalized regression model. Finding the optimal choice of the regularization parameter is a challenging problem in high-dimensional regimes where both the number of observations n and the number of parameters p are large. We propose two frameworks to obtain a computationally efficient approximation ALO of the leave-one-out cross validation (LOOCV) risk for nonsmooth losses and regularizers. Our two frameworks are based on the primal and dual formulations of the penalized regression model. We prove the equivalence of the two approaches under smoothness conditions. This equivalence enables us to justify the accuracy of both methods under such conditions. We use our approaches to obtain a risk estimate for several standard problems, including generalized LASSO, nuclear norm regularization and support vector machines. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of our results for non-differentiable cases.

The paper targets leave-one-out cross-validation risk, using an efficient approximation to support parameter selection in this setting.

The authors develop two approximation frameworks, one based on the primal formulation of penalized regression and the other on its dual formulation. Both address models with nonsmooth losses or regularizers. Under smoothness conditions, they prove that the two approaches are equivalent and use this connection to justify the accuracy of their approximations.

The frameworks yield risk estimates for generalized LASSO, nuclear norm regularization, and support vector machines. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in nondifferentiable cases, extending the practical evidence beyond the smooth setting covered by the stated equivalence argument. The contribution is therefore both a pair of computational approaches and an explanation of how they relate under specific mathematical conditions.
summary.tldr: Two primal and dual frameworks efficiently approximate leave-one-out risk for tuning penalized regression, including models with nonsmooth components.

title: Approximate Leave-One-Out for Fast Parameter Tuning in High Dimensions

abstract: We consider the PAC learnability of the local functions at the vertices of a discrete networked dynamical system, assuming that the underlying network is known. Our focus is on the learnability of threshold functions. We show that several variants of threshold functions are PAC learnable and provide tight bounds on the sample complexity. In general, when the input consists of positive and negative examples, we show that the concept class of threshold functions is not efficiently PAC learnable, unless NP = RP. Using a dynamic programming approach, we show efficient PAC learnability when the number of negative examples is small. We also present an efficient learner which is consistent with all the positive examples and at least (1-1/e) fraction of the negative examples. This algorithm is based on maximizing a submodular function under matroid constraints. By performing experiments on both synthetic and real-world networks, we study how the network structure and sample complexity influence the quality of the inferred system.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning the local update rules at vertices of a discrete networked dynamical system, assuming the network itself is known. Its focus is on threshold functions and PAC learnability, which connects the amount of training data to reliable learning guarantees. Several threshold-function variants are shown to be learnable, with tight sample-complexity bounds.

The authors identify a tractable case when the number of negative examples is small and provide an efficient dynamic-programming approach for that case.

They also give an efficient learner that satisfies every positive example and at least a 1−1/e fraction of negative examples. This algorithm uses submodular maximization under matroid constraints. Experiments on synthetic and real networks examine how network structure and sample requirements affect the inferred system. The results distinguish how much evidence learning needs from how difficult it is computationally, while offering exact or partial solutions for specified settings.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes statistical and computational limits of learning network threshold rules and supplies efficient learners for restricted or partial-consistency settings.

title: PAC Learnability of Node Functions in Networked Dynamical Systems

abstract: Compressed sensing (CS) provides an elegant framework for recovering sparse signals from compressed measurements. For example, CS can exploit the structure of natural images and recover an image from only a few random measurements. Unlike popular autoencoding models, reconstruction in CS is posed as an optimisation problem that is separate from sensing. CS is flexible and data efficient, but its application has been restricted by the strong assumption of sparsity and costly reconstruction process. A recent approach that combines CS with neural network generators has removed the constraint of sparsity, but reconstruction remains slow. Here we propose a novel framework that significantly improves both the performance and speed of signal recovery by jointly training a generator and the optimisation process for reconstruction via meta-learning. We explore training the measurements with different objectives, and derive a family of models based on minimising measurement errors. We show that Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs) can be viewed as a special case in this family of models. Borrowing insights from the CS perspective, we develop a novel way of improving GANs using gradient information from the discriminator.

Traditional approaches rely strongly on sparsity and can require expensive reconstruction. Neural generators offer another way to represent signal structure, removing the sparsity requirement in a recent approach, but recovery through those generators can still be slow.

This paper jointly trains a generator and the optimization process used to reconstruct signals. Meta-learning connects the model of possible signals with the procedure that searches for a reconstruction matching the measurements. The authors report significant improvements in both recovery performance and speed, addressing the reconstruction bottleneck alongside the choice of signal representation.

The work also explores learning measurements under different objectives and derives a family of models based on minimizing measurement errors. Within that family, generative adversarial networks appear as a special case. This connection leads to a proposed GAN improvement using gradient information from the discriminator, extending the compressed-sensing perspective beyond the original signal-recovery task.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a signal generator and its reconstruction process improves compressed sensing and yields a connection to GAN training.

title: Deep Compressed Sensing

abstract: We study the problem of efficiently estimating the effect of an intervention on a single variable using observational samples. Our goal is to give algorithms with polynomial time and sample complexity in a non-parametric setting. Tian and Pearl (AAAI ’02) have exactly characterized the class of causal graphs for which causal effects of atomic interventions can be identified from observational data. We make their result quantitative. Suppose 𝒫 is a causal model on a set V of n observable variables with respect to a given causal graph G, and let do(x) be an identifiable intervention on a variable X. We show that assuming that G has bounded in-degree and bounded c-components (k) and that the observational distribution satisfies a strong positivity condition: (i) [Evaluation] There is an algorithm that outputs with probability 2/3 an evaluator for a distribution P^ that satisfies TV(P(V | do(x)), P^(V)) < eps using m=O (n/eps^2) samples from P and O(mn) time. The evaluator can return in O(n) time the probability P^(v) for any assignment v to V. (ii) [Sampling] There is an algorithm that outputs with probability 2/3 a sampler for a distribution P^ that satisfies TV(P(V | do(x)), P^(V)) < eps using m=O (n/eps^2) samples from P and O(mn) time. The sampler returns an iid sample from P^ with probability 1 in O(n) time. We extend our techniques to estimate P(Y | do(x)) for a subset Y of variables of interest. We also show lower bounds for the sample complexity, demonstrating that our sample complexity has optimal dependence on the parameters n and eps, as well as if k=1 on the strong positivity parameter.
