The authors make that question quantitative by providing algorithms with polynomial time and sample requirements in a nonparametric setting.

The guarantees require an identifiable intervention, a given graph with bounded in-degree and bounded c-components, and a strong positivity condition on the observational distribution. Each construction succeeds with probability two-thirds.

Extensions cover effects on a subset of variables. Lower bounds establish optimal dependence on n and epsilon, and on the positivity parameter when the c-component bound is one, connecting causal identifiability to concrete resource guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under stated graph and positivity assumptions, the paper efficiently learns evaluators and samplers for identifiable single-variable intervention distributions.

title: Learning and Sampling of Atomic Interventions from Observations

abstract: Data containing human or social attributes may over- or under-represent groups with respect to salient social attributes such as gender or race, which can lead to biases in downstream applications. This paper presents an algorithmic framework that can be used as a data preprocessing method towards mitigating such bias. Unlike prior work, it can efficiently learn distributions over large domains, controllably adjust the representation rates of protected groups and achieve target fairness metrics such as statistical parity, yet remains close to the empirical distribution induced by the given dataset. Our approach leverages the principle of maximum entropy {–} amongst all distributions satisfying a given set of constraints, we should choose the one closest in KL-divergence to a given prior. While maximum entropy distributions can succinctly encode distributions over large domains, they can be difficult to compute. Our main contribution is an instantiation of this framework for our set of constraints and priors, which encode our bias mitigation goals, and that runs in time polynomial in the dimension of the data. Empirically, we observe that samples from the learned distribution have desired representation rates and statistical rates, and when used for training a classifier incurs only a slight loss in accuracy while maintaining fairness properties.

paragraphs: This paper addresses bias that can arise when datasets overrepresent or underrepresent social groups. It proposes a preprocessing framework that learns a new data distribution with controlled group representation and target fairness properties, such as statistical parity. At the same time, the framework aims to remain close to the empirical distribution of the original dataset.

The approach expresses bias-mitigation goals as constraints on a maximum-entropy distribution. Among distributions satisfying those constraints, it selects one closest to a specified prior in KL divergence. This makes the desired adjustments explicit rather than treating preprocessing as an unspecified balancing operation. The main computational contribution is a construction for the authors’ chosen constraints and priors that runs in time polynomial in the data dimension.

In the reported experiments, samples from the learned distribution attain the desired representation and statistical rates. Classifiers trained on those samples retain fairness properties while showing only a slight accuracy loss. These results support the framework as a way to make targeted changes to training data while preserving much of its predictive usefulness.
summary.tldr: A maximum-entropy preprocessing framework adjusts group representation and fairness statistics while keeping the learned data distribution close to the original.

title: Data preprocessing to mitigate bias: A maximum entropy based approach

abstract: We study the problem of learning adversarially robust halfspaces in the distribution-independent setting. In the realizable setting, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the adversarial perturbation sets under which halfspaces are efficiently robustly learnable. In the presence of random label noise, we give a simple computationally efficient algorithm for this problem with respect to any $\ell_p$-perturbation.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of learning adversarially robust halfspaces in the distribution-independent setting. In the realizable setting, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the adversarial perturbation sets under which halfspaces are efficiently robustly learnable. In the presence of random label noise, we give a simple computationally efficient algorithm for this problem with respect to any $\ell_p$-perturbation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn halfspaces, classifiers that separate inputs using a linear boundary, when an adversary can perturb the inputs. Robust learning must account for those allowed changes when finding a classifier. The setting is distribution-independent, so the investigation does not rely on choosing a particular input distribution.

The first result addresses the realizable setting, where the learning problem admits a suitable classifier. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions on the adversarial perturbation sets for efficient robust learning of halfspaces. This characterizes which permitted changes allow an efficient solution in that setting. Both directions matter: the conditions establish when learning is possible and identify requirements for that possibility.

The second result introduces random label noise, so the observed labels can be corrupted. For this case, the authors provide a simple, computationally efficient algorithm covering any perturbation defined by an ℓp norm. Together, the results address both the structure of allowable adversarial changes and the additional challenge of unreliable labels.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes efficient robust learning of halfspaces in the realizable setting and gives an efficient algorithm for ℓp perturbations with random label noise.

title: Efficiently Learning Adversarially Robust Halfspaces with Noise

abstract: Several approximate inference algorithms have been proposed to minimize an alpha-divergence between an approximating distribution and a target distribution. Many of these algorithms introduce bias, the magnitude of which becomes problematic in high dimensions. Other algorithms are unbiased. These often seem to suffer from high variance, but little is rigorously known. In this work we study unbiased methods for alpha-divergence minimization through the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) of the gradient estimator. We study several representative scenarios where strong analytical results are possible, such as fully-factorized or Gaussian distributions. We find that when alpha is not zero, the SNR worsens exponentially in the dimensionality of the problem. This casts doubt on the practicality of these methods. We empirically confirm these theoretical results.

In this work we study unbiased methods for alpha-divergence minimization through the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) of the gradient estimator. paragraphs: Approximate inference often fits a manageable distribution to a target by minimizing an alpha-divergence. Some optimization methods introduce bias that becomes problematic in high dimensions. Unbiased methods avoid that particular issue, but their gradient estimates can be highly variable. This paper studies whether the useful optimization signal survives that variability.

The authors analyze the signal-to-noise ratio of unbiased gradient estimators in representative settings that permit strong mathematical results, including fully factorized and Gaussian distributions. They find that for nonzero alpha, the ratio deteriorates exponentially as dimensionality increases. Within these analyzed settings, a gradient estimator can therefore be unbiased while still providing a progressively weaker signal relative to its noise.

Experiments confirm the theoretical behavior. The result casts doubt on the practicality of these unbiased approaches in high dimensions, because eliminating bias alone does not ensure an informative optimization direction. The scope of the finding matters: it concerns the studied scenarios and nonzero alpha. Its broader contribution is to make signal quality, alongside bias, a central criterion for assessing divergence-minimization methods.
summary.tldr: In analyzed settings with nonzero alpha, unbiased divergence-gradient estimators lose signal-to-noise ratio exponentially with dimension.

title: On the difficulty of unbiased alpha divergence minimization

abstract: We propose UCBMQ, Upper Confidence Bound Momentum Q-learning, a new algorithm for reinforcement learning in tabular and possibly stage-dependent, episodic Markov decision process. UCBMQ is based on Q-learning where we add a momentum term and rely on the principle of optimism in face of uncertainty to deal with exploration. Our new technical ingredient of UCBMQ is the use of momentum to correct the bias that Q-learning suffers while, \emph{at the same time}, limiting the impact it has on the second-order term of the regret. For UCBMQ, we are able to guarantee a regret of at most $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^3SAT}+ H^4 S A)$ where $H$ is the length of an episode, $S$ the number of states, $A$ the number of actions, $T$ the number of episodes and ignoring terms in poly$\log(SAHT)$. Notably, UCBMQ is the first algorithm that simultaneously matches the lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{H^3SAT})$ for large enough $T$ and has a second-order term (with respect to $T$) that scales \emph{only linearly} with the number of states $S$.

paragraphs: UCB Momentum Q-learning, or UCBMQ, is designed for episodic reinforcement learning with tabular states and actions. The environment may depend on the stage within an episode. The algorithm combines Q-learning with a momentum term and optimistic estimates that encourage exploration when the agent remains uncertain.

The technical contribution is using momentum to correct Q-learning’s bias while controlling its contribution to the second-order regret term. The guarantee has a leading term proportional to the square root of H³SAT and an additional H⁴SA term, apart from logarithmic factors. Here H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T counts episodes.

For sufficiently many episodes, the leading term matches the stated lower-bound scaling up to logarithmic factors. At the same time, the additional term grows only linearly with the number of states. The authors identify UCBMQ as the first algorithm to achieve both properties together. This matters because the guarantee controls both long-run regret and the extra contribution associated with the state-space size.
summary.tldr: UCBMQ uses momentum to correct Q-learning bias while combining near-optimal leading regret with a second-order term linear in state count.

title: UCB Momentum Q-learning: Correcting the bias without forgetting

abstract: Machine learning systems often do not share the same inductive biases as humans and, as a result, extrapolate or generalize in ways that are inconsistent with our expectations. The trade-off between exemplar- and rule-based generalization has been studied extensively in cognitive psychology; in this work, we present a protocol inspired by these experimental approaches to probe the inductive biases that control this trade-off in category-learning systems such as artificial neural networks. We isolate two such inductive biases: feature-level bias (differences in which features are more readily learned) and exemplar-vs-rule bias (differences in how these learned features are used for generalization of category labels). We find that standard neural network models are feature-biased and have a propensity towards exemplar-based extrapolation; we discuss the implications of these findings for machine-learning research on data augmentation, fairness, and systematic generalization.

paragraphs: A learning system can extend category labels by applying a rule or by relying on resemblance to examples it has encountered. These approaches can produce different predictions beyond the training data. This paper draws on experimental methods from cognitive psychology to probe which tendencies guide category-learning systems, including neural networks.

The protocol separates two sources of inductive bias. Feature-level bias concerns which features a model learns more readily. Exemplar-versus-rule bias concerns how the model uses the features it has learned when generalizing labels. Separating these questions helps distinguish a preference for certain information from a preference for a particular way of using that information.

The authors find that standard neural networks exhibit feature biases and a tendency toward exemplar-based extrapolation. These findings help explain why their generalization may differ from human expectations. The paper discusses implications for data augmentation, fairness, and systematic generalization, framing these as areas where understanding the source of a model's inductive bias can matter.
summary.tldr: A psychology-inspired protocol separates feature preferences from rule-versus-example preferences and finds both biases in standard neural networks.

title: Distinguishing rule and exemplar-based generalization in learning systems

abstract: The K-subspaces (KSS) method is a generalization of the K-means method for subspace clustering. In this work, we present local convergence analysis and a recovery guarantee for KSS, assuming data are generated by the semi-random union of subspaces model, where $N$ points are randomly sampled from $K \ge 2$ overlapping subspaces. We show that if the initial assignment of the KSS method lies within a neighborhood of a true clustering, it converges at a superlinear rate and finds the correct clustering within $\Theta(\log\log N)$ iterations with high probability. Moreover, we propose a thresholding inner-product based spectral method for initialization and prove that it produces a point in this neighborhood. We also present numerical results of the studied method to support our theoretical developments.

paragraphs: K-subspaces extends k-means by grouping points around subspaces rather than centers. Despite its natural formulation, understanding when it recovers the correct groups requires accounting for both initialization and the geometry of overlapping subspaces. This paper analyzes data drawn from a semi-random union-of-subspaces model.

If the initial assignments are sufficiently close to the true clustering, the authors prove superlinear convergence. With high probability, the algorithm finds the correct grouping within Θ(log log N) iterations for N sampled points. This is a local guarantee, so a good starting point is a necessary part of the result.

To address initialization, the paper proposes a spectral method based on thresholded inner products and proves that it enters the required neighborhood. Numerical experiments support the theoretical developments. Together, the initialization and convergence results explain how K-subspaces can recover clustering under the stated data model, rather than assuming a favorable initial assignment without a way to obtain it.
summary.tldr: A spectral initialization and local analysis give fast, high-probability recovery guarantees for K-subspaces clustering.

title: Convergence and Recovery Guarantees of the K-Subspaces Method for Subspace Clustering

abstract: Learning representations that can decompose a multi-object scene into its constituent objects and recompose them flexibly is desirable for object-oriented reasoning and planning. Built upon object masks in the pixel space, existing metrics for objectness can only evaluate generative models with an object-specific “slot” structure. We propose to directly measure compositionality in the representation space as a form of objections, making such evaluations tractable for a wider class of models. Our metric, COAT (Compositional Object Algebra Test), evaluates if a generic representation exhibits certain geometric properties that underpin object compositionality beyond what is already captured by the raw pixel space. Our experiments on the popular CLEVR (Johnson et.al., 2018) domain reveal that existing disentanglement-based generative models are not as compositional as one might expect, suggesting room for further modeling improvements. We hope our work allows for a unified evaluation of object-centric representations, spanning generative as well as discriminative, self-supervised models.

paragraphs: A useful representation of a scene should support separating its objects and combining them in different arrangements. Existing objectness metrics often assess pixel masks and assume that a generative model assigns objects to dedicated slots. That requirement restricts which models can be evaluated, even when other representations might contain meaningful object structure.

COAT, the Compositional Object Algebra Test, moves the evaluation into representation space. It checks geometric properties that support object composition in a generic representation. The intended distinction is between compositional structure learned by the model and structure already available in raw pixels. This makes the evaluation applicable to a wider class of models than methods requiring object-specific slots.

Experiments on CLEVR find that existing generative models based on disentanglement are less compositional than might be expected. Separating factors of variation therefore does not, in these experiments, deliver the anticipated degree of object composition. The authors hope COAT can support a common evaluation approach across generative, discriminative, and self-supervised representations, while exposing opportunities to improve their object structure.
summary.tldr: COAT evaluates object compositionality directly in representation space, revealing weaker-than-expected composition in tested disentanglement-based generative models.

title: COAT: Measuring Object Compositionality in Emergent Representations

abstract: Many resource management problems require sequential decision-making under uncertainty, where the only uncertainty affecting the decision outcomes are exogenous variables outside the control of the decision-maker. We model these problems as Exo-MDPs (Markov Decision Processes with Exogenous Inputs) and design a class of data-efficient algorithms for them termed Hindsight Learning (HL). Our HL algorithms achieve data efficiency by leveraging a key insight: having samples of the exogenous variables, past decisions can be revisited in hindsight to infer counterfactual consequences that can accelerate policy improvements. We compare HL against classic baselines in the multi-secretary and airline revenue management problems. We also scale our algorithms to a business-critical cloud resource management problem – allocating Virtual Machines (VMs) to physical machines, and simulate their performance with real datasets from a large public cloud provider. We find that HL algorithms outperform domain-specific heuristics, as well as state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods.

paragraphs: Many resource-management decisions unfold over time while external events determine uncertain outcomes. This paper focuses on problems where all uncertainty comes from variables outside the decision-maker’s control. It represents them as Markov decision processes with exogenous inputs, or Exo-MDPs, and develops Hindsight Learning algorithms to exploit that structure.

The key observation is that samples of external inputs can help evaluate decisions that were not actually taken. Looking back at a past situation, the learner can infer counterfactual consequences under those inputs and use them to improve its policy. This creates additional learning value from available samples, providing the basis for the approach’s data efficiency.

The authors evaluate Hindsight Learning on multi-secretary and airline revenue-management problems. They also apply it to allocating virtual machines across physical machines, simulating performance with real data from a large public cloud provider. The reported algorithms outperform domain-specific heuristics and leading reinforcement learning methods in the evaluations, supporting hindsight-based policy improvement for this structured class of decision problems.
summary.tldr: Hindsight Learning reuses external-event samples to infer counterfactual outcomes and improve policies efficiently in resource-management problems.

title: Hindsight Learning for MDPs with Exogenous Inputs

abstract: Minimax-fair machine learning minimizes the error for the worst-off group. However, empirical evidence suggests that when sophisticated models are trained with standard empirical risk minimization (ERM), they often have the same performance on the worst-off group as a minimax-trained model. Our work makes this counter-intuitive observation concrete. We prove that if the hypothesis class is sufficiently expressive and the group information is recoverable from the features, ERM and minimax-fairness learning formulations indeed have the same performance on the worst-off group. We provide additional empirical evidence of how this observation holds on a wide range of datasets and hypothesis classes. Since ERM is fundamentally easier than minimax optimization, our findings have implications on the practice of fair machine learning.

paragraphs: Minimax-fair learning focuses on reducing error for the group with the worst performance. Ordinary empirical risk minimization instead optimizes the overall training objective. Yet sophisticated models trained with the ordinary approach can empirically match minimax-trained models on the worst-off group. This paper gives a theoretical explanation for when that apparent coincidence occurs.

The result requires two conditions: the hypothesis class must be sufficiently expressive, and group membership must be recoverable from the input features. Under these conditions, the two learning formulations have the same performance on the worst-off group. The claim concerns this performance criterion and depends on both conditions being satisfied.

The authors also provide empirical evidence across a wide range of datasets and hypothesis classes. Because empirical risk minimization is fundamentally easier to optimize than a minimax objective, the equivalence has practical implications for choosing a training method. It identifies circumstances in which the simpler formulation can achieve the same worst-group performance, connecting model capacity and feature information to the need for explicit minimax optimization.
summary.tldr: ERM and minimax-fair learning match worst-group performance when models are sufficiently expressive and group membership is recoverable from features.

title: When do Minimax-fair Learning and Empirical Risk Minimization Coincide?

abstract: Diffusion models have exhibited excellent performance in various domains. The probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE) of diffusion models (i.e., diffusion ODEs) is a particular case of continuous normalizing flows (CNFs), which enables deterministic inference and exact likelihood evaluation. However, the likelihood estimation results by diffusion ODEs are still far from those of the state-of-the-art likelihood-based generative models. In this work, we propose several improved techniques for maximum likelihood estimation for diffusion ODEs, including both training and evaluation perspectives. For training, we propose velocity parameterization and explore variance reduction techniques for faster convergence. We also derive an error-bounded high-order flow matching objective for finetuning, which improves the ODE likelihood and smooths its trajectory. For evaluation, we propose a novel training-free truncated-normal dequantization to fill the training-evaluation gap commonly existing in diffusion ODEs. Building upon these techniques, we achieve state-of-the-art likelihood estimation results on image datasets (2.56 on CIFAR-10, 3.43/3.69 on ImageNet-32) without variational dequantization or data augmentation.

paragraphs: The probability flow ordinary differential equation associated with a diffusion model supports deterministic inference and exact likelihood evaluation. Nevertheless, the paper observes that diffusion ODEs have lagged behind leading likelihood-based generative models on likelihood performance. It addresses that gap through changes to both training and evaluation.

For training, the authors introduce velocity parameterization and investigate variance reduction to speed convergence. They also derive a higher-order flow-matching objective with an error bound for fine-tuning. This objective improves ODE likelihood and makes the trajectory smoother, connecting the training criterion with the behavior of the continuous transformation used by the model.

For evaluation, the paper introduces truncated-normal dequantization that requires no additional training and addresses a mismatch between training and evaluation. Combining the proposed techniques yields reported state-of-the-art likelihood results on image datasets, including 2.56 on CIFAR-10 and 3.43/3.69 on ImageNet-32. These results are achieved without variational dequantization or data augmentation. The contribution is a coordinated set of training and evaluation improvements for diffusion ODE likelihood modeling.
summary.tldr: Improved training objectives, parameterization, and evaluation dequantization strengthen diffusion ODE likelihood results on image datasets.

title: Improved Techniques for Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Diffusion ODEs

abstract: We introduce HyperFields, a method for generating text-conditioned Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) with a single forward pass and (optionally) some fine-tuning. Key to our approach are: (i) a dynamic hypernetwork, which learns a smooth mapping from text token embeddings to the space of NeRFs; (ii) NeRF distillation training, which distills scenes encoded in individual NeRFs into one dynamic hypernetwork. These techniques enable a single network to fit over a hundred unique scenes. We further demonstrate that HyperFields learns a more general map between text and NeRFs, and consequently is capable of predicting novel in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenes — either zero-shot or with a few finetuning steps. Finetuning HyperFields benefits from accelerated convergence thanks to the learned general map, and is capable of synthesizing novel scenes 5 to 10 times faster than existing neural optimization-based methods. Our ablation experiments show that both the dynamic architecture and NeRF distillation are critical to the expressivity of HyperFields.

paragraphs: HyperFields generates text-conditioned Neural Radiance Fields, or NeRFs, through a single forward pass, with optional fine-tuning. The goal is to learn a reusable connection between text and scene representations so that generating a new scene can benefit from knowledge already captured by a trained network.

The method combines a dynamic hypernetwork with NeRF distillation. The hypernetwork learns a smooth mapping from text-token embeddings into the space of NeRFs. Distillation transfers scenes represented by separate NeRFs into that shared network. Together, these components allow one network to fit more than a hundred distinct scenes.

The authors demonstrate generation of novel scenes both within and outside the training distribution, either directly or with a few fine-tuning steps. When fine-tuning is used, the learned mapping accelerates convergence, enabling novel-scene synthesis five to ten times faster than existing neural optimization-based methods in the reported comparisons. Ablations identify both the dynamic architecture and distillation as critical to expressivity. The findings support reusable scene-generation knowledge, while preserving the distinction between zero-shot generation and generation that benefits from additional optimization.
summary.tldr: HyperFields learns a shared text-to-NeRF mapping that supports zero-shot scene generation and faster optional fine-tuning.

title: HyperFields: Towards Zero-Shot Generation of NeRFs from Text

abstract: Attention-based architectures, in particular transformers, are at the heart of a technological revolution. Interestingly, in addition to helping obtain state-of-the-art results on a wide range of applications, the attention mechanism intrinsically provides meaningful insights on the internal behavior of the model. Can these insights be used as explanations? Debate rages on. In this paper, we mathematically study a simple attention-based architecture and pinpoint the differences between post-hoc and attention-based explanations. We show that they provide quite different results, and that, despite their limitations, post-hoc methods are capable of capturing more useful insights than merely examining the attention weights.

We show that they provide quite different results, and that, despite their limitations, post-hoc methods are capable of capturing more useful insights than merely examining the attention weights.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms expose weights that offer a view into a model’s internal behavior. That visibility makes them tempting to use as explanations, but the paper asks whether inspecting those weights provides the same understanding as an explanation produced after the model makes a prediction. The distinction matters because an accessible internal signal can still give an incomplete account.

The authors investigate this question mathematically using a simple attention-based architecture. They compare attention-based explanations with post-hoc explanations and identify differences between what the two approaches reveal. Their analysis finds that the resulting explanations can differ substantially, so the methods should not be treated as interchangeable ways of describing the model.

Within this analysis, post-hoc methods can capture more useful insights than attention weights alone, despite having limitations themselves. The contribution is a mathematical clarification of the debate over attention as explanation. It supports looking beyond attention weights when interpreting the studied architecture, while keeping the conclusion tied to the simple setting the authors analyze.
summary.tldr: A mathematical analysis of a simple attention architecture shows that post-hoc explanations can reveal more useful insights than attention weights alone.

title: Attention Meets Post-hoc Interpretability: A Mathematical Perspective

abstract: High utility and rigorous data privacy are of the main goals of a federated learning (FL) system, which learns a model from the data distributed among some clients. The latter has been tried to achieve by using differential privacy in FL (DPFL). There is often heterogeneity in clients’ privacy requirements, and existing DPFL works either assume uniform privacy requirements for clients or are not applicable when server is not fully trusted (our setting). Furthermore, there is often heterogeneity in batch and/or dataset size of clients, which as shown, results in extra variation in the DP noise level across clients’ model updates. With these sources of heterogeneity, straightforward aggregation strategies, e.g., assigning clients’ aggregation weights proportional to their privacy parameters ($\epsilon$) will lead to lower utility. We propose Robust-HDP, which efficiently estimates the true noise level in clients’ model updates and reduces the noise-level in the aggregated model updates considerably. Robust-HDP improves utility and convergence speed, while being safe to the clients that may maliciously send falsified privacy parameter $\epsilon$ to server. Extensive experimental results on multiple datasets and our theoretical analysis confirm the effectiveness of Robust-HDP. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/Saber-mm/HDPFL.git

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from clients whose data remain distributed. Adding differential privacy introduces noise, but clients can have different privacy requirements, dataset sizes, and batch sizes. This paper shows that these differences produce varying noise levels in their updates, complicating how the server should combine them.

Robust-HDP estimates the actual noise in client updates and uses that information to reduce noise in the aggregate. This addresses a weakness of simple aggregation rules, such as weighting clients in proportion to their privacy parameters. A reported privacy parameter alone does not capture all the factors determining an update's noise level.

The method targets a setting where the server is not fully trusted. It also remains safe against clients that submit falsified privacy parameters, according to the abstract. Theoretical analysis and experiments on multiple datasets support improved utility and faster convergence. The contribution is to make heterogeneous private aggregation responsive to estimated update noise, connecting the privacy setting to the quality of the shared learning signal.
summary.tldr: Robust-HDP estimates client-update noise to improve federated learning with heterogeneous privacy requirements and data sizes.

title: Noise-Aware Algorithm for Heterogeneous Differentially Private Federated Learning

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to improving the training stability of self-supervised learning (SSL) methods by leveraging a non-parametric memory of seen concepts. The proposed method involves augmenting a neural network with a memory component to stochastically compare current image views with previously encountered concepts. Additionally, we introduce stochastic memory blocks to regularize training and enforce consistency between image views. We extensively benchmark our method on many vision tasks, such as linear probing, transfer learning, few-shot classification, and image retrieval on many datasets. The experimental results consolidate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving stable SSL training without additional regularizers while learning highly transferable representations and requiring less computing time and resources.

We extensively benchmark our method on many vision tasks, such as linear probing, transfer learning, few-shot classification, and image retrieval on many datasets. The experimental results consolidate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving stable SSL training without additional regularizers while learning highly transferable representations and requiring less computing time and resources.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning aims to develop useful image representations, but keeping training stable is an important challenge. This paper introduces a memory of previously encountered concepts as an additional resource for learning. The memory gives the network a way to compare its current image views with information retained from earlier observations.

The approach augments the network with a non-parametric memory component and makes those comparisons stochastically. It also introduces stochastic memory blocks that regularize training and encourage consistency between image views. Memory therefore serves both as a source of comparison and as part of the mechanism that stabilizes representation learning.

The authors evaluate the approach across multiple datasets using linear probing, transfer learning, few-shot classification, and image retrieval. Their experiments support stable training without additional regularizers, transferable representations, and lower computing time and resource requirements. The range of evaluations matters because it examines whether the learned visual features remain useful beyond the original training process, including when transferred to other tasks or used with few labeled examples.
summary.tldr: A memory of previously seen concepts helps stabilize self-supervised visual learning and produces transferable features with lower reported computing requirements.

title: Learning from Memory: Non-Parametric Memory Augmented Self-Supervised Learning of Visual Features

abstract: Animals can swiftly adapt to novel tasks, while maintaining proficiency on previously trained tasks. This contrasts starkly with machine learning models, which struggle on these capabilities. We first propose a new task, the sequential Morris Water Maze (sWM), which extends a widely used task in the psychology and neuroscience fields and requires both rapid and continual learning. It has frequently been hypothesized that inductive biases from brains could help build better ML systems, but the addition of constraints typically hurts rather than helping ML performance. We draw inspiration from biology to show that combining 1) a content-addressable heteroassociative memory based on the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit with grid cells that retain shared across-environment structural representations and hippocampal cells that acquire environment-specific information; 2) a spatially invariant convolutional network architecture for rapid adaptation across unfamiliar environments; and 3) the ability to perform remapping, which orthogonalizes internal representations; leads to good generalization, rapid learning, and continual learning without forgetting, respectively. Our model outperforms ANN baselines from continual learning contexts applied to the task. It retains knowledge of past environments while rapidly acquiring the skills to navigate new ones, thereby addressing the seemingly opposing challenges of quick knowledge transfer and sustaining proficiency in previously learned tasks. These biologically motivated results may point the way toward ML algorithms with similar properties.

paragraphs: Learning a new environment quickly while retaining old navigation skills combines two demands that machine learning systems often struggle to satisfy together. The authors introduce the sequential Morris Water Maze to study this combination. It extends an established psychology and neuroscience task so that success requires both rapid adaptation and continual learning.

Their model combines three biologically motivated ingredients. A content-addressable memory separates structural knowledge shared across environments, represented by grid cells, from environment-specific information represented by hippocampal cells. A spatially invariant convolutional architecture supports rapid adaptation. Remapping makes internal representations orthogonal, supporting continued learning without forgetting earlier environments.

On the proposed task, the model outperforms neural-network baselines drawn from continual learning and retains prior environment knowledge while learning to navigate new ones rapidly. The results connect the memory design to generalization, the convolutional architecture to adaptation, and remapping to retention. They support this particular combination of biological ideas as a promising route toward systems that transfer knowledge quickly while preserving earlier skills.
summary.tldr: A biologically inspired navigation model combines shared structure, environment-specific memory, and remapping to learn new mazes quickly while retaining old ones.

title: Rapid Learning without Catastrophic Forgetting in the Morris Water Maze

abstract: Due to the rising privacy concerns on sensitive client data and trained models like Transformers, secure multi-party computation (MPC) techniques are employed to enable secure inference despite attendant overhead. Existing works attempt to reduce the overhead using more MPC-friendly non-linear function approximations. However, the integration of quantization widely used in plaintext inference into the MPC domain remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we propose the framework named Ditto to enable more efficient quantization-aware secure Transformer inference. Concretely, we first incorporate an MPC-friendly quantization into Transformer inference and employ a quantization-aware distillation procedure to maintain the model utility. Then, we propose novel MPC primitives to support the type conversions that are essential in quantization and implement the quantization-aware MPC execution of secure quantized inference. This approach significantly decreases both computation and communication overhead, leading to improvements in overall efficiency. We conduct extensive experiments on Bert and GPT2 models to evaluate the performance of Ditto. The results demonstrate that Ditto is about $3.14\sim 4.40\times$ faster than MPCFormer (ICLR 2023) and $1.44\sim 2.35\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art work PUMA with negligible utility degradation.
originalAbstract: Due to the rising privacy concerns on sensitive client data and trained models like Transformers, secure multi-party computation (MPC) techniques are employed to enable secure inference despite attendant overhead. Existing works attempt to reduce the overhead using more MPC-friendly non-linear function approximations. However, the integration of quantization widely used in plaintext inference into the MPC domain remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we propose the framework named Ditto to enable more efficient quantization-aware secure Transformer inference. Concretely, we first incorporate an MPC-friendly quantization into Transformer inference and employ a quantization-aware distillation procedure to maintain the model utility. Then, we propose novel MPC primitives to support the type conversions that are essential in quantization and implement the quantization-aware MPC execution of secure quantized inference. This approach significantly decreases both computation and communication overhead, leading to improvements in overall efficiency. We conduct extensive experiments on Bert and GPT2 models to evaluate the performance of Ditto. The results demonstrate that Ditto is about $3.14\sim 4.40\times$ faster than MPCFormer (ICLR 2023) and $1.44\sim 2.35\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art work PUMA with negligible utility degradation.

paragraphs: Ditto targets the computational and communication costs of running Transformer inference through secure multi-party computation. This setting addresses privacy concerns around client inputs and trained models, but secure execution introduces overhead. The paper investigates how quantization, already used for ordinary inference, can be incorporated effectively into this setting.

The framework combines changes to the model with changes to secure computation. It introduces an MPC-friendly quantization scheme and uses quantization-aware distillation to preserve model utility. It also supplies new MPC primitives for the type conversions required by quantization. These pieces work together to support secure execution of quantized Transformers, reducing both computation and communication.

Experiments on BERT and GPT2 report speedups of about 3.14–4.40 times over MPCFormer and 1.44–2.35 times over PUMA, with negligible utility degradation. These are results from the evaluated models and settings. The findings demonstrate that quantization can yield substantial efficiency gains when its numerical representation, model adaptation, and secure execution machinery are designed together.
summary.tldr: Ditto combines quantization-aware distillation with new secure-computation primitives to accelerate Transformer inference with negligible reported utility degradation.

title: Ditto: Quantization-aware Secure Inference of Transformers upon MPC

abstract: We study the problem of learning Single-Index Models under the $L_2^2$ loss in the agnostic model. We give an efficient learning algorithm, achieving a constant factor approximation to the optimal loss, that succeeds under a range of distributions (including log-concave distributions) and a broad class of monotone and Lipschitz link functions. This is the first efficient constant factor approximate agnostic learner, even for Gaussian data and for any nontrivial class of link functions. Prior work for the case of unknown link function either works in the realizable setting or does not attain constant factor approximation. The main technical ingredient enabling our algorithm and analysis is a novel notion of a local error bound in optimization that we term alignment sharpness and that may be of broader interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning single-index models under squared loss in the agnostic setting, where the data need not be perfectly described by a model in the chosen class. The goal is an efficient algorithm whose loss stays within a constant factor of the best achievable loss in that class.

The authors provide such an algorithm for a range of input distributions, including log-concave distributions, and a broad class of monotone, Lipschitz link functions. Their analysis relies on a new local error-bound concept called alignment sharpness. This optimization property is the central technical ingredient connecting the learning algorithm to its approximation guarantee.

The result advances beyond earlier work on unknown link functions that either assumed realizability or lacked a constant-factor guarantee. The authors identify it as the first efficient agnostic learner with this approximation quality even for Gaussian inputs and any nontrivial link-function class. Its significance is a conditional theoretical guarantee under the stated distribution and function assumptions, with alignment sharpness potentially useful beyond this problem.
summary.tldr: Alignment sharpness enables efficient constant-factor agnostic learning of single-index models under specified distribution and link-function conditions.

title: Robustly Learning Single-Index Models via Alignment Sharpness

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) effectively learn from relational data by leveraging graph symmetries. However, many real-world systems—such as biological or social networks—feature multi-way interactions that GNNs fail to capture. Topological Deep Learning (TDL) addresses this by modeling and leveraging higher-order structures, with Combinatorial Complex Neural Networks (CCNNs) offering a general and expressive approach that has been shown to outperform GNNs. However, TDL lacks the principled and standardized frameworks that underpin GNN development, restricting its accessibility and applicability. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized CCNNs (GCCNs), a simple yet powerful family of TDL models that can be used to systematically transform any (graph) neural network into its TDL counterpart. We prove that GCCNs generalize and subsume CCNNs, while extensive experiments on a diverse class of GCCNs show that these architectures consistently match or outperform CCNNs, often with less model complexity. In an effort to accelerate and democratize TDL, we introduce TopoTune, a lightweight software for defining, building, and training GCCNs with unprecedented flexibility and ease.

Topological deep learning models these higher-order structures. Combinatorial Complex Neural Networks provide an expressive approach, yet the lack of standardized development frameworks makes such models harder to build and apply.

The paper introduces Generalized Combinatorial Complex Neural Networks, or GCCNs, as a systematic way to transform neural networks, including graph networks, into topological counterparts. The authors prove that GCCNs generalize and subsume existing CCNNs. This establishes a model family that includes the earlier framework while supporting a broader range of architectures.

Experiments across diverse GCCNs show that they consistently match or outperform CCNNs, often with lower model complexity. TopoTune supplies lightweight software for defining, building, and training these models flexibly. The contribution combines a formal extension of the architecture family with practical development support, making higher-order modeling more accessible while retaining the performance benefits demonstrated in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TopoTune supports a generalized family of topological neural networks that subsumes CCNNs and often matches or improves their performance with less complexity.

title: TopoTune: A Framework for Generalized Combinatorial Complex Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a novel method for measuring the discrepancy between a set of samples and a desired posterior distribution for Bayesian inference. Classical methods for assessing sample quality like the effective sample size are not appropriate for scalable Bayesian sampling algorithms, such as stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, that are asymptotically biased. Instead, the gold standard is to use the kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD), which is itself not scalable given its quadratic cost in the number of samples. The KSD and its faster extensions also typically suffer from the curse-of-dimensionality and can require extensive tuning. To address these limitations, we develop the polynomial Stein discrepancy (PSD) and an associated goodness-of-fit test. While the new test is not fully convergence-determining, we prove that it detects differences in the first $r$ moments for Gaussian targets. We empirically show that the test has higher power than its competitors in several examples, and at a lower computational cost. Finally, we demonstrate that the PSD can assist practitioners to select hyper-parameters of Bayesian sampling algorithms more efficiently than competitors.

paragraphs: Bayesian sampling methods need diagnostics that assess whether their samples match a desired posterior distribution. Familiar measures such as effective sample size are unsuitable for methods that retain asymptotic bias. Kernel Stein discrepancy offers an alternative, but its quadratic cost in sample count, dimensionality challenges, and tuning requirements can limit practical use.

The authors introduce polynomial Stein discrepancy and an associated goodness-of-fit test. Its theoretical guarantee is deliberately specific: for Gaussian targets, the test detects differences in the first r moments. It is not fully convergence-determining, so this moment-sensitive guarantee should not be read as establishing complete distributional convergence.

In several empirical examples, the test has greater power than competing methods at lower computational cost. The paper also demonstrates its use in choosing hyperparameters for Bayesian sampling algorithms more efficiently. Together, these results position the method as a computationally useful diagnostic with a clear theoretical focus on moment differences, rather than a universal certificate that a sampler has recovered the entire target distribution.
summary.tldr: Polynomial Stein discrepancy offers an efficient sample-quality test with guarantees for detecting moment differences in Gaussian targets.

title: The Polynomial Stein Discrepancy for Assessing Moment Convergence

abstract: This paper introduces the SOAR framework for imitation learning. SOAR is an algorithmic template which learns a policy from expert demonstrations with a primal-dual style algorithm which alternates cost and policy updates. Within the policy updates the SOAR framework prescribe to use an actor critic method with multiple critics to estimate the critic uncertainty and therefore build an optimistic critic fundamental to drive exploration. When instantiated to the tabular setting, we get a provable algorithms dubbed FRA with guarantees matching the best known results in $\epsilon$. Practically, the SOAR template is shown to boost consistently the performance of primal dual IL algorithms building on actor critic routines for the policy updates. Approximately, thanks to SOAR, the required number of episodes to achieve the same performance is reduced by a half.

paragraphs: Imitation learning aims to learn behavior from expert demonstrations. SOAR provides an algorithmic template that alternates between updating a cost function and updating a policy in a primal-dual procedure. Its main change concerns how the policy update handles uncertainty while deciding what behavior to explore.

Within that update, SOAR uses an actor-critic method with multiple critics. Their estimates provide information about critic uncertainty, which is used to construct an optimistic critic that drives exploration. This connects exploration to uncertainty in the learned evaluations instead of treating the policy update as a fixed component of the imitation-learning procedure.

For a tabular setting, the framework yields an algorithm called FRA whose guarantees match the best known dependence on the accuracy parameter epsilon. In practical evaluations, SOAR consistently improves the tested primal-dual imitation-learning algorithms built on actor-critic updates. The authors report approximately halving the episodes needed to reach the same performance. The theory and experiments thus support the template at different levels: formal accuracy dependence and observed interaction efficiency.
summary.tldr: SOAR uses uncertainty from multiple critics to guide imitation-learning exploration, approximately halving required episodes in the reported practical evaluations.

title: IL-SOAR : Imitation Learning with Soft Optimistic Actor cRitic

abstract: Interactions between modalities—redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy—collectively determine the composition of multimodal information. Understanding these interactions is crucial for analyzing information dynamics in multimodal systems, yet their accurate sample-level quantification presents significant theoretical and computational challenges. To address this, we introduce the Lightweight Sample-wise Multimodal Interaction (LSMI) estimator, rigorously grounded in pointwise information theory. We first develop a redundancy estimation framework, employing an appropriate pointwise information measure to quantify this most decomposable and measurable interaction. Building upon this, we propose a general interaction estimation method that employs efficient entropy estimation, specifically tailored for sample-wise estimation in continuous distributions. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate LSMI’s precision and efficiency. Crucially, our sample-wise approach reveals fine-grained sample- and category-level dynamics within multimodal data, enabling practical applications such as redundancy-informed sample partitioning, targeted knowledge distillation, and interaction-aware model ensembling. The code is available at https://github.com/GeWu-Lab/LSMI_Estimator.

paragraphs: Different modalities can repeat information, contribute information individually, or provide information through their combination. These interactions are described as redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy. The paper addresses the difficulty of measuring them for individual examples, where accurate estimates must also be computationally practical.

The Lightweight Sample-wise Multimodal Interaction estimator, or LSMI, is grounded in pointwise information theory. The authors first develop a framework for estimating redundancy, choosing an information measure suited to decomposing this interaction. They then build a more general interaction estimator using efficient entropy estimation designed for individual samples from continuous distributions.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support LSMI’s precision and efficiency. Measuring interactions at the sample level reveals differences between individual examples and between categories that broader summaries can conceal. The paper connects these measurements to practical uses: dividing samples according to redundancy, targeting knowledge distillation, and forming model ensembles with awareness of modality interactions. Its contribution is therefore both an estimation method and a way to make fine-grained information relationships useful in multimodal systems.
summary.tldr: LSMI efficiently estimates multimodal information interactions for individual samples, supporting finer analysis and interaction-aware learning strategies.

title: Efficient Quantification of Multimodal Interaction at Sample Level

abstract: The proliferation of LLM bias probes introduces three challenges: we lack (1) principled criteria for selecting appropriate probes, (2) a system for reconciling conflicting results across probes, and (3) formal frameworks for reasoning about when and why experimental findings will generalize to real user behavior. In response, we propose a systematic approach to LLM social bias probing, drawing on insights from the social sciences. Central to this approach is EcoLevels—a novel framework that helps (a) identify appropriate bias probes (b) reconcile conflicting results, and (c) generate predictions about bias generalization. We ground our framework in the social sciences, as many LLM probes are adapted from human studies, and these fields have faced similar challenges when studying bias in humans. Finally, we outline five lessons that demonstrate how LLM bias probing can (and should) benefit from decades of social science research

paragraphs: Researchers have many ways to probe social bias in language models, but the growing collection creates interpretive problems. This paper identifies three: choosing an appropriate probe, reconciling results that disagree, and determining when experimental findings will carry over to real user behavior. These problems concern how evidence is selected and interpreted, not simply how many tests are available.

The authors propose EcoLevels, a framework intended to organize bias probing around those three needs. It helps identify relevant probes, make sense of conflicting findings, and generate predictions about generalization. The approach draws on social sciences, where researchers have faced similar challenges in studying human bias and where many language model probes originated.

The paper also outlines five lessons from social science research for improving this work. Its contribution is a systematic approach to connecting particular experimental observations with broader claims about bias. That connection matters because disagreement between probes and uncertainty about real-world relevance require a framework for reasoning about evidence, rather than an assumption that any individual probe provides a complete assessment.
summary.tldr: EcoLevels draws on social science to guide bias-probe selection, reconcile conflicting results, and predict generalization to real user behavior.

title: Position: Rethinking LLM Bias Probing Using Lessons from the Social Sciences

abstract: In this work, we consider the problems of learning junta distributions, their quantum counterparts (quantum junta states), and $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits, which we show to be close to juntas. (1) Junta distributions. A probability distribution $p:$-1,1$^n\to \mathbb [0,1]$ is a $k$-junta if it only depends on $k$ bits. We show that they can be learned to within additive error $\varepsilon$ in total variation distance from $O(2^k\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples, which quadratically improves the upper bound of Aliakbarpour et al. (COLT’16) and matches their lower bound in every parameter. (2) Junta states. We initiate the study of $n$-qubit states that are $k$-juntas, those that are the tensor product of a $k$-qubit state and an $(n-k)$-qubit maximally mixed state. We show that these states can be learned with error $\varepsilon$ in trace distance with $O(12^{k}\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ single copies. We also prove a lower bound of $\Omega((4^k+\log (n))/\varepsilon^2)$ copies. Additionally, we show that, for constant $k$, $\widetilde{\Theta}(2^n/\varepsilon^2)$ copies are necessary and sufficient to test whether a state is $\varepsilon$-close or $7\varepsilon$-far from being a $k$-junta. (3) $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits. We show that $n$-qubit $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits with size $s$, depth $d$ and $a$ auxiliary qubits can be learned from $2^{O(\log(s^22^a)^d)}\log(n)$ copies of the Choi state, improving the $n^{O(\log(s^22^a)^d)}$ by Nadimpalli et al. (STOC’24). Along the way, we give new proof of the optimal performance of Classical Shadows based on Pauli analysis. We also strengthen the lower bounds against $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ to compute the address function.

paragraphs: A junta distribution has probabilities that depend on only a small subset of its input bits. This paper studies how efficiently such distributions, their quantum counterparts, and related quantum circuits can be learned. For a distribution depending on k of n bits, it proves a sample bound proportional to 2^k log(n)/ε² for total-variation error ε, matching the existing lower bound in every parameter.

The quantum analogue consists of an arbitrary k-qubit state together with maximally mixed remaining qubits. The authors establish learning bounds of O(12^k log(n)/ε²) copies and complementary lower bounds. Testing whether an unknown state is close to this family is much more demanding: for constant k, distinguishing ε-closeness from 7ε-farness requires exponentially many copies in n, up to logarithmic factors.

The paper also shows that QAC⁰ circuits are close to juntas and improves their learning bounds using copies of a circuit’s Choi state. Additional results give a Pauli-analysis proof of optimal Classical Shadows performance and stronger circuit lower bounds for the address function. Together, the results clarify both the benefits and limits of exploiting dependence on few variables.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal classical junta learning rates, quantum junta learning and testing bounds, and improved learning bounds for QAC⁰ circuits.

title: Learning Junta Distributions, Quantum Junta States, and QAC$^0$ Circuits

abstract: Recurrent and deep neural networks (RNNs/DNNs) are cornerstone architectures in machine learning. Remarkably, RNNs differ from DNNs only by weight sharing, as can be shown through unrolling in time. How does this structural similarity fit with the distinct functional properties these networks exhibit? To address this question, we here develop a unified mean-field theory for RNNs and DNNs in terms of representational kernels, describing fully trained networks in the feature learning ($\mu$P) regime. This theory casts training as Bayesian inference over sequences and patterns, directly revealing the functional implications induced by the RNNs’ weight sharing. In DNN-typical tasks, we identify a phase transition when the learning signal overcomes the noise due to randomness in the weights: below this threshold, RNNs and DNNs behave identically; above it, only RNNs develop correlated representations across timesteps. For sequential tasks, the RNNs’ weight sharing furthermore induces an inductive bias that aids generalization by interpolating unobserved time steps. Overall, our theory offers a way to connect architectural structure to functional biases.

paragraphs: Unrolling a recurrent neural network through time makes it resemble a deep network whose layers share weights. This paper asks how that structural difference produces different learned behavior. It develops a unified mean-field theory for fully trained recurrent and deep networks in the feature-learning regime, where training changes the representations themselves.

The theory describes representations through kernels and interprets training as Bayesian inference over sequences and patterns. For tasks typical of deep networks, it identifies a transition controlled by the strength of the learning signal relative to noise from random weights. Below the threshold, the two architectures behave identically within the theory. Above it, only recurrent networks develop correlated representations across time steps.

For sequential tasks, sharing weights also produces a bias that helps generalization by interpolating time steps that were not observed. These results connect an architectural choice to the organization of learned features. The contribution is a common theoretical account of when recurrent and deep networks behave alike, when their representations diverge, and how recurrence can support sequential generalization.
summary.tldr: A unified theory links recurrent weight sharing to a representation-learning phase transition and an inductive bias that aids sequential generalization.

title: A unified theory of feature learning in RNNs and DNNs

abstract: Deep learning methods have vastly expanded the capabilities of motion planning in robotics applications, as learning priors from large-scale data has been shown to be essential in capturing the highly complex behavior required for solving tasks such as manipulation or navigation for autonomous vehicles. At the same time, model-based planning algorithms based on search or optimization remain an essential tool due to their flexibility, efficiency, and the ability to incorporate domain knowledge via expert-designed algorithms and objective functions. We propose a new generative framework to unify these two paradigms. First, we learn an autoencoder with a high compression ratio and a latent space of hierarchically ordered, discrete-valued tokens. Leveraging both the dimensionality reduction and the hierarchical coarse-to-fine structure learned by this autoencoder, we then perform motion planning by directly searching in the latent space of tokens. This search can optimize arbitrary objective functions specified at test time, providing a large degree of flexibility while maintaining efficiency and producing realistic solutions by relying on the generative capabilities of the highly compressed autoencoder. We evaluate our method on nuPlan and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, showing how latent space search can be used for a variety of guided behavior generation tasks, achieving strong performance for closed-loop motion planning and multi-agent guided scenario synthesis without requiring any task-specific training.

paragraphs: Motion planning benefits from learned patterns of realistic behavior and from search algorithms that optimize explicitly chosen objectives. This paper combines those strengths by learning a compressed representation of motion and then searching directly within that representation. The goal is to preserve realistic behavior while allowing planning requirements to change at test time.

An autoencoder maps motion into a small set of discrete tokens arranged hierarchically from coarse to fine. Planning searches over those tokens, taking advantage of both reduced dimensionality and the hierarchy. The learned generator provides realistic solutions, while the search can optimize arbitrary objectives supplied at test time.

Evaluations on nuPlan and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset demonstrate several forms of guided behavior generation. The authors report strong results for closed-loop motion planning and guided synthesis of multi-agent scenarios, without task-specific training. These findings show how a learned motion representation can serve as a reusable search space for different planning objectives, combining generative modeling with explicit optimization.
summary.tldr: Searching a hierarchical, compressed token representation enables realistic motion planning under test-time objectives without task-specific training.

title: Motion Planning in Compressed Representation Spaces

abstract: Detecting AI-generated images (AIGI) remains challenging because detectors often fail to generalize to unseen generators. Although existing methods are trained on large datasets, their performance still degrades when generation settings change, indicating that data scale alone is insufficient and that limited coverage of generative variations during training is a key factor. Studies on generative model editing show that small changes in internal representations can produce diverse and meaningful image variations, many of which are not explored under standard sampling. Leveraging this insight, we propose PROBE (Probing Robustness via Boundary Exploration), a framework that improves detector generalization by actively exploring challenging regions of the generative process. Instead of treating the generator as a fixed data source, PROBE uses the detector as a critic to steer the generator through manifold-level modifications, producing realistic samples that are difficult to classify. These samples expose failure cases that are uncommon under standard data sampling strategies and are used to refine the detector. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks indicate that PROBE enhances generalization to unseen generators, resulting in more generalizable AIGI detection performance.

paragraphs: Image detectors can perform well on familiar generators and still fail when confronted with a new generator or changed generation settings. This paper argues that larger training datasets alone do not solve the problem when they cover too little of the variation a generator can produce. It focuses on finding realistic images that expose detector weaknesses.

PROBE uses the detector as a critic to guide changes within the generator’s internal representation space. These modifications steer generation toward challenging regions while producing realistic samples that are difficult to classify. The resulting examples reveal failure cases that standard sampling seldom encounters and are then used to refine the detector.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks indicate improved generalization to unseen generators. The findings support actively shaping the training distribution around weaknesses in the detector, rather than relying solely on the volume of routinely generated examples. The contribution is a feedback process linking detection and generation: the detector helps identify informative variations, and those variations supply the evidence needed to improve its subsequent decisions.
summary.tldr: PROBE uses detector feedback to generate realistic, difficult training examples that improve detection of images from unseen generators.

title: Where Detectors Fail: Probing Generative Space for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection

abstract: Long input sequences are central to in-context learning, document understanding, and multi-step reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the quadratic attention cost of Transformers makes inference memory-intensive and slow. While context distillation (CD) can transfer information into model parameters, per-prompt distillation is impractical due to training costs and latency. To address these limitations, we propose Doc-to-LoRA (D2L), a lightweight hypernetwork that meta-learns to perform approximate CD within a single forward pass. Given an unseen prompt, D2L generates a LoRA adapter for a target LLM, enabling subsequent queries to be answered without re-consuming the original context, reducing latency and KV-cache memory consumption during target LLM inference. On a long-context needle-in-a-haystack task, D2L successfully learns to map contexts into adapters that store the needle information, achieving near-perfect zero-shot accuracy at sequence lengths exceeding the target LLM’s native context window by more than 4x. On real-world QA datasets with limited compute, D2L outperforms standard CD while significantly reducing peak memory consumption and update latency. We envision that D2L can facilitate rapid adaptation of LLMs, opening up the possibility of frequent knowledge updates and personalized chat behavior. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/SakanaAI/doc-to-lora.

paragraphs: Answering repeated questions about a long document can be expensive when a language model must keep processing the original context. Context distillation transfers information into model parameters, but training separately for each prompt adds substantial delay. Doc-to-LoRA tackles that adaptation cost by learning how to produce a compact model update directly from a new context.

Its lightweight hypernetwork generates a LoRA adapter for a target language model in one forward pass. This approximates context distillation without running a separate distillation training process for each prompt. Subsequent queries can use the adapter without consuming the original context again, reducing inference latency and the memory required for cached attention states.

Under limited compute on real-world question-answering datasets, it outperforms standard context distillation while reducing peak memory and update latency. Frequent knowledge updates and personalized behavior are proposed possibilities, rather than established outcomes of these evaluations.
summary.tldr: Doc-to-LoRA turns new contexts into lightweight model adapters in one forward pass, enabling later queries without repeatedly processing the original context.

title: Doc-to-LoRA: Learning to Instantly Internalize Contexts

abstract: Transformer-based models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains, yet our understanding of their training dynamics remains limited. In this work, we identify a recurrent focus–dilution cycle in attention learning and provide a rigorous explanation in a one-layer Transformer setting for Markovian data via gradient-flow analysis. Using stage-wise linearization around critical points, we show that a single focus–dilution cycle can be decomposed into a sequence of distinct stages. First, embedding and projection rapidly condense to a rank-one structure, while attention parameters remain effectively frozen. Then, the attention parameters begin to increase, inducing a frequency-driven focus toward high-frequency tokens. As attention continues to evolve, it generates next-order perturbations in embeddings, leading to a mass-redistribution mechanism that progressively dilutes this focus. Finally, small asymmetries among low-frequency tokens lift a degenerate critical point, opening new embedding directions and initiating the next cycle. Experiments on synthetic Markovian data as well as WikiText and TinyStories corroborate the predicted stages and cyclical dynamics.

paragraphs: Attention does not necessarily develop through a steady progression toward sharper focus. This paper identifies a repeated cycle in which attention first concentrates and then becomes more dispersed. It explains the cycle mathematically for a one-layer Transformer trained on Markovian data, using gradient-flow analysis and local approximations around critical points.

Early in a cycle, embeddings and projections rapidly concentrate into a rank-one structure while attention parameters barely change. Attention parameters then grow, producing a focus on frequently occurring tokens. Continued attention learning creates further changes in the embeddings, triggering a redistribution of mass that gradually weakens the initial concentration.

Small differences among less frequent tokens eventually break a degeneracy at a critical point. This opens new embedding directions and starts another cycle. Experiments on synthetic Markovian data, WikiText, and TinyStories support the predicted stages and recurring dynamics. The work connects changing attention patterns to interactions between attention parameters and embeddings, with its rigorous explanation grounded in the specified one-layer setting.
summary.tldr: Attention learning exhibits recurring focus–dilution cycles explained through staged interactions between embeddings and attention in a one-layer Transformer.

title: Focus and Dilution: The Multi-stage Learning Process of Attention

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically trained on shuffled corpora, yielding models whose knowledge is frozen at training time and whose temporal grounding remains poorly understood. In this work, we study the impact of pretraining dynamics on the acquisition of time-sensitive factual knowledge, focusing specifically on data ordering. Our main contributions are twofold. First, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark of over 7,000 temporally grounded questions and an evaluation protocol that enables analysis of whether models correctly associate facts with their corresponding time periods. Second, we pretrain 6B-parameter language models on temporally ordered Common Crawl snapshots and compare them against standard shuffled pretraining. Our results show that sequentially trained models match shuffled baselines on general language understanding and common knowledge while consistently exhibiting more up-to-date and temporally precise knowledge. Temporally ordered pretraining yields improved factual freshness, while shuffled pretraining peaks on older data, possibly due to increased factual repetition. These findings, along with the release of our checkpoints and datasets, provide a foundation for future research on continual learning for large language models.

paragraphs: A language model can know a fact yet associate it with the wrong time period. This paper studies how pretraining order affects that distinction, focusing on the acquisition of time-sensitive factual knowledge. The central comparison is between standard shuffled training and training that follows the temporal order of the source data.

The authors introduce a benchmark with more than 7,000 temporally grounded questions and a protocol for checking whether facts are linked to the correct periods. They also pretrain 6-billion-parameter models on time-ordered Common Crawl snapshots and compare them with models trained on shuffled data. This connects the evaluation directly to a controlled choice in pretraining dynamics.

Sequential training matches the shuffled baselines on general language understanding and common knowledge while producing consistently fresher and more temporally precise knowledge. Shuffled training performs best on older data, which the authors suggest may reflect greater repetition of older facts. That explanation remains tentative. The results establish data ordering as a consequential factor in the tested models' temporal knowledge, and the released checkpoints and datasets support further continual-learning research.
summary.tldr: Temporally ordered pretraining gives tested 6B language models fresher, more time-precise knowledge while matching shuffled baselines on general capabilities.

title: Understanding Data Temporality Impact on Large Language Models Pre-training

abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning with Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) remains the standard post-training paradigm for Large Language Models, yet it imposes a disproportionately aggressive update force on low-probability target tokens. This focus forces the model to prioritize minimizing the loss of difficult samples over optimizing the overall quality of the generation, often leading to unwarranted overconfidence. On the other hand, alternatives like Dynamic Fine-Tuning suffer from vanishing gradients on these tokens, which severely hinders the acquisition of new concepts. To bridge this gap, we propose Spectrum-Adaptive Fine-Tuning (SAFT), a unified framework that interpolates between the aggressive learning signal of NLL and the robust nature of probability-weighted optimization. By adaptively balancing these objectives, SAFT effectively mitigates outlier sensitivity without sacrificing learning efficiency. Empirically, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating superior generalization on out-of-distribution tasks. Furthermore, evaluations on general conversational alignment validate SAFT’s broad adaptability across diverse data regimes. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjtu-scx/SAFT.
