paragraphs: SAFT addresses how strongly fine-tuning should push a language model toward target tokens it currently considers unlikely. Standard negative log-likelihood can apply disproportionately aggressive updates to these tokens, encouraging sensitivity to difficult examples and unwarranted confidence. The paper argues that alternatives such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning can move too far in the other direction, weakening gradients needed to learn new concepts.

Spectrum-Adaptive Fine-Tuning interpolates between the strong learning signal of negative log-likelihood and probability-weighted optimization. Its adaptive balance aims to reduce sensitivity to outliers while keeping updates effective enough for learning. The contribution is therefore a way to manage competing properties of the training objective through one unified framework.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and improved generalization to out-of-distribution tasks. Evaluations of general conversational alignment also support applicability across different data regimes. Together, these findings suggest that adjusting the strength of learning signals can improve both reasoning and broader alignment, while addressing the specific tension between aggressive fitting and insufficient learning.
summary.tldr: SAFT adaptively balances strong and probability-weighted learning signals to improve fine-tuning robustness without sacrificing learning efficiency.

title: Navigating the Pareto Frontier of Alignment: Spectrum-Adaptive Fine-Tuning for LLMs

abstract: How does the amount of compute available to a reinforcement learning (RL) policy affect its learning? Can policies using a fixed amount of parameters, still benefit from additional compute? The standard RL framework does not provide a language to answer these questions formally. Empirically, deep RL policies are often parameterized as neural networks with static architectures, conflating the amount of compute and the number of parameters. In this paper, we formalize compute bounded policies and prove that policies which use more compute can solve problems and generalize to longer-horizon tasks that are outside the scope of policies with less compute. Building on prior work in algorithmic learning and model-free planning, we propose a minimal architecture that can use a variable amount of compute. Our experiments complement our theory. On a set 31 different tasks spanning online and offline RL, we show that $(1)$ this architecture achieves stronger performance simply by using more compute, and $(2)$ stronger generalization on longer-horizon test tasks compared to standard feedforward networks or deep residual network using upto 5 times more parameters.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning policies are often implemented with fixed neural architectures, making parameter count and computation difficult to study separately. This paper formalizes policies with bounded computation so that the amount of processing available to a policy becomes an explicit part of the analysis.

The theory proves that policies with more computation can solve problems and generalize to longer-horizon tasks beyond the capabilities of policies with less computation. Building on algorithmic learning and model-free planning, the authors also propose a minimal architecture that can vary how much computation it uses. This creates a practical way to investigate computational scaling separately from simply increasing model size.

Experiments cover 31 tasks across online and offline reinforcement learning. The architecture improves performance by using more computation and generalizes better to longer-horizon test tasks than feedforward or deep residual networks with up to five times as many parameters. These results support computation as a meaningful resource for policy capability, alongside parameter count, in the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: A formal model and variable-compute architecture show how additional computation can improve reinforcement learning without simply adding parameters.

title: On the Role of Computation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large language models often hallucinate with high confidence on "random facts" that lack inferable patterns. We formalize the memorization of such facts as a membership testing problem, unifying the discrete error metrics of Bloom filters with the continuous log-loss of LLMs. By analyzing this problem in the regime where facts are sparse in the universe of plausible claims, we establish a rate-distortion theorem: the optimal memory efficiency is characterized by the minimum KL divergence between score distributions on facts and non-facts. This theoretical framework provides a distinctive explanation for hallucination under an idealized setting: even with optimal training, perfect data, and a simplified “closed world” setting, the information-theoretically optimal strategy under limited capacity is not to abstain or forget, but to assign high confidence to some non-facts, resulting in hallucination. We validate this theory empirically on both synthetic and real-world data, showing that hallucinations persist as a natural consequence of lossy compression. The same theorem recovers and sharpens classical space lower bounds for Bloom-type filters, pinning down an additive constant left open for two-sided filters.

paragraphs: Some facts have no useful pattern from which a model can infer them; they must be remembered. This paper studies that situation as membership testing: distinguishing facts from the larger set of plausible claims. The formulation connects the discrete errors of Bloom-type filters with the continuous log-loss used for language models.

Under their idealized, limited-capacity, closed-world setting, the information-theoretically optimal strategy assigns high confidence to some non-facts, even with perfect data and optimal training.

summary.tldr: A rate-distortion theorem shows how memory-optimal compression of sparse, unstructured facts can produce confident false claims in an idealized setting.

title: Hallucination is a Consequence of Space-Optimality: A Rate-Distortion Theorem for Membership Testing

abstract: AI arenas, which rank generative models from pairwise preferences of users, are a popular method for measuring the relative performance of models in the course of their organic use. Because rankings are computed from noisy preferences, there is a concern that model producers can exploit this randomness by submitting many models (e.g., multiple variants of essentially the same model) and thereby artificially improve the rank of their top models. This can lead to degradations in the quality, and therefore the usefulness, of the ranking. In this paper, we begin by establishing, both theoretically and in simulations calibrated to data from the platform Arena (formerly LMArena, Chatbot Arena), conditions under which producers can benefit from submitting clones when their goal is to be ranked highly. We then propose a new mechanism for ranking models from pairwise comparisons, called You-Rank-We-Rank (YRWR). It requires that producers submit rankings over their own models and uses these rankings to correct statistical estimates of model quality. We prove that this mecha-nism is approximately clone-robust, in the sense that a producer cannot improve their rank much by doing anything other than submitting each of their unique models exactly once. Moreover, to the extent that model producers are able to correctly rank their own models, YRWR improves overall ranking accuracy. In further simulations, we show that indeed the mechanism is approximately clone-robust and quantify improvements to ranking accuracy, even under producer mis-ranking.

A producer may benefit by submitting many nearly identical models and allowing the luckiest variant to rise in the ranking. This paper establishes conditions for that advantage through theory and simulations calibrated to Arena data, showing how submission strategy can undermine ranking quality.

The contribution connects incentive design with statistical estimation, using information from model producers to reduce the influence of repeated submissions and improve the usefulness of preference-based rankings.
summary.tldr: You-Rank-We-Rank uses producers' internal model rankings to limit gains from clone submissions and improve preference-based ranking accuracy.

title: Strategic Candidacy in Generative AI Arenas

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts architectures have become the standard for efficient LLM scaling, typically employing expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. However, the absence of explicit load balancing constraints during inference allows adversarial inputs to trigger severe routing concentration. We demonstrate that out-of-distribution prompts can manipulate the routing mechanism such that all tokens are routed to the same set of top-k experts, which creates computational bottlenecks on certain devices while forcing others to idle. This converts an efficiency mechanism into a denial-of-service attack vector, leading to violations of service-level agreements for time-to-first-token (TTFT). We propose RepetitionCurse, a black-box strategy to exploit this vulnerability. By identifying a universal flaw in MoE router behavior, RepetitionCurse constructs attack prompts using simple repetitive token patterns in a model-agnostic manner. On widely deployed MoE models hosted on 8-GPU clusters, our method increases TTFT by 20% to 148%, significantly degrading service quality.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models distribute specialized components across devices and route each token to a selected subset. Their efficiency depends partly on how that work is distributed. This paper investigates a vulnerability arising when inference lacks explicit load-balancing constraints: unusual inputs can concentrate routing on the same experts and leave other devices underused.

The authors demonstrate that out-of-distribution prompts can send all tokens to the same top-k expert set. This creates a hardware bottleneck even though the architecture is designed for efficient scaling. RepetitionCurse is their black-box, model-agnostic strategy for exposing the issue through repetitive token patterns, linking input structure to harmful routing concentration.

On widely deployed mixture-of-experts models running on eight-GPU clusters, the method increases time to first token by 20% to 148%. That delay affects how long users wait before a response begins and can violate service-level expectations. The results identify inference-time routing balance as an operational security concern: selective computation can become a denial-of-service weakness when adversarial inputs repeatedly concentrate the selected work.
summary.tldr: RepetitionCurse demonstrates how repetitive inputs concentrate MoE routing, increasing time to first token by 20%–148% in tested eight-GPU deployments.

title: RepetitionCurse: Measuring and Understanding Router Imbalance in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs under DoS Stress

abstract: We study last-iterate convergence for stochastic smooth and monotone variational inequalities (VIs), a framework that captures convex-concave saddle points and Nash equilibrium computation in monotone games with noisy payoff feedback. In contrast to the well-understood average-iterate guarantees, anytime last-iterate guarantees in stochastic settings remain limited, despite their relevance for uncoupled learning dynamics that output a single current strategy. We analyze two single-call regularized methods, the regularized gradient (RG) and the regularized optimistic gradient (ROG) methods, and establish anytime last-iterate convergence rates in terms of the squared gap function. For monotone VIs, RG attains $O(t^{-2/5})$ while ROG achieves the variance-adaptive rate $O(\sigma^{4/5} t^{-2/5} + t^{-1})$, where $\sigma^2$ is the noise variance. For $\lambda$-strongly monotone VIs, ROG yields $O(\sigma^2 / (\lambda^2 t) + t^{-c})$ for any constant $c \ge 2$. These results give anytime last-iterate guarantees without knowing the horizon and show that optimism improves convergence in the low-noise regime.

paragraphs: In equilibrium learning, the current strategy may matter more than an average of all previous strategies. This paper studies guarantees for that current, or last, iterate when feedback is noisy. Its setting is smooth monotone variational inequalities, which include convex-concave saddle-point problems and equilibrium computation in monotone games.

The authors analyze regularized gradient and regularized optimistic gradient methods, each using a single feedback call per step. Their guarantees hold at any time without requiring advance knowledge of the stopping horizon. Measured by the squared gap function, regularized gradient has a rate of order t to the power −2/5, while the optimistic method combines a noise-dependent term of that order with a term of order 1/t.

For strongly monotone problems, the optimistic method obtains a noise term proportional to variance divided by the squared monotonicity strength and elapsed steps, plus a faster-decaying term. These bounds explain the benefit of optimism when noise is small: its faster component can become more influential. The result gives guarantees directly for the strategy available when learning stops.
summary.tldr: Regularized gradient methods gain anytime guarantees for their current iterate in noisy monotone problems, with optimism improving low-noise convergence.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Regularized Gradient Methods for Stochastic Monotone Variational Inequalities

abstract: Single-cell perturbation modeling is fundamental for understanding and predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations. However, existing approaches, from causal representation learning to foundation models, often struggle with an overlooked challenge: gene expression is dominated by perturbation-invariant information, while perturbation-specific signals are intrinsically sparse. As a result, learned representations either entangle invariant and perturbation-specific information, leading to spurious and non-generalizable predictors, or suppress perturbation-specific signals altogether, rendering them ineffective for prediction. To address this, we propose PerturbedVAE, a general framework designed to resolve this signal imbalance. The framework explicitly separates perturbation-specific information from dominant invariant structure and recovers causal representations to effectively utilize such information for prediction. We further provide an identifiability analysis that characterizes the conditions under which sparse perturbation effects can be reliably recovered, thereby clarifying how the framework can be concretely specified under such conditions. Empirically, PerturbedVAE achieves state-of-the-art performance on a widely used benchmark across multiple evaluation settings, yielding significant gains on out-of-distribution combinatorial predictions and uncovering interpretable perturbation-response programs.

The authors also analyze identifiability, characterizing conditions under which sparse perturbation effects can be reliably recovered. This conditional analysis connects the framework's design to the circumstances in which the desired separation can be established.

On a widely used benchmark, PerturbedVAE achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple evaluation settings, with significant gains for out-of-distribution predictions involving combinations of perturbations. It also reveals interpretable perturbation-response programs. The results support preserving small but consequential changes during representation learning, while the theory makes clear that reliable recovery of those effects depends on the characterized conditions.
summary.tldr: PerturbedVAE separates sparse perturbation effects from dominant unchanged expression patterns to improve cellular-response prediction and interpretation.

title: What Makes a Representation Good for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction?

abstract: Existing deep learning models have demonstrated potential in Diabetic retinopathy (DR) diagnosis, but they still suffer from three key challenges: reliance on single-source inputs, opaque and untraceable reasoning processes, and the absence of a mechanism for result verification. Thus, we propose a provenance-enabled concept-based framework for multi-view DR diagnostic (ProConMV), which integrates DR lesion masks, clinical text and multi-view data, utilizing multimodal prompt analysis and visual-text concept interaction to learn the interpretable multi-source input. During the reasoning stage, the proposed framework introduces lesion concepts for causal reasoning chains combining clinical guidelines, and adds doctor intervention for human-machine collaboration. For dynamic fusion decision and verification in multi-view DR diagnosis, we derive via generalization theory that incorporating each view’s lesion concept uncertainty and grading uncertainty reduces the generalization error upper bound. Accordingly, we design a dual uncertainty-aware module to enable provenance-based verification, ultimately enabling verifiable analysis of DR diagnostic results. Extensive experiments conducted on two public multi-view DR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code will be released at https://github.com/SoY0ung/ProConMV.

title: ProConMV: Provenance-Enabled Conceptual Framework for Interpretable Multi-View Diabetic Retinopathy Diagnosis

abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable success on final-answer mathematical problems, largely due to the ease of applying reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, the reasoning underlying these solutions is often flawed. Advancing to rigorous proof-based mathematics requires reliable proof verification capabilities. We begin by analyzing multiple evaluation setups and show that focusing on a single benchmark can lead to brittle or misleading conclusions. To address this, we evaluate both proof-based and final-answer reasoning to obtain a more reliable measure of model performance. We then scale two major generative verification methods (GenSelect and LLM-as-a-Judge) to millions of tokens and identify their combination as the most effective framework for solution verification and selection. We further show that the choice of prompt for LLM-as-a-Judge significantly affects the model’s performance, but reinforcement learning can reduce this sensitivity. However, despite improving proof-level metrics, reinforcement learning does not enhance final-answer precision, indicating that current models often reward stylistic or procedural correctness rather than mathematical validity. Our results establish practical guidelines for designing and evaluating scalable proof-verification and selection systems.

The authors interpret this mismatch as evidence that current models often reward stylistic or procedural features rather than mathematical validity. The work therefore provides both a practical combination of verification methods and a reason to assess gains using multiple complementary measures.
summary.tldr: Combined generative verifiers perform best in the study, but improved proof metrics do not necessarily improve final-answer precision.

title: Scaling Generative Verifiers For Natural Language Mathematical Proof Verification And Selection

abstract: The growing size of Large Language Models (LLMs) makes efficient inference challenging, primarily due to the memory demands of the autoregressive Key-Value (KV) cache. Existing eviction or compression methods reduce cost but rely on heuristics, such as recency or past attention scores, which serve only as indirect proxies for a token’s future utility and introduce computational overhead. We reframe KV cache eviction as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem: learning to rank tokens by their predicted usefulness for future decoding. To this end, we introduce KV Policy (KVP), a framework of lightweight per-head RL agents trained on pre-computed generation traces using only key and value vectors. Each agent learns a specialized eviction policy guided by a holistic reward, derived from future utility, that evaluates the quality of the ranking across all cache budgets, requiring no modifications to the underlying LLM or additional inference. Evaluated across two model families on the long-context benchmark RULER (up to 128K tokens) and the multi-turn dialogue benchmark OASST2-4k, KVP significantly outperforms strong baselines. Zero-shot tests on standard downstream tasks (BoolQ, LongBench passage retrieval, GovReport) further show that KVP generalizes beyond its training distribution and to considerably longer sequence lengths. These results demonstrate that learning to predict future token utility is a powerful and scalable paradigm for adaptive KV cache management.

paragraphs: A language model’s key-value cache stores information from earlier tokens for use during subsequent generation. As context grows, this cache becomes a major memory cost. Existing eviction methods often decide what to retain using recency or previous attention scores, which provide indirect evidence about whether a token will matter later.

KV Policy instead learns to rank cached tokens by predicted future usefulness. It trains lightweight reinforcement-learning agents for individual attention heads using precomputed generation traces and only key and value vectors. A reward based on future utility evaluates the entire ranking across cache budgets, encouraging policies that support different amounts of available memory without modifying the underlying language model.

Across two model families, the method significantly outperforms strong baselines on RULER contexts up to 128,000 tokens and on the OASST2-4k dialogue benchmark. Zero-shot evaluations on BoolQ, LongBench passage retrieval, and GovReport also show transfer beyond the training distribution and to substantially longer sequences. The results support learning future utility directly as a practical basis for deciding which cached information to discard.
summary.tldr: KV Policy learns attention-head-specific eviction rankings that predict which cached tokens will help future generation.

title: Learning to Evict from Key-Value Cache

abstract: Equivariant neural networks exploit underlying task symmetries to improve generalization, but strict equivariance constraints can induce more complex optimization dynamics that can hinder learning. Prior work addresses these limitations by relaxing strict equivariance during training, but typically relies on prespecified, explicit, or implicit target levels of relaxation for each network layer, which are task-dependent and costly to tune. We propose Recurrent Equivariant Constraint Modulation (RECM), a layer-wise constraint modulation mechanism that learns appropriate relaxation levels solely from the training signal and the symmetry properties of each layer’s input-target distribution, without requiring any prior knowledge about the task-dependent target relaxation level. We demonstrate that under the proposed RECM update, the relaxation level of each layer provably converges to a value upper-bounded by its symmetry gap, namely the degree to which its input-target distribution deviates from exact symmetry. Consequently, layers processing symmetric distributions recover full equivariance, while those with approximate symmetries retain sufficient flexibility to learn non-symmetric solutions when warranted by the data. Empirically, RECM outperforms prior methods across diverse exact and approximate equivariant tasks, including the challenging molecular conformer generation on the GEOM-Drugs dataset.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks encode how outputs should change when inputs undergo symmetry transformations. These constraints can improve generalization, but enforcing them strictly can also complicate optimization. Existing relaxation approaches often need a task-dependent target for each layer. RECM learns layer-specific relaxation levels from the training signal and the symmetry properties of the layer’s input-target distribution.

Experiments report improvements over earlier methods on tasks with both exact and approximate equivariance, including molecular conformer generation on GEOM-Drugs. The contribution combines a layer-level convergence guarantee with empirical evidence that adapting symmetry constraints can improve learning across differing symmetry conditions.
summary.tldr: RECM learns how much to relax each layer’s symmetry constraints, with convergence tied to the layer’s departure from exact symmetry.

title: Recurrent Equivariant Constraint Modulation: Learning Per-Layer Symmetry Relaxation from Data

abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer mortality, driving the development of automated screening tools to alleviate radiologist workload. Standing at the frontier of this effort is Sybil, a deep learning model capable of predicting future risk solely from computed tomography (CT) with high precision. However, despite extensive clinical validation, current assessments rely purely on observational metrics. This correlation-based approach overlooks the model’s actual reasoning mechanism, necessitating a shift to causal verification to ensure robust decision-making before clinical deployment. We propose S(H)NAP, a model-agnostic auditing framework that constructs generative interventional attributions validated by expert radiologists. By leveraging realistic 3D diffusion bridge modeling to systematically modify anatomical features, our approach isolates object-specific causal contributions to the risk score. Providing the first interventional audit of Sybil, we demonstrate that while the model often exhibits behavior akin to an expert radiologist, differentiating malignant pulmonary nodules from benign ones, it suffers from critical failure modes, including dangerous sensitivity to clinically unjustified artifacts and a distinct radial bias.

paragraphs: Sybil predicts future lung cancer risk from CT scans, but strong predictive results do not by themselves explain which image features drive its scores. This paper examines that distinction through an interventional audit. Its central question is how Sybil's prediction changes when particular anatomical features are deliberately modified.

The authors introduce S(H)NAP, an auditing framework that can be applied without being tied to a particular model architecture. It uses realistic three-dimensional diffusion bridge modeling to modify anatomy and isolate the contributions of specific objects to the predicted risk. Expert radiologists validate the resulting generative interventional attributions. This makes controlled image changes the basis for examining the model's behavior.

The audit finds both clinically meaningful behavior and serious failures. Sybil often distinguishes malignant pulmonary nodules from benign ones in a way resembling expert assessment. However, it also reacts dangerously to clinically unjustified artifacts and shows a distinct radial bias. These findings explain why an audit of what changes a model's score can reveal problems that observational performance measurements alone overlook.
summary.tldr: Generative interventions reveal that Sybil combines clinically meaningful nodule assessment with sensitivity to unjustified artifacts and a radial bias.

title: Auditing Sybil: Explaining Deep Lung Cancer Risk Prediction Through Generative Interventional Attributions

abstract: A key tool in developing safe AI models is data auditing, i.e., using statistical tools to determine whether harmful content may have been used in the training data of a black-box model. Unfortunately, most membership inference attacks (MIAs) used to perform this type of auditing themselves assume access to examples of harmful content from the same distribution as the query data. In real-world auditing scenarios, auditors often face legal and ethical restrictions preventing them from accessing a representative set of samples of harmful content to train MIA models effectively. We abstract and formalize this setting into a new data access model, the “unseen class” setting, and show that the state-of-the-art MIAs fail due to the lack of access to the full target distribution. We show that in this setting, quantile regression attacks outperform approaches typically considered to be state of the art. We demonstrate this both empirically and theoretically, showing that quantile regression attacks achieve up to 11$\times$ the TPR of shadow model-based approaches in practice, and providing a theoretical model that outlines the generalization properties required for this approach to succeed. Our work identifies an important failure mode in existing MIAs and provides a cautionary tale for practitioners who aim to directly use existing tools for real-world applications of AI safety.

paragraphs: Membership inference can help auditors assess whether particular content was used to train a black-box model. However, many attack methods require representative examples from the same distribution as the content being checked. This creates a practical problem when legal or ethical restrictions prevent auditors from collecting examples of harmful material.

The paper formalizes this constraint as the unseen-class setting. It shows that methods considered state of the art can fail when their training data do not cover the full target distribution. The authors investigate quantile regression attacks as an alternative and provide a theoretical model describing the generalization properties needed for these attacks to succeed.

Empirically, quantile regression attacks achieve up to eleven times the true-positive rate of shadow-model approaches in this setting. This is a qualified improvement within the studied auditing conditions, rather than a universal ranking of membership inference techniques. The broader finding is that access assumptions materially affect audit reliability: a method that works with representative training examples may perform poorly when the very class under investigation is unavailable during attack development.
summary.tldr: Quantile regression improves membership inference when auditors lack representative examples of the target class.

title: Membership Inference Attacks for Unseen Classes

abstract: Preference-based post-training aligns LLMs with human intent, yet safety behavior often remains brittle. A model may refuse a harmful request in a standard prompt but comply when the same intent is wrapped in adversarial wording. We suggest that robust safety requires context-invariant alignment, where behavior depends on the underlying intent rather than surface form. Enforcing invariance is difficult in alignment because not all training signals are equally trustworthy; for some prompt variants we can obtain verifiable feedback (e.g., multiple-choice), while for open-ended variants we typically rely on noisy, gameable reward proxies (e.g., learned judges). As a result, standard symmetric invariance regularizers can reduce cross-context discrepancies by lowering performance on reliable variants instead of improving open-ended robustness. To address this, we introduce Anchor Invariance Regularization (AIR), which treats verifiable prompts as anchors and uses a stop-gradient target to regularize only the open-ended variants toward the anchor performance. AIR is implemented as a plug-in auxiliary loss and combined with group-based preference optimization (e.g., GRPO) via heterogeneous prompt grouping. Across Safety, Moral Reasoning, and Math, AIR improves context invariance, boosting in-distribution group accuracy by 12.71% and out-of-distribution consistency by 33.49%, making safety constraints robust to adversarial framings.

paragraphs: A language model may reject a harmful request in ordinary wording yet comply when the same intent appears in an adversarial framing. This paper aims to make alignment depend more consistently on underlying intent. Its key observation is that feedback quality differs across prompt forms: some permit verifiable answers, while open-ended responses often rely on noisy reward proxies.

Across safety, moral reasoning, and mathematics, the authors report a 12.71% improvement in in-distribution group accuracy and a 33.49% improvement in out-of-distribution consistency. This offers a concrete way to strengthen consistency across adversarial framings while avoiding the specific failure mode of reducing anchor performance to obtain agreement.
summary.tldr: AIR uses verifiable prompts as fixed anchors to improve alignment consistency across differently framed requests.

title: Towards Context-Invariant Safety Alignment for Large Language Models

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising non-autoregressive generative paradigm. Given the prohibitive computational cost of full fine-tuning, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has become the standard approach. However, existing PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA), originally tailored for autoregressive models, rely on static parameters that are agnostic to the noise level. Consequently, they ignore the intrinsic dynamics of the diffusion process, where input distributions and generation difficulty shift significantly along the denoising trajectory, rendering them suboptimal for dLLMs. To address this, we propose Noise-aware Low-Rank Adaptation (NaRA), which introduces a low-rank core matrix generated by a lightweight, globally shared hypernetwork conditioned on the noise level. This design enables the update matrices to vary continuously along the diffusion process while keeping parameter and latency overhead negligible. We provide a theoretical justification for the proposed NaRA framework and empirically demonstrate consistent improvements over noise-agnostic baselines across commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/generaldi/NaRA.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text through a denoising process, during which input distributions and generation difficulty change. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adapting these models, but standard LoRA uses static adaptation parameters. This paper argues that ignoring the current noise level leaves those adaptations poorly matched to the changing demands of generation.

NaRA introduces a low-rank core matrix produced by a lightweight hypernetwork conditioned on noise level. The hypernetwork is shared globally, allowing the adaptation matrices to vary continuously throughout denoising without requiring a separate full adaptation for every stage. The authors describe the additional parameter and latency costs as negligible.

The paper provides a theoretical justification and evaluates the method on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation benchmarks. It reports consistent improvements over noise-agnostic baselines across these tasks. The findings support making the fine-tuning mechanism responsive to diffusion progress, so that a compact adaptation can change with the type of input the model is currently processing.
summary.tldr: NaRA makes low-rank adaptations depend on diffusion noise level, improving reasoning and code generation with negligible reported overhead.

title: NaRA: Noise-Aware LoRA for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Diffusion LLMs

abstract: Fine-tuned LLMs can covertly encode prompt secrets into outputs via steganographic channels. Prior work demonstrated this threat but relied on trivially recoverable encodings. We formalize payload recoverability via classifier accuracy and show previous schemes achieve 100% recoverability. In response, we introduce low-recoverability steganography, replacing arbitrary mappings with embedding-space-derived ones. For Llama-8B (LoRA) and Ministral-8B (LoRA) trained on TrojanStego prompts, exact secret recovery rises from 17$\rightarrow$30% (+78%) and 24$\rightarrow$43% (+80%) respectively, while on Llama-70B (LoRA) trained on Wiki prompts, it climbs from 9$\rightarrow$19% (+123%), all while reducing payload recoverability. We then discuss detection. We argue that detecting fine-tuning-based steganographic attacks requires approaches beyond traditional steganalysis. Standard approaches measure distributional shift, which is an expected side-effect of fine-tuning. Instead, we propose a mechanistic interpretability approach: linear probes trained on later-layer activations detect the secret with up to 33% higher accuracy in fine-tuned models compared to base models, even for low-recoverability schemes. This suggests that malicious fine-tuning leaves actionable internal signatures amenable to interpretability-based defenses.

The paper examines how easily these hidden payloads can be recovered by a classifier, finding that earlier encoding schemes reach 100% recoverability under this measure. It introduces mappings derived from embedding geometry to make the payload less readily recoverable.

Linear probes on later layers detect secrets with up to 33% higher accuracy in fine-tuned models than in base models, including low-recoverability schemes. The findings suggest that malicious fine-tuning leaves internal evidence that could support interpretability-based defenses.
summary.tldr: Embedding-based secret encodings reduce classifier recoverability while improving secret transmission, and internal probes reveal potential detection signals.

title: Hide and Seek in Embedding Space: Geometry-based Steganography and Detection in Large Language Models

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) aims to construct a joint model for multiple tasks by sharing a common representation across domains. To achieve this goal, existing optimization-centric methods either balance task gradients or modify the shared architecture. However, as these approaches remain agnostic to the content of the shared representation, they fail to disentangle task-relevant structure from spurious context, leading to negative transfer and poor generalization. To overcome this limitation, we propose Causal Orthogonal Representations for Multi-Task Learning (CORE-MTL) , a representation-centric framework that structurally disentangles the shared representation into semantic and residual streams, concentrating task-relevant structure in the semantic stream while relegating nuisance variation to the residual stream. We instantiate this framework in the visual domain by leveraging physical priors for structured scenes and statistical constraints for attributes. Theoretically, our method enjoys a tighter out-of-distribution generalization bound than optimization-centric methods and reduces task gradient interference without explicit gradient projection or reweighting. Empirically, CORE-MTL consistently outperforms existing methods on visual multi-task benchmarks in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.

paragraphs: A model trained on several tasks shares internal representations, but that sharing can also let tasks interfere with one another. CORE-MTL argues that adjusting gradient magnitudes or changing shared architecture leaves an underlying problem unresolved: shared features can mix useful task information with incidental context. This mixture can harm transfer and performance on unfamiliar data.

The proposed framework separates the representation into semantic and residual streams. The semantic stream concentrates information relevant to the tasks, while the residual stream carries nuisance variation. For visual tasks, the authors implement this separation using physical priors for structured scenes and statistical constraints for attributes. The approach changes what information is shared, making representation content central to how tasks interact during learning.

The theoretical analysis gives a tighter out-of-distribution generalization bound than optimization-centered methods and shows reduced gradient interference without explicit gradient projection or reweighting. On visual multi-task benchmarks, CORE-MTL consistently improves over the compared methods both within and outside the training distribution. These findings support separating useful structure from context as a route to more effective task sharing.
summary.tldr: CORE-MTL separates task-relevant features from nuisance variation to reduce interference and improve visual multi-task generalization.

title: CORE-MTL: Rethinking Gradient Balancing via Causal Orthogonal Representations

abstract: Dataset pruning (DP) and dataset distillation (DD) fundamentally differ in their outputs: DP selects original image subsets, while DD generates synthetic images. Recently, DD’s increasing reliance on original images suggests a convergence of the two directions. To investigate this convergence trend, we propose a unified dataset compression (DC) benchmark. This benchmark reveals an interesting trade-off for soft-label-DD: while soft labels provide valuable information, they can make the distillation process less essential, as distilled images may not always outperform random subsets. In addition, the benchmark reveals that in current stages, dataset pruning outperforms dataset distillation at small dataset sizes. Given these observations, we explore hard-label-DC as a complementary approach that emphasizes image quality while offering substantial storage efficiency. Our PCA (Prune, Combine, and Augment) is the first framework that does not rely on soft labels but instead focuses on image quality. (1) "P” means selecting easy samples based on dataset pruning metrics, (2) "C” indicates combining these samples effectively, and (3) "A” is to apply constrained image augmentation during training.

summary.tldr: A unified compression benchmark reveals the influence of soft labels and motivates PCA, a hard-label approach that selects, combines, and augments images.

title: Unifying Dataset Pruning and Distillation for Efficient Large-scale Compression

abstract: Tree ensembles are machine learning models with strong predictive performance and interpretability, and remain widely used for tabular data. Standard pruning methods for tree ensembles typically optimize an accuracy-compression trade-off and may change a subset of predictions, potentially compromising decision consistency. Faithful pruning methods address this issue by preserving prediction equivalence over the entire input space, but this requirement leads to lower compression ratios. We propose PINE, a pruning method that provides strong guarantees within an in-distribution region. PINE preserves prediction equivalence within this region and controls the region size using a single parameter $\alpha$ via conformal calibration. Experiments on 12 public tabular datasets show that PINE improves the compression ratio by up to 30% while preserving predictions at a comparable level to existing faithful pruning methods.

paragraphs: Pruning a tree ensemble reduces its size, but ordinary compression methods can change some predictions. That can matter when preserving existing decisions is a priority. Faithful pruning addresses this by requiring prediction equivalence across the entire input space, although such a broad requirement restricts how much the model can be compressed.

PINE changes the scope of the guarantee. It preserves prediction equivalence inside an in-distribution region, with the size of that region controlled by a single parameter, alpha, through conformal calibration. The compression procedure can therefore focus its equivalence requirement on a calibrated region rather than every possible input.

The finding illustrates the value of choosing where equivalence must hold: a regional guarantee can permit greater compression while maintaining strong decision consistency. The stated guarantee applies within the calibrated region, which is the central distinction from methods requiring agreement everywhere.
summary.tldr: PINE improves tree-ensemble compression by guaranteeing prediction equivalence within a conformally calibrated in-distribution region.

title: PINE: Pruning Boosted Tree Ensembles with Conformal In-Distribution Prediction Equivalence

abstract: The rapid progress of generative models such as GANs and diffusion models has led to the widespread proliferation of AI-generated images, raising concerns about misinformation, privacy violations, and trust erosion in digital media. Although large-scale multimodal models like CLIP offer strong transferable representations for detecting synthetic content, fine-tuning them often induces catastrophic forgetting, which degrades pre-trained priors and limits cross-domain generalization. To address this issue, we propose the Distillation-guided Gradient Surgery Network (DGS-Net), a novel framework that preserves transferable pre-trained priors while suppressing task-irrelevant components. Specifically, we introduce a gradient-space decomposition that separates harmful and beneficial descent directions during optimization. By projecting task gradients onto the orthogonal complement of harmful directions and aligning with beneficial ones distilled from a frozen CLIP encoder, DGS-Net achieves unified optimization of prior preservation and irrelevant suppression. Extensive experiments on 50 generative models demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by an average margin of 6.6%, achieving superior detection performance and generalization across diverse generation techniques.

paragraphs: CLIP provides representations that can transfer to detecting AI-generated images, but adapting it to that task can erase useful pretrained knowledge. This catastrophic forgetting can reduce generalization across different kinds of image generators. DGS-Net addresses the optimization process directly, aiming to retain transferable information while reducing components that do not help the detection task.

The significance is that preserving pretrained knowledge and suppressing irrelevant information are handled within the same update mechanism. The reported results support modifying how fine-tuning proceeds as a way to improve transfer across synthetic-image sources.
summary.tldr: DGS-Net reshapes CLIP fine-tuning gradients to preserve useful pretrained knowledge and improve AI-generated image detection across diverse generators.

title: DGS-Net: Distillation-Guided Gradient Surgery for CLIP Fine-Tuning in AI-Generated Image Detection

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can be seen as compressed knowledge bases, but it remains unclear what knowledge they truly contain and how far their knowledge boundary extends. Existing benchmarks are mostly static and provide limited support for systematic knowledge probing. In this paper, we propose an interactive agentic framework to systematically extract and quantify the knowledge of LLMs. Our method includes four adaptive exploration policies to probe knowledge at different granularity. To ensure the quality of extracted knowledge, we introduce a three-stage knowledge processing pipeline that combines vector-based filtering to remove strict duplicates, LLM-based adjudication to resolve ambiguous semantic overlap, and domain relevance auditing to retain valid knowledge units. Through extensive experiments, we find that Recursive Taxonomy is the most effective exploration strategy. We also observe a clear knowledge scaling law, where larger models consistently recover more knowledge. In addition, we identify a Pass@1 versus Pass@k trade-off: domain-specialized models achieve higher initial accuracy but experience rapid degradation, while general-purpose models maintain stable performance over extended extraction. Finally, our results show that differences in training data composition lead to distinct and measurable knowledge profiles across model families, reflecting how pretraining shapes each model’s parametric knowledge.

Together, these results show why both exploration strategy and extraction duration matter when assessing a model's accessible knowledge.
summary.tldr: Adaptive knowledge probing reveals differences in recoverable knowledge, sustained extraction, and domain profiles across language models.

title: Probing the Knowledge Boundary: An Interactive Agentic Framework for Deep Knowledge Extraction

abstract: With the recent fast development of generative models, instruction-based image editing has shown great potential in generating high-quality images. However, the quality of editing highly depends on carefully designed instructions, placing the burden of task decomposition and sequencing entirely on the user. To achieve autonomous image editing, we present PhotoAgent, a system that advances image editing through explicit aesthetic planning. Specifically, PhotoAgent formulates autonomous image editing as a long-horizon decision-making problem. It reasons over user aesthetic intent, plans multi-step editing actions via tree search, and iteratively refines results through closed-loop execution with memory and visual feedback, without requiring step-by-step user prompts. To support reliable evaluation in real-world scenarios, we introduce UGC-Edit, an aesthetic evaluation benchmark consisting of 7,000 photos and a learned aesthetic reward model. We also construct a test set containing 1,017 photos to systematically assess autonomous photo editing performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PhotoAgent significantly outperforms existing methods in both instruction faithfulness and visual quality across a diverse range of editing scenarios.

paragraphs: Instruction-based image editing can produce strong results, but users often have to decide which changes to request and in what order. PhotoAgent takes on that planning work. It interprets a user’s aesthetic intent and treats editing as a sequence of decisions whose combined effects determine the final image, without requiring step-by-step prompts from the user.

The system uses tree search to plan multiple editing actions and then refines the result through closed-loop execution. Memory and visual feedback inform subsequent decisions, allowing the process to respond to the edited image rather than relying only on an initial plan. Explicit aesthetic planning connects the user’s broad goal to an evolving sequence of concrete edits.

Across diverse editing scenarios, experiments report significant improvements over existing methods in both instruction faithfulness and visual quality. The findings support combining planning with feedback when assessing autonomous editing against both user intent and appearance.
summary.tldr: PhotoAgent plans and revises multi-step image edits using visual feedback, improving instruction faithfulness and visual quality in the reported experiments.

title: PhotoAgent: Exploratory Visual Aesthetic Planning with Large Vision Models

abstract: Constraint-based causal discovery relies on conditional independence (CI) tests whose reliability degrades as conditioning sets grow, particularly in hub-dominated graphs. Existing methods constrain adjacency or global structure, but leave conditioning-set dimensionality uncontrolled. In this paper, we propose Ordering-Constrained Markov Blanket discovery (OCMB), a paradigm that treats conditioning-set dimensionality as a first-class constraint. OCMB decouples discovery into two stages: lightweight global ordering estimation providing directional priors, followed by local Markov blanket validation within small, ordering-constrained candidate sets. By enforcing directional constraints before any CI test, OCMB ensures bounded conditioning sets even with hub nodes. We show that OCMB recovers correct parent sets provided a high-recall ordering assumption holds, without requiring the ordering to be globally correct. Experiments demonstrate that OCMB significantly improves precision and robustness over constraint-based and hybrid methods in high-dimensional regimes where conventional CI-based approaches fail.

paragraphs: Constraint-based causal discovery uses conditional independence tests to help identify relationships between variables. These tests become less reliable when they must account for many other variables at once. The problem is particularly acute around highly connected hub nodes. Restricting possible edges or global graph structure does not necessarily control the size of each test’s conditioning set.

Ordering-Constrained Markov Blanket discovery makes that size an explicit design constraint. It first estimates a lightweight global ordering that provides directional guidance. It then validates local relationships within small candidate sets restricted by that ordering. Applying directional constraints before the independence tests keeps conditioning sets bounded even when the graph contains hubs.

The theoretical recovery claim depends on a high-recall ordering assumption: under that assumption, OCMB recovers correct parent sets without needing a globally correct ordering. This makes the quality required of the preliminary ordering central to the guarantee. Experiments show significantly improved precision and robustness over constraint-based and hybrid approaches in high-dimensional settings where conventional independence-testing methods fail.
summary.tldr: OCMB uses approximate global ordering to keep local causal tests small, with parent recovery guaranteed under a high-recall ordering assumption.

title: Global Directional Priors with Local Statistical Validation for Scalable Causal Discovery

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training for large language models (LLMs) is computationally expensive, as it generates many rollout sequences that frequently share long token prefixes. Existing RL frameworks usually process these sequences independently during policy training, i.e., repeatedly recomputing identical prefixes in both the forward and backward passes of policy gradient computation, leading to substantial inefficiencies in computation resources and memory usage. Although prefix sharing naturally induces a tree structure over rollouts, packed tree-mask approaches scale poorly in RL settings. In this paper, we introduce AReaL-DTA, which efficiently exploits prefix sharing in RL training. AReaL-DTA employs a depth-first search (DFS)-based execution strategy that dynamically traverses the rollout prefix tree during both forward and backward computation, materializing only a single root-to-leaf path at a time. To further improve scalability, AReaL-DTA incorporates a load-balanced distributed batching mechanism that dynamically constructs and processes prefix trees across multiple GPUs. On $\tau^2$-bench, AReaL-DTA improves training throughput by up to $8.31\times$ over dense training and up to $1.70\times$ over sparse training. Our code is available at https://github.com/areal-project/AReaL/tree/feat/dta.

summary.tldr: AReaL-DTA shares rollout-prefix computation through dynamic tree traversal, substantially increasing reinforcement-learning training throughput in the reported benchmark.

title: AReaL-DTA: Dynamic Tree Attention for Efficient Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models

abstract: In point clouds, noise directly perturbs point coordinates that encode both spatial location and geometry, making one-to-one correspondence construction more challenging than in images. Existing methods impose statistical mappings across noisy variants via noise or optimal transport, but suffer from correspondence ambiguity. In this work, we propose Self-Induced Mirror-Point Consistency (SIMPC) to learn deterministic correspondences between points and the underlying surface in an unsupervised manner. For each noisy point, SIMPC generates a mirror-point on the opposite side of the underlying surface, guided by geometric priors during the denoising process. By encouraging consistency between the denoising targets of the original point and its mirror counterpart, SIMPC effectively localizes the position of underlying surface. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that SIMPC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and surpasses several strong supervised counterparts.

paragraphs: Noise in a point cloud changes the coordinates that describe both where points are and what shape they form. This makes matching noisy points to their underlying surface difficult. The paper argues that existing statistical mappings between noisy variants suffer from ambiguous correspondences, motivating a more direct geometric constraint for unsupervised denoising.

SIMPC generates a mirror counterpart for each noisy point on the opposite side of the underlying surface, using geometric priors during denoising. It then encourages the original point and its mirror to share a consistent denoising target. The agreement between these paired targets helps localize the surface and learn deterministic correspondences.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art unsupervised methods, as well as performance exceeding several strong supervised methods. The result supports the use of constructed geometric pairs as a learning signal for recovering surfaces. The method’s distinctive contribution is to reduce correspondence ambiguity through mirror-point consistency, making the relationship between two generated views of a point central to the denoising objective.
summary.tldr: SIMPC denoises point clouds by making noisy points and generated mirror counterparts agree on their underlying surface.

title: SIMPC: Learning Self-Induced Mirror-Point Consistency for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising

abstract: Deep time series models are vulnerable to noisy data ubiquitous in real-world applications. Existing robustness strategies either prune data or rely on costly prior quantification, failing to balance effectiveness and efficiency. In this paper, we introduce DropoutIS, a model-agnostic plug{ı}n that shifts the paradigm from what to learn to how much to learn. DropoutTS employs a Sample-Adaptive Dropout mechanism: leveraging spectral sparsity to efficiently quantify instance-level noise via reconstruction residuals, it dynamically calibrates model learning capacity by mapping noise to adaptive dropout rates, selectively suppressing spurious fluctuations while preserving fine-grained fidelity. Extensive experiments across diverse noise regimes and open benchmarks show DropoutTS consistently boosts superior backbones’ performance, delivering advanced robustness with negligible parameter overhead and no architectural modifications. Code is available at https://github.com/CityMind-Lab/DropoutTS.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting models can learn misleading fluctuations when their training data contain noise. DropoutTS addresses this by adjusting how strongly the model learns from each sample. The central idea is to vary dropout according to estimated noise, providing a lightweight alternative to removing data or relying on expensive prior noise measurements.

The method uses spectral sparsity to estimate noise through reconstruction residuals: the differences left after reconstructing an instance provide a signal of its noise level. That estimate determines a sample-specific dropout rate, which changes the model's effective learning capacity. The intended balance is to suppress spurious fluctuations while retaining the fine detail needed for accurate forecasting.

Across open benchmarks and different noise regimes, the reported experiments show consistent improvements to strong forecasting backbones. The method adds negligible parameter overhead and requires no architectural changes, making it a plug-in for existing models. Its contribution is a connection between instance-level noise estimation and training regularization, allowing the learning process to respond differently to samples with different noise characteristics.
summary.tldr: DropoutTS adjusts dropout for each time-series sample using estimated noise, improving reported forecasting robustness with negligible parameter overhead.

title: DropoutTS: Sample-Adaptive Dropout for Robust Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Adaptation methods have been a workhorse for unlocking the transformative power of pre-trained diffusion models in diverse applications. Existing approaches often abstract adaptation objectives as a reward function and steer diffusion models to generate high-reward samples. However, these approaches can incur high computational overhead due to additional training, or rely on stringent assumptions on the reward such as differentiability. Moreover, despite their empirical success, theoretical justification and guarantees are seldom established. In this paper, we propose $\texttt{DOIT}$ ($\textbf{D}$oob-$\textbf{O}$riented $\textbf{I}$nference-time $\textbf{T}$ransformation), a training-free adaptation method for generic, non-differentiable rewards. We develop two variants of this method: $\texttt{DOIT-Proto}$, a full-rollout simulation-based algorithm and $\texttt{DOIT-Practical}$, an efficient surrogate algorithm. The key idea is a measure transport formulation that seeks to transport the pre-trained generative distribution to a high-reward target distribution. We leverage Doob’s $h$-transform to realize this transport, which induces a dynamic correction to the diffusion sampling process and admits simulation-based computation without modifying the pre-trained model. Theoretically, we establish a high-probability convergence guarantee to the target high-reward distribution for $\texttt{DOIT-Proto}$ by characterizing the approximation error in the dynamic Doob correction. Empirically, $\texttt{DOIT-Practical}$ consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on D4RL offline RL benchmarks while preserving sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: DOIT adapts pretrained diffusion models to favor high-reward outputs without additional training. It accommodates rewards that are not differentiable, addressing a restriction of some guidance methods. The authors frame adaptation as transporting the model’s original generation distribution toward a target distribution that emphasizes reward.

The paper introduces two versions: DOIT-Proto uses full rollout simulations, while DOIT-Practical uses an efficient surrogate. summary.tldr: DOIT uses Doob’s h-transform to steer diffusion sampling toward high-reward outputs without retraining or requiring differentiable rewards.

title: Training-Free Adaptation of Diffusion Models via Doob’s $h$-Transform

abstract: Large language models are useful because we taught them to give us what we want. That works when success can be judged immediately, but people increasingly bring these systems their relationships, their hard decisions, and their long-term goals, where what a user wants to hear and what serves them best are frequently different. We argue that LLM providers should offer at least one widely accessible, opt-in mode optimized and evaluated for long-term well-being rather than next-turn approval. This is a pressing need, as models have been found to endorse questionable framings well above human baselines, users take AI advice readily without their well-being improving, and sycophantic models raise dependence while lowering prosocial intent. We propose three principles—change the objective, give users explicit relational roles, avoid paternalism—and organize the design space around three choices the current paradigm makes implicitly: the horizon over which well-being is measured (When), whose interests it represents (Who), and what role the assistant plays (How).

paragraphs: This position paper questions whether immediate user approval is a suitable objective when people ask language models about relationships, difficult decisions, or long-term goals. In these settings, what someone wants to hear may differ from what benefits them over time. The authors propose a widely accessible, optional mode explicitly optimized and evaluated for long-term well-being.

Their motivation draws on findings described in the abstract: models endorse questionable framings above human baselines, people readily accept AI advice without improved well-being, and sycophantic models can increase dependence while reducing prosocial intent. These concerns support evaluating assistance beyond whether a particular reply pleases the user in the moment.

The proposal has three principles: change the objective, let users choose explicit relational roles, and avoid paternalism. It organizes design around when well-being is measured, whose interests count, and how the assistant participates. This makes choices currently embedded implicitly in model behavior explicit, while preserving user choice through an opt-in design and attention to the assistant’s role.
summary.tldr: The authors propose an opt-in language-model mode optimized for long-term well-being, with explicit user-selected roles and safeguards against paternalism.

title: Position: We Need Large Language Models Optimized For Our Well-Being

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable results on a range of standardized tests originally designed to assess human cognitive and psychological traits, such as intelligence and personality. While these results are often interpreted as strong evidence of human-like characteristics in LLMs, this paper argues that such interpretations constitute an ontological error. Human psychological and educational tests are theory-driven measurement instruments, calibrated to a specific population. Applying these tests to non-human subjects without empirical validation, risks mischaracterizing what is being measured. Furthermore, a growing trend frames AI performance on benchmarks as measurements of traits such as “intelligence”, despite known issues with validity, data contamination, cultural bias and sensitivity to superficial prompt changes. We argue that interpreting benchmark performance as measurements of human-like traits, lacks sufficient theoretical and empirical justification. This leads to our position: Stop Evaluating AI with Human Tests, Develop Principled, AI-specific Tests instead. We call for the development of principled, AI-spec by laying out, end-to-end, how valid measurement instruments are constructed and validated and where the ontological error enters when a human-calibrated instrument is applied to LLMs.

paragraphs: The paper challenges the interpretation of strong language-model scores on human psychological and educational tests as evidence of human-like traits. Such tests are built around theories of particular traits and calibrated using particular populations. Applying them to language models without empirical validation can change what the results mean, even when the model produces answers that receive high scores.

The authors describe this transfer of interpretation as an ontological error: assumptions about the kind of subject being measured are carried over without sufficient justification. They also identify validity concerns, training-data contamination, cultural bias, and sensitivity to small prompt changes as obstacles to interpreting benchmark results as measurements of intelligence or personality.

The paper outlines the process of constructing and validating measurement instruments and identifies where transferring a human-calibrated instrument to AI becomes problematic. It calls for tests designed specifically for AI with explicit theoretical and empirical foundations. The practical lesson is that a score needs a validated interpretation before it can support claims about an underlying trait.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that human test scores do not establish human-like AI traits without validation and calls for principled AI-specific measurements.

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a similarity function from a set of positive equivalence constraints, i.e. ’similar’ point pairs. We define the similarity in information theoretic terms, as the gain in coding length when shifting from independent encoding of the pair to joint encoding. Under simple Gaussian assumptions, this formulation leads to a non-Mahalanobis similarity function which is efficient and simple to learn. This function can be viewed as a likelihood ratio test, and we show that the optimal similaritypreserving projection of the data is a variant of Fisher Linear Discriminant. We also show that under some naturally occurring sampling conditions of equivalence constraints, this function converges to a known Mahalanobis distance (RCA). The suggested similarity function exhibits superior performance over alternative Mahalanobis distances learnt from the same data. Its superiority is demonstrated in the context of image retrieval and graph based clustering, using a large number of data sets.

We define the similarity in information theoretic terms, as the gain in coding length when shifting from independent encoding of the pair to joint encoding. Under simple Gaussian assumptions, this formulation leads to a non-Mahalanobis similarity function which is efficient and simple to learn. This function can be viewed as a likelihood ratio test, and we show that the optimal similaritypreserving projection of the data is a variant of Fisher Linear Discriminant. We also show that under some naturally occurring sampling conditions of equivalence constraints, this function converges to a known Mahalanobis distance (RCA). paragraphs: The paper learns similarity from pairs of points known to be similar. Its central idea is to measure how much coding length is saved by encoding a pair jointly instead of encoding its members independently. Similarity is therefore expressed through shared information: a pair receives its relationship score from the benefit of describing the two points together.

Under simple Gaussian assumptions, this construction yields a non-Mahalanobis similarity function that is simple and efficient to learn. The authors also interpret it as a likelihood ratio test and show that the optimal projection preserving the similarity is a variant of Fisher Linear Discriminant. These connections give several mathematical views of the same learned relationship.

Under certain naturally occurring sampling conditions for the similar pairs, the function converges to the known RCA Mahalanobis distance. This is a conditional relationship, rather than an equivalence in every setting. Experiments across many datasets show better performance than alternative Mahalanobis distances learned from the same data, with demonstrations in image retrieval and graph-based clustering.
summary.tldr: The method learns similarity from the coding savings of jointly describing similar pairs, yielding strong retrieval and clustering results.

title: Learning distance function by coding similarity

abstract: Many kernel learning methods have to assume parametric forms for the target kernel functions, which significantly limits the capability of kernels in fitting diverse patterns. Some kernel learning methods assume the target kernel matrix to be a linear combination of parametric kernel matrices. This assumption again importantly limits the flexibility of the target kernel matrices. The key challenge with nonparametric kernel learning arises from the difficulty in linking the nonparametric kernels to the input patterns. In this paper, we resolve this problem by introducing the graph Laplacian of the observed data as a regularizer when optimizing the kernel matrix with respect to the pairwise constraints. We formulate the problem into Semi-Definite Programs (SDP), and propose an efficient algorithm to solve the SDP problem. The extensive evaluation on clustering with pairwise constraints shows that the proposed nonparametric kernel learning method is more effective than other state-of-the-art kernel learning techniques.

This assumption again importantly limits the flexibility of the target kernel matrices. The key challenge with nonparametric kernel learning arises from the difficulty in linking the nonparametric kernels to the input patterns. In this paper, we resolve this problem by introducing the graph Laplacian of the observed data as a regularizer when optimizing the kernel matrix with respect to the pairwise constraints. We formulate the problem into Semi-Definite Programs (SDP), and propose an efficient algorithm to solve the SDP problem. paragraphs: Kernel learning determines a representation of similarity that can guide downstream learning. Many approaches restrict this representation to a chosen parametric family or a linear combination of predefined kernel matrices. The paper argues that these restrictions reduce flexibility when the observed data contain diverse patterns that the chosen forms may not fit well.

The proposed method learns a nonparametric kernel matrix from pairwise constraints. Its key challenge is maintaining a connection between this flexible matrix and the original input patterns. The authors address that by using the observed data's graph Laplacian as a regularizer. They formulate the optimization as semidefinite programs and provide an efficient algorithm for solving the resulting problem.

The regularizer supplies data-based structure while the pairwise constraints guide the learned similarities. This allows the approach to avoid the specified parametric restrictions without disconnecting the kernel from the inputs. Extensive evaluations on clustering with pairwise constraints find it more effective than other state-of-the-art kernel-learning techniques in the comparisons reported.
summary.tldr: Graph Laplacian regularization links a nonparametric kernel matrix to observed inputs, improving constrained clustering in the reported evaluations.

title: Learning nonparametric kernel matrices from pairwise constraints

abstract: Beam search is used to maintain tractability in large search spaces at the expense of completeness and optimality. We study supervised learning of linear ranking functions for controlling beam search. The goal is to learn ranking functions that allow for beam search to perform nearly as well as unconstrained search while gaining computational efficiency. We first study the computational complexity of the learning problem, showing that even for exponentially large search spaces the general consistency problem is in NP. We also identify tractable and intractable subclasses of the learning problem. Next, we analyze the convergence of recently proposed and modified online learning algorithms. We first provide a counter-example to an existing convergence result and then introduce alternative notions of “margin” that do imply convergence. Finally, we study convergence properties for ambiguous training data.

We study supervised learning of linear ranking functions for controlling beam search. The goal is to learn ranking functions that allow for beam search to perform nearly as well as unconstrained search while gaining computational efficiency. We first study the computational complexity of the learning problem, showing that even for exponentially large search spaces the general consistency problem is in NP. We also identify tractable and intractable subclasses of the learning problem. Next, we analyze the convergence of recently proposed and modified online learning algorithms. Finally, we study convergence properties for ambiguous training data.

paragraphs: Beam search limits computation in large search spaces by retaining only selected candidates, sacrificing completeness and optimality. This paper studies supervised learning of linear ranking functions that control those selections. The goal is to retain much of unconstrained search's performance while benefiting from beam search's reduced computational demands.

The first part analyzes the complexity of learning an appropriate ranking function. The authors show that the general consistency problem belongs to NP even when the search space is exponentially large. They also identify tractable and intractable subclasses. Membership in NP is a complexity characterization; the separate subclass results distinguish settings in which the learning problem is manageable from those in which it is difficult.

The second part examines convergence of online learning algorithms. The paper gives a counterexample to a previously claimed convergence result, then introduces alternative definitions of margin that do support convergence. It also studies ambiguous training data. Together, these results clarify which computational and separation conditions can justify learning guarantees for ranking functions used inside beam search.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the complexity of learning beam-search rankings and replaces a flawed convergence claim with margin conditions that imply convergence.

title: On learning linear ranking functions for beam search

abstract: We propose a new algorithm for independent component and independent subspace analysis problems. This algorithm uses a contrast based on the Schweizer-Wolff measure of pairwise dependence, a non-parametric measure based on pairwise ranks of the variables. Our algorithm frequently outperforms state of the art ICA methods in the normal setting, is significantly more robust to outliers in the mixed signals, and performs well even in the presence of noise. Since pairwise dependence is evaluated explicitly, using Cardoso's conjecture, our method can be applied to solve independence subspace analysis (ISA) problems by grouping signals recovered by ICA methods. We provide an extensive empirical evaluation using simulated, sound, and image data.

This algorithm uses a contrast based on the Schweizer-Wolff measure of pairwise dependence, a non-parametric measure based on pairwise ranks of the variables. Our algorithm frequently outperforms state of the art ICA methods in the normal setting, is significantly more robust to outliers in the mixed signals, and performs well even in the presence of noise.
