paragraphs: Independent component analysis and independent subspace analysis seek useful separations of mixed signals. This paper proposes an algorithm whose objective uses the Schweizer-Wolff measure of pairwise dependence. That measure is nonparametric and based on the pairwise ranks of variables, so rank relationships provide the dependence information used by the method.

Explicitly evaluating pairwise dependence also gives the approach a role in independent subspace analysis. Using Cardoso's conjecture, the authors apply the method to group signals recovered by ICA into subspaces. This links the component separation stage to the grouping stage through a shared measure of dependence, with the conjecture forming part of the stated basis for that extension.

The empirical evaluation covers simulated signals, sound, and image data. The authors report that their algorithm frequently outperforms leading ICA methods in the normal setting, is significantly more robust to outliers in mixed signals, and works well with noise. These findings support the rank-based objective across the tested conditions, while the comparative success is explicitly frequent rather than universal.
summary.tldr: A rank-based dependence measure supports ICA and subspace grouping, with reported robustness to outliers and good performance under noise.

title: ICA and ISA using Schweizer-Wolff measure of dependence

abstract: The $k$ $q$-flats algorithm is a generalization of the popular $k$-means algorithm where $q$ dimensional best fit affine sets replace centroids as the cluster prototypes. In this work, a modification of the $k$ $q$-flats framework for pattern classification is introduced. The basic idea is to replace the original reconstruction only energy, which is optimized to obtain the $k$ affine spaces, by a new energy that incorporates discriminative terms. This way, the actual classification task is introduced as part of the design and optimization. The presentation of the proposed framework is complemented with experimental results, showing that the method is computationally very efficient and gives excellent results on standard supervised learning benchmarks.

In this work, a modification of the $k$ $q$-flats framework for pattern classification is introduced. The basic idea is to replace the original reconstruction only energy, which is optimized to obtain the $k$ affine spaces, by a new energy that incorporates discriminative terms. This way, the actual classification task is introduced as part of the design and optimization. The presentation of the proposed framework is complemented with experimental results, showing that the method is computationally very efficient and gives excellent results on standard supervised learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Ordinary k-means represents each cluster with a centroid. The k q-flats algorithm extends that idea by representing a cluster with a fitted q-dimensional affine set, allowing a more structured geometric prototype. This paper adapts that framework for pattern classification, where the goal is to distinguish classes rather than simply reconstruct the observed data well.

The central change is to the objective used to learn the affine spaces. The original framework optimizes reconstruction alone; the proposed objective also contains discriminative terms. As a result, the classification task directly influences how the geometric representations are chosen. The spaces are optimized with their eventual predictive use included in the learning criterion.

Experiments on standard supervised learning benchmarks show strong classification results and very efficient computation. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating class discrimination into the fitting process. The paper's contribution is a classification-oriented modification of an existing geometric framework, with reported benefits in both predictive performance and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: Discriminative k-metrics adapts affine-space clustering for classification by adding class-discriminating terms to its optimization objective.

title: Discriminative k-metrics

abstract: The Dueling Bandits Problem is an online learning framework in which actions are restricted to noisy comparisons between pairs of strategies (also known as bandits). It models settings where absolute rewards are difficult to elicit but pairwise preferences are readily available. In this paper, we extend the Dueling Bandits Problem to a relaxed setting where preference magnitudes can violate transitivity. We present the first algorithm for this more general Dueling Bandits Problem and provide theoretical guarantees in both the online and the PAC settings. Furthermore, we show that the new algorithm has stronger guarantees than existing results even in the original Dueling Bandits Problem, which we validate empirically.
originalAbstract: The Dueling Bandits Problem is an online learning framework in which actions are restricted to noisy comparisons between pairs of strategies (also known as bandits). It models settings where absolute rewards are difficult to elicit but pairwise preferences are readily available. In this paper, we extend the Dueling Bandits Problem to a relaxed setting where preference magnitudes can violate transitivity. We present the first algorithm for this more general Dueling Bandits Problem and provide theoretical guarantees in both the online and the PAC settings. Furthermore, we show that the new algorithm has stronger guarantees than existing results even in the original Dueling Bandits Problem, which we validate empirically.

paragraphs: The dueling bandits problem studies learning through noisy comparisons between pairs of strategies. This is useful when asking for an absolute reward is difficult but asking which of two alternatives is preferable is practical. An algorithm must decide which comparisons to make while learning from answers that are not perfectly reliable.

This paper relaxes the existing problem formulation by allowing preference magnitudes to violate transitivity. The qualification concerns the magnitudes of preferences, so the contribution should be understood at that stated level. The authors introduce an algorithm for this more general setting, extending the kinds of pairwise feedback relationships that their theory can accommodate.

They provide theoretical guarantees for both online learning and the probably approximately correct, or PAC, setting. The algorithm also has stronger guarantees than earlier results within the original dueling bandits formulation, with empirical validation supporting the improvement. Its significance is therefore twofold: it broadens the permitted preference structure while also improving guarantees in the narrower setting that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: A dueling-bandit algorithm handles relaxed transitivity requirements for preference magnitudes and strengthens guarantees in both the relaxed and original settings.

title: Beat the Mean Bandit
